News.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle appears in court over child sex abuse material
News.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

Markle was arrested on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.

The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for almost 20 years.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".

Markle's court hearing lasted for 30 minutes, and the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

He was brought into court a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.

The court ordered Markle to submit to home detention at his assisted living facility in Florida and electronic monitoring.

No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.

FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.

"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.

He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids â any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".

Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

News.title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
News.content:
Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".

"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.

She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.

In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".

On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.

The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."

Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

News.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
News.content:
Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts

No British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.

His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.

Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.

On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.

As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.

News.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
News.content:
In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.

On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.

"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."

News.title: Harry and five others seek to challenge Mail publisher privacy ruling
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex and five other high-profile figures who lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday are seeking to challenge the High Court ruling.

Prince Harry, singer Sir Elton John and actress Elizabeth Hurley were among the group facing paying joint legal costs of up to Â£34.5m after the court ruled in July they had failed to prove the allegations of unlawful information gathering.

Associated Newspapers Limited strongly denied the claims, which were heard at an 11-week trial in London that ended with judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissing all the allegations.

At the time, a spokesperson for the publisher described the judgement as an "overwhelming victory for the Daily Mail and its journalists".

The prince testified in person during the civil hearing and claimed the details that appeared in 14 articles about him "plainly" proved journalists were listening in to phone calls - but a High Court judge said he had failed to prove that.

On Friday, a spokesperson for Prince Harry, Hurley, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish, actress Sadie Frost and political campaigner Baroness Lawrence said the claimants had filed applications with the Court of Appeal applying for permission to challenge the judgements.

The statement said the planned appeal was both on Mr Justice Nicklin's dismissal of their claims and a subsequent indemnity costs order.

The spokesperson said: "The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed."

In August, a month on from his judgement, Mr Justice Nicklin ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before the trial.

He also ordered at that time the claimants should make an initial payment of Â£9.54m while the final total was calculated.

The statement from the group's joint spokesperson did not make any reference to Liberal Democrat politician Sir Simon Hughes who was part of the action. The BBC has contacted Sir Simon to establish whether he is joining the appeal.

After the costs ruling, he told the BBC he was "disappointed" and would take "the time necessary to consider both the substantive and the costs judgment and whether to pursue appeals against decisions in either judgment or both".

The trial saw many current and former Mail and Mail on Sunday journalists and executives giving evidence denying accusations of illegal activity that was put to them by lawyers representing the prince and his fellow claimants.

Lawyers for the publisher said in court that the journalists had provided a "compelling account of a pattern of legitimate sourcing of articles", including using information provided by friends and "leaky" social circles surrounding those they had written about.

In a civil case such as this, the legal convention is that the losing party must reimburse "reasonable" legal fees incurred by the other side. They also have to settle their own legal costs.

News.title: Child, 6, dies weeks after Waterford arson attack
News.content:
A six-year-old boy who was critically injured in a suspected arson attack at his family home in County Waterford has died.

Elliot English died on Friday at Children's Health Ireland (CHI) hospital in Crumlin in Dublin.

His parents, Kim English and Philip English, and two of his siblings, 12-year-old Callum and nine-year-old Jayden, died in the house fire on Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford on 13 October.

Another child, who was also critically injured in the attack, remains in hospital.

News.title: Watch: Is it the end of the road for Tesla's Cybertruck?
News.content:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said production of the firm's Cybertruck is "winding down" in Texas, to focus on its self-driving Cybercab cars.

The model is only produced at Tesla's Austin base, and he did not clarify if manufacturing would be moved elsewhere or simply cease.

The Cybertruck has received a mixed response since its launch in 2023, with some praising its individuality and others simply labelling it ugly.

It has also suffered from disappointing sales, quality problems and recalls.

BBC technology reporter Shiona McCallum has this report.

More on this story.

News.title: Manhunt after boy injured by sword, sparking Gloucester school lockdowns
News.content:
Police described both suspects as white males. One is aged in his late teens to early 20s, of a medium to large build, and about 6ft tall. He was wearing white sliders at the time of the incident.

The other suspect is described as being about 5ft 5ins tall, of slim build and wearing black clothing.

St Peter's High School pupil Jimmy said the situation was "really scary" and he was still in shock.

After getting into the Tuffley school for the day, he said his friends came in and told him something had happened near his home.

He said the school's alarm then went off and the computer he was on displayed a message saying "This is a lockdown".

"The computers are not accessible at all and we've all had to turn the lights off, lock the doors, turn all the blinds down, and we've had to get on the ground," he said.

"At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he added.

Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for two to three hours.

"[When police cars arrived] I thought this is getting serious, I'm getting worried, I don't know what's going on," he said.

The 15-year-old said he was able to message his mother when the school let students use their phones after about an hour.

"When I was able to eventually get out, she was giving me a bunch of hugs," he said.

"What I am is shocked. I'm surprised that this happened," he added.

Jimmy said the school had previously run lockdown drills but a real event had never happened before.

News.title: Met Police boss 'wouldn't be surprised' if more allegations made about Brand
News.content:
During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.

Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.

Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Bayles and another member of Brand's staff had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did.

Shortly after, he sexually assaulted her.

She had complained to her manager, who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.

In recent years, Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.

In a statement, Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.

"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."

Bayles said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".

He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

Bayles said this was why he decided to stop working with Brand in 2010 and had not had any contact with him since. He added that during his time with Brand, no complaints were made about the entertainer's behaviour.

"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

News.title: Man, 41, and boy, 16, arrested after car damaged by gunshots
News.content:
Two people have been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.

South Wales Police said a vehicle on the A48 in Morriston, Swansea, sustained damage "consistent with a firearms discharge" on Friday.

A 41-year-old man from Llansamlet, Swansea, had been arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life, while a 16-year-old boy, also from Llansamlet, had been arrested on suspicion of affray.

The force said officers were still investigating and that it had been declared a critical incident.

Residents have been told to avoid the area and events, including a local firework display, have been cancelled.

Video circulating online shows police officers next to a stationary car that appears to have been struck by a shotgun blast on Clase Road near an Asda superstore.

A National Police Air Service helicopter was circling the area but has since returned to base.

South Wales Police said the incident was ongoing, with road closures in place.

Ch Supt Stephen Jones said: "A policing presence will be visible in the area whilst this investigation is ongoing."

"It is important that people avoid the area so we can effectively deal with this incident and return the area to normality."

The local football club, Morriston Town AFC, cancelled a planned firework display on Friday.

"Unfortunately, the police have advised due to an issue ongoing, the event has to be cancelled. With immediate effect," it said in a social media post, advising people to stay at home.

News.title: Man, 35, charged with murder of Carrie Mullane
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder by police investigating the disappearance and suspected murder of Carrie Mullane (Noonan).

Mullane, who is 39, has been missing since she arrived in Enniskillen from Limerick on 10 October 2026.

The 35-year-old man is also charged with preventing the lawful burial of a corpse.

He is due to appear via video link before Dungannon Magistrates' Court on 7 November.

Earlier on Friday, police carried out a number of searches in County Fermanagh, including Lough Erne.

A small boat and a camper van were recovered and taken away for examination.

News.title: 'Misleading' student loans information left out examples of higher-salary repayments
News.content:
Several universities in England have only been using below-average salaries in examples of student loan repayments on their websites, the BBC has found.

Treasury Committee chair Dame Meg Hillier, who led a recent inquiry into student loans, said some information about repayments was "misleading", including one instance where they were compared to the "cost of a daily coffee".

She also said the Department for Education (DfE) must include higher-salary examples on its own website, too.

The DfE said it would review the information it provides, while universities said their websites referred to government information and would be reviewed where necessary.

Student loan repayments are tied to earnings, so the more you earn, the more you repay every month - and graduates generally go on to earn more than non-graduates.

Current and prospective students in England take out Plan 5 loans to pay for their tuition fees and living costs. They repay 9% of anything they earn over Â£25,000 for 40 years, or until the loan is paid off.

The BBC looked at publicly available information on more than 110 university websites in England and found cases of inaccurate information about the salary at which they start repaying and the length of time they repay for.

It also found that 12 universities only gave students worked examples of repayments based on earnings that are less than the UK average, which is Â£39,039.

News.title: Tube drivers to stage strikes in Christmas run-up
News.content:
A series of strikes in the spring over the same issue caused significant disruption across the network, with some lines being entirely closed.

Despite further talks being held since, RMT has not accepted TfL's proposals.

General secretary Eddie Dempsey said: "London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers' working conditions as a voluntary four-day week.

"Our members are being asked to spend more time driving trains, accept longer and more unpredictable shifts and surrender agreements that have been negotiated and defended over many years."

The union also said it believed the changes would "pave the way for hundreds of job cuts".

TfL said that drivers choosing to remain on a five-day week would be given a guarantee of remaining at the same depot.

Nick Dent, director of customer operations for London Underground, said: "This will give our colleagues a real, meaningful choice on their working pattern without having to change where they work.

"This will also mean less time at work for Tube drivers, while delivering a more efficient, reliable Tube service for our customers."

BBC London's transport correspondent Tom Edwards said the issue of a four-day working week had turned into a "long-running, festering dispute".

"The RMT union regards it as an intensification of the job; TfL sees the changes as being minor and part of a good deal.

"The RMT has been here before and strikes have been called off before. But this is a knotty issue and patience is wearing thin."

News.title: Firms should publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law, says PM
News.content:
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.

Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".

"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.

The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.

He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.

A number of politicians are currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary., external

Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."

News.title: This is what dying feels like, says train victim
News.content:
A passenger stabbed multiple times by a knifeman accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train has told jurors he thought "this is what it feels like to die".

Scott Bletcher was on the York to London King's Cross LNER service on 1 November last year when the attacks happened, leading to an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire.

On Friday, Cambridge Crown Court also heard from staff member Samir Zitouni, who said he fought back using a frying pan, stating he did not want to "give up until the train stopped".

Anthony Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder.

He is also charged with four other alleged attempted murders following earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

Bletcher said he was travelling alone after doing Christmas shopping in Newark-on-Trent, in Nottinghamshire, and was "quite looking forward to the tapas I'd bought actually".

After Peterborough he noticed people running down the aisle, but he remained seated because he was "still not concerned", presuming there had been a disagreement.

He then saw a knife being held in front of him at eye level and said he felt "trappedâ¦ there is no way of escape", followed by a "scratch" to the head from the knife.

Bletcher said he moved his arm to shield his face and added: "There was nothing said to me and I didn't respond because there was nothing to respond to."

The court heard the victim - who is the first to give live evidence at the trial - was stabbed five more times.

News.title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
News.content:
The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.

The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.

Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.

But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.

Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.

On Thursday, Environment Secretary Angela Eagle told a radio presenter he should "get a life" when he asked about the potential impact of the new rules on snacks, such as smoky bacon crisps.

But it highlights the political dangers for the government of realigning with regulations that British politicians have not been able to shape, with the Conservatives and Reform UK keen to pounce on cases showing Britain to be a "rule taker" from Brussels.

It is not the first regulatory skirmish over smoky bacon crisps - following previous headlines over how the well-loved British flavour could be affected by an EU decision in 2024 to phase out a number of artificial smoke flavourings.

Now, the flavour name itself has been called into question by a separate EU attempt to restrict how descriptions of meat are used to market food.

Under rules adopted this summer, the EU plans to restrict the use of 31 terms, including bacon, drumstick and steak, to products that contain meat, claiming consumers could be confused by plant-based alternatives using the same names.

The European snack industry is seeking clarity on how the rules, which will also cover terms such as pork, chicken and beef, would apply to meat-flavoured crisps, including those flavoured without the use of any meat extracts.

The UK government has said it expects the new regulations to be in scope of its proposed food standards deal.

This means they would also apply to companies marketing their products in Britain, which is among the biggest consumers of crisps in Europe, according to analysts Euromonitor., external

News.title: UK satellite launched into space to help armed forces monitor worldwide military activity
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A new British military observation satellite named Titania has been deployed into orbit, the Ministry of Defence has announced.

Described as a fresh "pair of eyes" orbiting the Earth, the reconnaissance probe will support the armed forces in monitoring military activity back on earth.

Weighing 100kg and roughly the size of a household washing machine, the satellite was launched from California in October aboard a reusable SpaceX rocket.

The mission follows the deployment of a comparable spacecraft, Tyche, two years prior.

The pair will form part of a wider network of British military satellites, manufactured by UK firms and overseen by Britain’s Space Command.

BAE Systems-built Titania and Surrey Satellite Technology (SSTL)-built Tyche will eventually be joined by Juno, also produced by SSTL, alongside Oberon, engineered by Airbus.

Drawing their names from classical and Shakespearean characters, the orbiters belong to the wider Intelligence, Surveillance, Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance Information (ISTARI) initiative.

The MoD also announced it is trialling new advanced ground-based sensors across three worldwide sites under Project Inaros to monitor space.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “The new space age is here. Space underpins everything from weather forecasts and financial transactions to sat-navs and mobile phone connections, and it is critical for our national security and military operations.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting ( PA )

“Having Titania now in orbit and Project Inaros stepping up how we watch over our satellites means we can see threats sooner, making the UK safer.

“Titania and Inaros are British-built and British-designed, backed by more than £3 billion of investment in space capabilities. That means highly skilled jobs across the UK, a stronger industrial base, and a more secure United Kingdom.”

Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, the Chief of the Air Staff, said: “The ability to observe the Earth from space is critical to both national resilience and military advantage. This will be demonstrated by Tyche and Titania, alongside Juno and Oberon in the years ahead.

“We will monitor these vital satellites using state-of-the-art technology around the world, including our Inaros sensors – to ensure our Armed Forces can fight and win wherever they are. ”

In September, Sir Harv warned that Britain’s enemies are posing an increasing threat in space, and announced that a new No 3 Space Effects Squadron would be formed to “disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity” outside of Earth’s atmosphere.

News.title: Burnham considers rape trial law change after Russell Brand backlash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Burnham has said he will look at how rape cases are conducted in court after Russell Brand’s conviction, to ensure they do not leave women feeling like they are the ones on trial.

The prime minister refused to rule out changes to the law, saying he would study the case “in great detail”.

He also described Brand’s actions as “horrifying” and praised the bravery of the women who had the “courage to speak out” against the comedian.

open image in gallery Russell Brand is facing a lengthy jail term for rape (James Manning/PA) ( PA Wire )

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy has also called for the case to be a “wake up call” to the media and entertainment industries, saying “we owe it to all of the women who so bravely came forward in this case, and other victims of abuse, to ensure this is the line in the sand”.

Brand faces a lengthy jail sentence after being convicted of raping one of his fans and sexually assaulting three women at the height of his fame.

The Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley said on Friday that some of what he had heard reported from Brand’s trial was “getting very close to victim blaming” as he backed calls for judges to have to issue directions on rape myths and misconception to juries.

Speaking to Times Radio, Mr Burnham said: "I think we need to constantly look at the way rape trials are conducted to make sure that they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court, as has been the experience of people in the past.

“So I will look closely at what Sir Mark Rowley is saying. Always prepared to make changes.”

Asked whether that meant changes to the law, he said: “I wouldn't rule anything out, of course not... I will study what's happened here in great detail."

He added: “We need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape. We need to get the conviction rate up. It has improved, but not enough. We need to do more to support victims of sexual assault and rape, and we will do that as well.”

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to rule out changes to the law (Carlos Jasso/PA) ( PA Wire )

Appearing on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, Sir Mark was told Brand’s defence lawyer Ian Winter KC had told jurors that “none of the complainants had, in his words, resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Sir Mark replied: “I think what I’ve heard reported heads towards... victim blaming.”

He warned that “people fall into myths” about how rape victims will behave.

“The evidence is really clear,” he said. “Some people will fight. Some people will freeze. Some people will tell people straight away. Some people bottle it up for years. There isn’t one way of reacting.”

He added that “it shouldn’t be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn’t behave in one way, that somehow that undermines their case, when the evidence is very clear. We’re all (of a) very different sort of psychological and personal make-up, and in the most extraordinary horrific moments, of course, people react very differently”.

open image in gallery Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley backed calls for judges to have to issue directions on rape myths and misconception to juries (Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Wire )

Asked if he would support Victims’ Commissioner Claire Waxman, who wants a legal duty in the Courts and Tribunals Bill that would require judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial, Sir Mark said: “I strongly support Claire”.

He also said he would not be surprised if “many more” alleged victims of Mr Brand now came forward.

High-profile cases such as this often lead to a rise in reporting because they give victims confidence to speak up about attackers, he said.

On Brand, he added: “There’s two more cases we’re investigating at the moment. I clearly wouldn’t be surprised if many more came forward.”

Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a high-profile trial at Southwark Crown Court.

The star, 51, who denied all charges against him, was acquitted of two rape charges and a further accusation of attempted indecent assault.

A jury of eight men and four women took around nine hours to deliver their verdicts for each of the seven allegations against him.

The judge in the case, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand that he faces a “significant custodial term” when he is sentenced on Monday.

The PM is the most senior government figure to comment on the case since the jury delivered their verdict.

Before any of the allegations came to light, Mr Burnham was one of a number of politicians, including the foreign secretary Ed Miliband, who praised Brand. In 2014, Mr Burnham said he has used his celebrity status “to help others”, while the then-Labour leader Mr Miliband was interviewed by Brand as he courted his supporters in the run up to the 2015 general election.

News.title: Secret Service arrests man near White House after he said he heard voices telling him to kill Trump
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The U.S. Secret Service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill President Donald Trump.

The arrest Thursday night happened after Secret Service officers approached a man “acting suspicious” in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement. U.S. officials say the suspect — Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos — then went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation's capital and kill the Republican president.

Shortly after, officers discovered the suspect's vehicle had been reported stolen and he had three different firearms and dozens of rounds of ammunition. This is the latest in a series of arrests the Secret Service and other law enforcement agencies have made against individuals who have threatened Trump or his family members' lives since he returned to office last year.

The statement described Chrinos as a migrant from Venezuela who is in the country illegally after entering the U.S. through Texas in March 2024. DHS said he has been charged and currently remains in U.S. Marshals Service custody.

The White House did not provide comment, instead referring to DHS and U.S.S.S.

“Thanks to our brave Secret Service officers, this illegal alien with three firearms in his vehicle was arrested near the White House before he could harm anyone,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the statement.

News.title: Usman Khawaja insists ‘all of us’ involved in 2018 Australia sandpaper scandal
News.content:

Usman Khawaja has claimed the entire Australia team and coaching staff were aware of the sandpaper plot that shocked the cricketing world in 2018, finally stating: “It was all of us.”

A huge ball-tampering scandal flared up in an ill-tempered series against South Africa eight years ago, with television cameras clearly showing Cameron Bancroft using sandpaper to help generate reverse swing during the third Test in Cape Town.

The aftermath saw captain Steve Smith and his deputy David Warner banned for a year while Bancroft, as a junior player, served nine months. Until now nobody else involved in the tour has ever admitted culpability.

open image in gallery Steve Smith faced much of the criticism after the ball-tampering incident (Jason O’Brien/PA) ( PA Archive )

The bowling unit of Pat Cummins – now Australia captain – Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon even released a statement in 2021 denying they knew anything about the tactic.

But Khawaja, who retired after last winter’s Ashes and is promoting his new autobiography, has reopened the story and delivered his own seismic recollections. It is reported that the book will include an admission that the same tactic was first used in the previous Test at Gqeberha and that he was never interviewed by Cricket Australia in their subsequent investigation.

“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” he told the Sydney Morning Herald, which is serialising the title.

“In an ideal world, I don’t want to do this. I don’t want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

“Maybe I thought Davey (Warner) would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn’t think it was going to come down to this.”

Khawaja added that he was in favour of facing the subsequent storm as a team and expressed sympathy for those who took the flak, which went as far as then-Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull branding the matter “a disgrace” and an “affront” to the nation. Smith said in September the episode was a “traumatic experience” and he was “thrown to the wolves” in the aftermath.

open image in gallery Cameron Bancroft was caught damaging the ball with sandpaper in 2018 (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Archive )

open image in gallery Australia captain Pat Cummins has claimed no knowledge of the plot. (Ben Whitley/PA) ( PA Archive )

In his memoir, named Sabr after an Arabic term for resilience and endurance, Khawaja has dedicated the chapter on Cape Town to Smith, Warner and Bancroft.

He added: “Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game, I said, ‘Take this as a team. We did this as a team’.

“I’m not doing this for any other reason than I think it’s the right thing to do. I’ve always felt like there’s more to life than just cricket, and these guys, in some respect, deserve that justice. And it just doesn’t feel like anyone’s going to give it to them.”

In response, a spokesperson for Cricket Australia told the Press Association: “There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month’s series in South Africa.

“During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process.”

open image in gallery Pat Cummins, right, told Khawaja ‘tell your story’ (Adam Davy/PA) ( PA Archive )

Speaking ahead of Australia’s recent Test return to South Africa, Cummins revealed that he had given Khawaja his blessing to revisit the past after taking a phone call from his former team-mate.

“(I said) tell your story. It’s fine,” he said.

“It’s obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything, was done back then. We answered every question a million times. It was dealt with then, and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on.”

Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood have all been rested from this month’s white-ball series against England but Mitch Marsh, who played at Newlands, is set to serve as captain and is likely to face questioning on Khawaja’s revelations.

News.title: Meghan Markle’s father Thomas appears in court charged with possession of child sexual abuse images
News.content:

Thomas Markle will be subject to home detention and electronic tagging after appearing in court accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including images of himself with naked young girls.

Travel restrictions were also imposed by the judge on the Duchess of Sussex’s father, who did not enter a plea at the hearing in Tampa, Florida.

He has been bailed and was ordered to undergo a psychiatric exam, amid concerns he may not be unable to understand the proceedings or properly assist his lawyer.

A future court appearance in California is not due for at least several weeks, according to the US justice department.

Meghan’s 82-year-old father was arrested at the Maravida Senior Living care home in Lakeland near Tampa, Florida, on Thursday, having returned to the state to recuperate from a recent medical treatment. He was pictured in a wheelchair being led away by FBI agents.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney for California Bill Essayli announced Markle Snr’s arrest in X and posted a copy of the criminal complaint levelled against him, adding that if found guilty, he faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

open image in gallery Markle Snr appeared at the United States District Court in the Middle District of Florida in Tampa ( Reuters )

FBI special agents raided two storage units allegedly rented by the suspect in the Los Angeles area and had recovered 78 items that allegedly contained child sexual abuse material, including three alleged images of Markle Snr with underage girls.

Two of the images allegedly depict an adult man – whom a witness “positively identified” as Markle – with a nude young girl.

In one of them, according to court documents, the man “appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s”, which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades given Markle is now 82.

A third image is said to show a nude young girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines.

Other photographs allegedly show Markle with children in various stages of undress.

“These allegations are serious and disturbing,” Essayli wrote. “We intend to prosecute Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

open image in gallery Thomas Markle Sr has been arrested by the FBI for allegedly possessing child pornography, according to reports ( ITV/GMB )

FBI Director Kash Patel said in an accompanying statement: “Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida.

“This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”

The duchess’s father was reported to police in the Philippines and to the FBI last month by his son, Thomas Markle Jnr, 60, who handed over a haul of alleged child abuse images he found in his father’s belongings in Cebu City, where an investigation is underway.

A second alleged hoard was discovered last week in a storage unit Markle Snr is said to have rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico, during a raid by Mexican police.

Markle Snr, a retired television lighting and photography director, has admitted to paying for sex in the Philippines but denied ever possessing child abuse imagery, calling the accusations by his son “sick lies.”

Meghan said last month she was left “deeply distressed” at the allegations and revealed she was sent a letter via the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection seven years ago that made “troubling and disturbing allegations” about her father. She was given assurances these were being investigated, she said.

open image in gallery The Duchess of Sussex was left ’deeply disturbed’ by the allegations against her father, she said last month ( PA )

The Metropolitan Police has admitted it never shared the details with other law enforcement agencies, and the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, is now investigating its conduct.

The duchess had wanted to “speak out” immediately after reading the letter but police advised her against doing so, sources said.

The Independent reached out to the Metropolitan Police for comment. The DOJ directed us to the FBI’s statement while Buckingham Palace and the duchess both declined to comment.

Addressing the allegations against her father, from whom she is estranged, the duchess said last month: “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

On Thursday, the Philippines’ interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, said that Mr Markle Jnr, the duchess’s half-brother, had been named as a person of interest in its investigation into his father.

“There are indications suggesting that the son may also be involved in the crime,” he said at a press conference in Manila. “But only as a person of interest so far, he is not yet treated as a suspect. We will know in the next few days.”

According to Remulla, more than 7,000 photos and one video – all of underage males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered among Mr Markle Snr’s possessions.

He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen.”

If you are a child and you need help because something has happened to you, you can call Childline free of charge on 0800 1111. You can also call the NSPCC if you are an adult and you are worried about a child, on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adults on 0808 801 0331

News.title: Concerns only a third of homes could be eligible under Labour’s new scheme for first-time buyers
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Less than a third of homes will qualify under the Labour’s new scheme to help first-time buyers get on the property market, research shows.

Under the Your First Home Scheme, the government has promised to provide an interest-free loan on new build homes for individuals or couples earning a combined income of £110,00 or less a year.

Buyers will face different property price caps depending on where they live, with a survey from SAM Conveyancing in The Times revealing that just 30 per cent of homes will be eligible.

The property company found that the cap was below the price of an average new build home in 264 of the 285 local authorities that it analysed, meaning less than half of homes were eligible.

In 97 local authorities, less than a quarter of homes would qualify, it said.

Andrew Boast, the chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, has called for the government to open up the scheme to all homes.

He said: “Limiting Your First Home to new builds was always going to restrict where first-time buyers could use it, and the price caps show just how tight that restriction is.

“Fewer than a third of the new homes sold in England come in under them, so in much of the country buyers will be choosing from a small slice of an already small market.”

open image in gallery Less than a third of new homes are eligible under the scheme ( AFP/Getty )

The lowest proportion of qualifying homes was in Oxford, where none of the 66 new build properties sold over the last two years was under than the cap of £415,000. According to the research, the average new build cost £777,867.

Similarly, in Worthing, only one of the 90 new build homes would have been eligible under the scheme. The government has a £300,000 cap in the area, but the typical new build costs £409,472.

The caps reach as high as £650,000 in areas in central London, including Westminster, Kensington and Chelsea and the City of London. Only 3.6 per cent of homes would qualify in Islington, 3.8 per cent in Westminster, 5.3 per cent in Hammersmith and Fulham, and 5.6 per cent in Kensington and Chelsea.

The area with the highest proportion of eligible homes was in Melton, where 35 per cent of new build sales fell below the area’s £300,000 cap.

A government spokesperson said: “Your First Home will help first-time buyers across the country without the bank of mum and dad onto the housing ladder and is specifically designed to target support to those who need it most, based on the median price paid by first-time buyers for new build homes in their area.

open image in gallery The Your First Home scheme has local property price caps ( PA Archive )

“The analysis presented does not consider the type of new build home being sold in the areas highlighted and whether those would actually be purchased by first time buyers rather than the broader market.

“Industry estimates have found almost half of all new build homes sold in England last year and two-thirds of new build flats would be covered by the price caps.”

It said the caps are based on the median price paid by first-time buyers for new build homes with an additional 10 per cent added above this and rounded up to the nearest £5,000.

The government says to scheme will help 70,000 people get onto the property ladder and save first time buyers hundreds of pounds a month.

Eligible buyers will be able to purchase their home using a deposit of at least 2.5 per cent of the purchase price.

Mr Boast said: “Opening the scheme to existing homes, with the equity loan based on an independent valuation instead of the agreed price, would give first-time buyers far more choice and help keep prices in check.

“Until then, anyone hoping to use it should check early which homes fall under the cap in their area, and speak to a conveyancer before reserving a plot.”

News.title: Monty Don gives final goodbye as Gardeners’ World role comes to an end after 23 years
News.content:
Monty Don signed off for the final time on Gardeners’ World this evening (6 November) as his two decade-long run hosting the BBC show came to an end.

Don announced he was hanging up his shears in September after deciding ‘it was time to stop’, having taken over from Alan Titchmarsh in 2002.

Thanking viewers at the end of the episode, the 71-year-old said: “There has been one constant factor and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here as well as working with so many superb people.

“Thank you for coming on that journey with me.”

News.title: Hugo Keenan scores hat-trick as Ireland seal emphatic victory over Argentina
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick as Ireland preserved their unbeaten home record against Argentina with a comfortable 42-12 bonus-point victory in the Nations Championship.

The Pumas had famously stunned Andy Farrell’s 2025 British and Irish Lions squad on their previous visit to the Aviva Stadium, yet they entered the match having lost all 11 of their past meetings with Ireland in Dublin.

Felipe Contepomi’s side took an early lead when Mateo Carreras caught a cross-field kick from Tomas Albornoz over diminutive scrum-half Craig Casey to touch down in the left corner.

However, full-back Keenan crossed the line either side of a try by captain Dan Sheehan, allowing the hosts to establish a 21-5 advantage by half-time.

Sam Prendergast registered his maiden international try alongside five successful conversions, before Keenan’s third score and a powerful finish from Ronan Kelleher sealed a resounding win for the home team.

Carreras managed a late consolation try for Argentina, but the visitors' attempt to cause a surprise was hampered by yellow cards for Justo Piccardo and Efrain Elias, alongside an early head injury to skipper Julian Montoya.

This outcome was Ireland’s third victory from four Nations Championship matches, following summer successes against Australia and Japan and a defeat to New Zealand.

With head coach Farrell accepting that his side must improve to compete at next year’s World Cup, the opening fixture of the autumn provided an opportunity to assess several squad options.

Argentina’s 10th-minute score further subdued a flat crowd which was significantly below capacity.

However, Ireland swiftly hit back. Casey initially won a turnover penalty and then started a flowing team move from right to left which culminated with Mack Hansen sending Keenan racing across the try line.

open image in gallery Ireland’s win was a third from four matches in the Nations Championship after summer successes against Australia and Japan were followed by defeat against New Zealand ( Getty )

Hooker Sheehan – captaining his country in the absence of the injured Caelan Doris – crashed over 10 minutes later after Nick Timoney was held up following a lineout maul.

Argentina lost hooker Montoya before falling further behind when Keenan collected another Hansen pass to dance past three defenders and powerfully pirouette over.

While the Pumas have a wretched record away to Ireland, they have won three of four World Cup meetings between the nations.

Their hopes of securing a landmark success on Irish soil were hampered further by centre Piccardo being sent to the sin bin in the 35th minute for not retreating following a penalty.

Sheehan was then denied his second try when he was forced into touch just before grounding in an incident which led to him and Montoya’s replacement Leonel Oviedo each departing for head injury assessments.

Fly-half Prendergast secured Ireland’s bonus point within two minutes of the restart, spotting a gap between Marcos Kremer and Juan Martin Gonzalez to superbly race away and dot down.

Keenan was unable to prevent Pumas wing Carreras scoring his second before completing his treble following quick hands from forwards Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and Ryan Baird.

Replacement hooker Kelleher then bulldozed over in the aftermath of Elias being sent to the bin for a high tackle on Keenan, with Ciaran Frawley converting.

Ireland prop Sam Illo – on for his home debut – became the third player shown a yellow card before Farrell’s men cruised through the closing stages ahead of upcoming appointments with Fiji and world champions South Africa.

News.title: Ireland send out ominous warning with second-gear walloping of Argentina
News.content:
Is it time to fire up the emerald green bandwagon? Not quite yet. But this was not a bad start to Ireland’s autumn; a 42-12 walloping of Los Pumas with Andy Farrell’s team still nowhere near their best. That should be highly encouraging for those of an Irish persuasion.

A year out from the World Cups of 2015, 2019 and 2023, Ireland had enjoyed banner seasons, eyeing up global glory. They never made it past the quarter-finals.

The build-up this time has been tougher going – the Aviva, unusually for this time of year – was not even full for this Nations Championship encounter. But perhaps Ireland will be better for it. They had far too much on a crisp Friday night in Dublin for an Argentina team who were missing a few of their stars, notably Bath’s Santiago Carreras and Lyon prop Thomas Gallo, but still packing 750 caps’ worth of Test experience in their starting XV.

Farrell was missing a few big names himself. Caelan Doris and Jack Conan were out injured, with the Englishman opting to hand Sean Jansen and Nick Timoney starts in the back row. Farrell also chose to start Craig Casey rather than Jamison Gibson-Park – arguably their best player of the last 18 months – at scrum-half, with Sam Prendergast starting again at 10 given Jack Crowley’s absence.

All in all there was a slightly experimental feel to proceedings, making Argentina potentially dangerous visitors. But Ireland had far too much in reserve. Hugo Keenan grabbed a hat-trick and took the player of the match award. Robert Baloucoune was consistently excellent. Mack Hansen’s return on the wing was hugely welcome. Tominey stood out in the back row.

Farrell said he was delighted with the result, if not the entire performance, making special mention of the likes of Keenan, Hansen, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, all of whom were returning from long injury lay-offs.

“The game’s never going to be perfect. But if you look at the bigger picture, to win 42-12 against a really good side in Argentina, I don’t think too many teams have done that,” Farrell said. “You have to be pleased.”

Asked whether he was happier with the 42 points scored or the meagre 12 conceded, Farrell added that it was probably the latter: “We want to be known for our defence. It shows our mentality.”

Los Pumas scored the first try of the game, Mateo Carreras getting the jump on Casey in the corner to field a Tomás Albornoz crossfield kick.

News.title: ‘Air Caluori’ puts on show as England A offer exciting glimpse into future
News.content:
England A 59 Argentina XV 24

Noah Caluori and Luke Northmore both scored twice as England A produced an emphatic victory over Argentina XV at the Rec.

On a night when England’s back line showcased plenty of attacking flair and free-flowing rugby, the hosts ran in nine tries to shrug off a dogged Argentina outfit.

Bath’s Max Ojomoh shone bright on his own turf and combined effortlessly with Northmore in a midfield partnership which showed plenty of promise for the future.

A young and inexperienced touring Argentina side hung tough in a see-sawing first half which yielded seven tries, but England found another gear after the break, with Jack Kenningham and Jamie Blamire among those on the scoresheet.

The hosts enjoyed a dream start when Caluori dotted down inside the opening two minutes, setting the tone for a helter-skelter first half.

News.title: Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place
News.content:
Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

News.title: A tech editor’s guide to finding genuine Black Friday discounts
News.content:
The Black Friday shopping season is here. The world’s biggest technology brands, including Amazon, Samsung, Apple and Sony, are all expected to drop their prices, with British retailers such as John Lewis, Currys and Argos throwing their hats in the ring as we speed towards the new year.

While you might already have your eye on a gadget or two in the hope they drop in price during the sales, it’s important to shop wisely – and, crucially, manage expectations.

As Telegraph Recommended’s tech editor, who has been covering the Black Friday sales for well over a decade, I have picked up a number of must-know tips.

Whether that’s buying last year’s iPhone for less than the latest model, or accepting the sad truth that game consoles won’t be discounted ahead of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch, here’s everything you need to know – including early discounts.

News.title: White House postpones tech boss meeting after AI crash
News.content:
The White House has postponed a meeting of Silicon Valley tech bosses including Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang following Thursday’s stock market sell-off.

Donald Trump’s administration was scheduled to convene a session on Friday with an industry panel known as the “President’s Council ​of ⁠Advisers on Science and Technology”, which advises Mr Trump on tech matters.

However, the meeting was cancelled by the White House and is yet to be rescheduled. Thursday’s tech rout, which saw the Nasdaq 100 fall the most in six years, wiped more than $1 trillion off the Magnificent 7.

The tech ​panel also includes top Silicon Valley bosses such as AMD’s ‌Lisa Su and Marc ​Andreessen, co-foudner of Andreessen ​Horowitz.

The move comes after the President reaffirmed his commitment to the buildout of data centres, saying that “only foolish leadership will say “NO” to the riches they bring.”

Tech shares fell sharply on Thursday over fears the Democratic “blue wave” will halt the construction of data centres, which have fuelled the AI boom

It comes as US stocks staged a small rebound, with the Nasdaq Composite up 1.77pc.

Meta shares were up 2.5pc on Friday following a 4pc fall on Thursday, while Nvidia rebounded 3.6pc after a drop of 9.3pc a day earlier.

News.title: Cheap version of game-changing HIV preventive drug granted approval by US authorities
News.content:
Millions of people in low and middle income countries are set to get access to a game-changing HIV prevention drug within weeks, after US health authorities green lit a cheap form of the product.

Earlier this week the US Food and Drug Administration granted tentative approval to a generic form of the drug lenacapavir, made by Indian manufacturer Dr Reddy’s Laboratories.

Under an agreement hammered out between drug manufacturers and philanthropic donors in 2025 120 low and middle income countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East and the Caribbean, will get access to the generic drug, at just $40 per patient per year – compared to the US list price of $28,000.

Lenacapavir, a long-acting injection administered twice a year, was hailed as the scientific breakthrough of 2024 and a potential turning point in the fight against HIV. Clinical trials have shown it provides almost 100 per cent protection against catching the HIV virus for six months and it is more effective and convenient than taking daily pre-exposure prophylactic (PrEP) pills.

Last year, Gilead Sciences, which developed lenacapavir, signed royalty-free, non-exclusive voluntary licencing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable the production and supply of a generic. Dr. Reddy’s is the first to get FDA approval and it is hoped the first batches will be ready by the end of the year.

Jessica Burry, HIV technical officer at Unitaid, which in conjunction with the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI supported Dr Reddy’s in its bid to manufacture the generic, said it normally takes 10 years for a generic form of a drug to be launched.

“So we’re celebrating this milestone,” she said. “There’s a lot of demand in the countries where we’re working and we think having an affordable generic could make a real difference.”

Standard PrEP involves daily pills which some people find difficult to stick to.

“You can overcome the stigma, you can overcome the potential adherence difficulties so it’s really a game changer in terms of things to have in the toolbox,” she said.

News.title: The perilous road to parenthood: Mongolia’s fight to make childbirth safer
News.content:
As the 4x4 raced south, bouncing across Mongolia’s rocky valley roads and dusty forest steppes, an obstetrician was doing her best to ease Otgonbayar Odbayar’s pain and panic.

Hours earlier, the reindeer herder’s waters had broken. But Otgonbayar was six weeks early – and almost 250 miles away from the doctors who could provide the caesarean she knew she needed.

She contacted the nearest clinic, kicking off a relay of calls that spanned the length of Khuvsgul, a region bordering Russia. Soon, a plan came back through the chain: one health team would collect the 26-year-old and sprint south, while doctors from the provincial hospital in Murun would hurtle north. They’d meet in the middle.

Otgonbayar Odbayar with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But Otgonbayar’s three-hour journey was touch and go. “Halfway through, her contractions got very intense and very close together,” said Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh, the obstetrician who collected her. “She was in a lot of pain. We put her on an IV and were driving so fast.”

They made it to the small clinic in Tugul a little after 11pm, but then faced an excruciating 90 minute wait for the team from Murun, who had further to travel on Mongolia’s rutted roads. Dr Tsogbadrakh didn’t have a Plan B: the baby was in breech position, and the scar from Otgonbayar’s previous c-section still hadn’t fully healed.

Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“When [the doctors] arrived, I felt relief,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh. “If we had waited only 30 more minutes to start surgery, no one could tell what would have happened.”

Yet Otgonbayar’s ordeal is now the exception in Mongolia, underscoring just how far the vast country has come in its three-decade drive to tackle the childbirth risks posed by geography.

In 1990, 200 women died for every 100,000 births, but that ratio plunged to 47 by 2015 – making Mongolia one of only nine countries to hit global targets to reduce maternal mortality by 75 per cent over the 25-year period, according to analysis in the Lancet.

Strides have slowed but continued, and the rate now hovers at around 37. By contrast, other countries with a similar maternal mortality ratio in 1990, including Algeria, Brazil, the Philippines and Kiribati, still see more than 70 deaths per 100,000 births, according to Our World in Data.

In a country as vast and sparse as Mongolia – which is more than six times the size of the UK, but home to just 3.5 million people – health gains have been reliant “on overcoming the distance between women and the care they need”, said the health minister Batshugar Enkhbayar.

That has meant introducing telemedicine initiatives to bring specialist advice to remote clinics, waiting homes where pregnant women can stay in the final weeks before delivery, and better trained staff to spot risks before they become acute. In the last year, the country has also started to trial portable ultrasounds.

Northern Mongolia near the Russian border Credit : Simon Townsley

“We cannot always eliminate that distance,” said Mr Enkhbayar, “so we have to plan around it.”

The Telegraph spent a week in Mongolia to find out what this looks like in practice, driving hundreds of miles to meet pregnant women and new mothers in provincial hospitals, village clinics and remote herder communities.

There are also lessons for other countries: the latest data shows that globally, 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023 – one death every two minutes. In the UK, around 250 women died in childbirth between 2022 and 2024, equal to more than one expectant mother a week.

Obstetrician Otgongerel Uvgii with Otgonbayar Odbayar following her recent birth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But in low and middle income countries, the vast majority of fatalities are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as preeclampsia, which are all entirely preventable. Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives.

And, when a mother survives childbirth – like Otgonbayar eventually did – her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At 2:10am on October 4, the doctors safely delivered Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy weighing 2.3kg. The family hadn’t yet decided on a name when we visited the stuffy maternity room a day later – but they were already thinking about his future.

Sports.title: Lampard: VAR didn't do its job
Sports.content:
Coventry boss Frank Lampard says VAR 'didn't do its job' in his side's defeat to Everton as three reviews controversially went against his side.

Two penalty appeals and a possible handball for Everton's second goal were all reviewed by VAR officials Timothy Wood and Gary Beswick, but nothing was given. They were also not awarded on-field by referee Stuart Attwell.

Coventry opened the scoring after the two penalty appeals, but were ultimately beaten 3-1 on Merseyside on Friday Night Football.

Lampard told Sky Sports: "I hate to sound like a moaner. It's a football match and if you win the game, that can happen here. I've worked here and know the momentum swings in the game.

"I'm not trying to talk about the circumstances of the actual football, but when big decisions change games, they absolutely do. It's disappointing. VAR is there for that and it didn't do its job."

Here, we breaks down each incident and what the pundits, managers and players had to say...

Tarkowski avoids punishment for elbow and hair pull

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Should Tarkowski have seen red for a hair pull during Everton's Premier League match against Coventry

Towards the end of the first half, James Tarkowski rose to defend a high ball into the box. As he did, he caught Ethan Pinnock with an elbow, before also appearing to pull the hair of Caleb Yirenkyi.

VAR did look at the incident, especially the elbow, but nothing was given in terms of a card or a penalty.

There was no communication from the Premier League Match Centre on if the hair pull was reviewed, but there was new guidance from the Premier League this summer, which says: "A red card will be issued when there is a clear and deliberate action to pull an opponent's hair with excessive force and/or brutality.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Everton’s match against Coventry in the Premier League

"A yellow card will be issued if the action is deemed to be without excessive force and/or brutality.

"Referees will enhance recognition of clear holding actions that have a clear material impact, and/or non-footballing holding actions with no place on the football pitch. This includes penalising defenders where they are clearly only focused on opponents and making a holding action that is impactful on the attacker's ability to play or challenge for the ball."

Lampard: I thought the rules were clear

"The first-half decision on Tarkowski got checked. Seeing it back, he pulls on Caleb's hair while competing with Ethan.

"I thought the rules were clear. I know they've changed the rules so it's no red card, I get that too. But he's pulling on his hair and [Yirenkyi] can't get his momentum to jump. I think it's a foul and a penalty and they decided no."

What did the pundits say?

Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp on Friday Night Football: "Yirenkyi goes up, Tarkowski gets hold of his hair. He yanks it down. Is it excessive force? Probably not, but he pulls his hair, stopping any elevation. It's a definite penalty for me.

"Yirenkyi knows he has his hair pulled. It's unusual for Tarkowski to do. It's not the best piece of defending that's for sure... It's a foul. It's not a red card anymore but it's definitely a foul."

Lee Hendrie on Sky Sports co-commentary: "There's a clear pull... Tarkowski is in the heart of this. There's an elbow, which isn't a problem, but the hair pull will raise awareness.

"You can clearly see he's utilising the hair. It's a tight one. VAR have completely not looked at it or felt the need to look at it."

Moyes: We want the right result, but we've had decisions go against us Everton boss David Moyes to Sky Sports on whether he is bothered by Coventry's calls:



“I’m bothered because we want it [the result] to be right, but we’ve had a few decisions recently where we don’t think have gone our way.



"There was one possibly at Newcastle but there was one at Man City last season in a league game which was hugely important for us regarding getting into Europe.



"Sometimes they go for you, sometimes they don’t. If they were going against me, I’d be complaining a bit more.”

Mykolenko clip on Awoniyi not given

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Coventry denied a penalty by VAR after Mykolenko foul deemed as outside the box

At the start of the second half, Taiwo Awoniyi drove into the box with Vitalii Mykolenko behind him. There was some contact from behind which sent the striker down.

Referee Stuart Attwell said no penalty, while the VAR review deemed the contact to be outside the box.

Lampard: I can't believe it's not given

"I thought the one on Taiwo running through - it's a clear foul that the referee doesn't give in-game. I can't believe that because it's clear. Maybe he waited for VAR because it was on the borderline.

"But as I see it, Taiwo's foot is entering the box and his knee and the back of his knee is on the line of the box, which is a penalty."

Sports.title: WTA chair apologises to Pegula after 'diva' comment broadcast
Sports.content:
Audio recording on practice courts will be deactivated at the WTA Finals after private comments made by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva were picked up, with the governing body's chair apologising to the American for the "regrettable" incident.

US player Pegula describing Russian teenager Andreeva as "a diva" while conversing with coach Mark Knowles during a practice session were heard on a YouTube livestream at Indian Wells, the venue for the WTA Tour season-ending event from November 8-15.

The WTA shouldered the blame for failing to properly inform players about active microphones, with chair Valerie Camillo saying there was "a lack of advanced notice and clear signage" as she confirmed audio will now be switched off for practice sessions.

Image: Pegula hopes the incident allows players to push for more privacy

Camillo added: "I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles. What happened was regrettable and unacceptable.

"Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction.

"As a member ​organisation, one of the primary responsibilities of the WTA is to protect ​players whenever possible. The players deserve better and we will continue to work to raise the bar for the WTA."

Image: Andreeva won the French Open this year, beating Maja Chwalińska in the final

Pegula: Let's keep pushing for more privacy

Pegula, who was also heard saying French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and that her coach, former Wimbledon winner, Conchita Martinez, encouraged her player's behaviour, addressed the incident on ESPN on Friday.

The world No 5 said: "Obviously I had no idea and was not informed that audio was being recorded. But it is what it is.

"I think it's something that we have fought a lot over the last couple years as there's a lot more surveillance, audio and, I guess, access to the players at tournaments than there has been in the past.

"I know for broadcasting that it's great for fans, but I think we've seen a couple incidents now throughout the year, the last couple of years really, where it seems highly unnecessary.

"I think [this will] definitely reignite the topic. Hopefully we can use this incident to keep pushing for more player privacy."

Image: Coco Gauff had called for more privacy back in January

Two-time Grand Slam champion Coco Gauff - in Pegula's group at the WTA Finals, alongside Linda Noskova and world No 1 Elena Rybakina - called for more privacy in January after cameras caught her smashing her racket following defeat to Elina Svitolina at the Australian Open quarter-finals in Melbourne.
