“Incessant fuel tanker fire (fires) worries (worry) Obi of Onitsha”

“…so that our people will live a prosperous, safe and secure lives (life) in their environment (environments)….”

“…as cost of raw materials skyrocket (skyrockets)”

“RUGA: Why farmers, herders (herders’) crisis (crises) persist—Don”

“Even a child in this nation knows that the police derives (derive) its (their) enabling and operational authority from the dictates of the Centre….” The paper’s Metro Section institutionalized this same lexical bondage in one of its headlines: “In Kano, Police allegedly shoots (sic) tanker driver over bribe” Its Editorial was equally not left out in this particular police howler: “Nigerians would no doubt be happier to hear from the Nigerian Police what it is (they are) doing to enhance its (their) capacity….”

“The ban on tinted glasses is even more reprehensible because the security benefits it can deliver is (are) far from certain.”

“Gov, Reps demand his arrest over (for) inciting comments on 2027”

“A week’s trail on the heels of pirates reveal (reveals) how Nigerians lose billions of Naira to the kingpin….”

“Court remands Edo lawmaker in prison over unlawful possession of firearm” The lawmaker was remanded in custody—not in prison!

“That is why the Presidency must show more leadership and tact before jumping into a battle just because it thinks it has the power to crush the enemy—real or imagined.” Get it right: the enemy—real or imaginary.

“Nigerian scientists have failed woefully.” THE SUNDAY INTERVIEW: …have failed abysmally (not woefully)

“Let me also make this point that our scientists have not done creditably well over the years.” No overkill: either creditably or well.

The final entry from last week’s edition of this medium: “Insurgents await ransom, assure on ex-minister’s safety” ‘Assure’ is a transitive verb. It must take an object.

“Restoring sanity on (to) the road should be the first tangible step if he is serious about….”

“The result was that what was supposed to be a consensus agreement willingly entered into by….” ‘Consensus agreement’? Next time, just choose one.

“It was flurry of activities in Abuja last week.…” A flurry or a hive of activity….

“The minister said government’s desire to licence (sic) a second carrier is born out of the…” General view: borne out.

“Knowing fully well that Abacha was a key factor in the Babangida regime.…” Intelligent commentary: knowing full well.

“What is good for the goose should be good for the gander.” Fixed expression: what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

“Some blind beggars on a street in Lagos Island” Beggars in a street on (not in) Lagos Island.

“…Catholic cardinals who converged at (on) the Vatican for a three-day meeting….”

“Manhunt begins for killers of award winning (award-winning) police chief.”

“…writes (writes to) the president to intimate him of (to) the hardship ravaging the land.”

“The civil servants have got pay rise, yet their purchasing power have (has) been decimated.”

“The ITSC equipment was damaged early this week by a heavy rainstorm….” In the interest of telecoms, delete ‘heavy’-–which is contextually otiose, just like ‘heavy downpour’!

“Every moneybag (moneybags) wants you to know when he is celebrating….” ‘Moneybag’ is the sac used in putting money, while the owner is a moneybags.

“A professional must update his knowledge in his chosen career otherwise he becomes a mediocre.” The way we write: otherwise he becomes a mediocrity or mediocrist. ‘Mediocre’ is an adjective that cannot function as a noun except in a collective manner (the mediocre).

“The emergence of vigilante (vigilance) groups to combat the activities of men of the underworld is only symptomatic of lack of faith in the ability of the police to guarantee….”

“NLC suspends siege on (to) First Bank, as NUJ lays siege to Daily Champion over non-payment of six-month salary”

“The assurance from the IGP is therefore supposed to act as a soothing balm.” Is a balm not supposed to soothe? Does it do the opposite?

“…it will be much more so with one involving a police personnel.” ‘Personnel’ is a collective term. Use ‘policeman’, ‘officer’ or ‘cop’.

“But how do we prevent hunger next year when politicians will engage themselves (one another) in a do or die (do-or-die) battle for re-election.”

“VP condemns do or die politics” This way: do-or-die politics.

“The race to Government House in Kano has began in earnest as….” Without any effort: The race has begun….

“…those who would have uttered (what?) them reduced everyone to spectators while they reached for each other’s throats.” Get it right: each other’s throat or one another’s throat (depending on context).

“After all, as they say, ‘what is good for the goose is good for the gander’ ’’. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.

“Knowing what to wear and how to compliment (complement) it goes a long way….”

“The state, therefore, does not deserve the treatment being currently meted to it”. Classical expression: being meted out to it.

“Chief of Naval Staff advocates for increased productivity via industrialization” When used as a verb, ‘advocate’ does not admit ‘for’. Let us avoid verbiage in headline casting: Naval Chief advocates increased productivity.

“For the university to recommend that students should pay for the damages while they have….” A common mistake: except in legalese, ‘damage’ cannot be pluralized.

“…rather than investigating and finding out who were involved and check against future re-occurrence: Beyond recurrence, can an event yet to take place happen in the past?

“…the university is pointing its accusing fingers in the direction of the lecturers.” True idiom: point a/the finger. No inclusion of ‘accusing’ or inflection of ‘finger’.

“It is our belief that we members of the alumni association of our Alma Mata (Alma Mater) have unique roles to play in the restoration of sanity on our university campus.” It is…restoration of sanity to (not on) our campus.

“Isn’t it funny that it is the beak with which a bird builds it’s (sic) nest that it uses to scatter it.” Possessive: its

“…the AU summiteers concentrated almost exclusive (sic) on the political independence and liberation of countries in (on) the continent.”

“Monday’s action, which started at dawn, was as a result of the breakdown of series of negotiations…” An agendum: a series of negotiations.

“According to investigations, the deceased was said to be resting alone in his room at about 9.p.m….” Every reporter should be decisive based on timing which description to use: either at or about 9 p.m. The two cannot co-function.

“According to the source, the institution has a very high percentage of failure in the last academic year.” Reported speech: the institution had (not has).

“… that the authorities of the institution was (were) still waiting the result of the police analysis of the bomb”.

“…in the next three years, its per capital income would have …” This way: per capita income.

“Then it was catalogue of misses for the Super Eagles.” In the spirit of qualification: a catalogue of misses.

World.title: 2027: Stop The Violence Before It Consumes The Election
World.content:
Femi Akintunde-Johnson

There is something deeply disturbing about a political environment in which a candidate cannot travel to meet supporters, a party cannot organise a gathering, or citizens cannot attend a campaign event without the possibility of being attacked. Nigeria is still some distance from the 2027 general election, yet the atmosphere surrounding political activities is already acquiring an unsettling character. Violence, intimidation, disruption of meetings and physical attacks are becoming recurring features of political engagement. We should be concerned, not merely because politicians and their supporters are at risk, but because the freedom to participate in democracy is being threatened.

The incidents are no longer easy to dismiss as isolated disagreements between overenthusiastic supporters. In Katsina, supporters All Progressives Congress travelling towards a campaign flag-off in Funtua were reportedly attacked along the Yashi-Funtua route in late October. A female passenger was injured, vehicles were damaged, and the police subsequently announced 14 arrests. In Cross River, the convoy of Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, came under attack in Calabar on 4 November. Police confirmed damage to vehicles and announced the arrest of a suspect, while investigations continued. The suspect, it should be emphasised, remains entitled to the presumption of innocence. These incidents follow other reported confrontations and disruptions of political activities in different parts of the country.

The National Peace Committee has reportedly recorded 60 election-related incidents within one month, including violence, intimidation and threats. That is a sobering indication of the climate developing around the next electoral cycle. We should not wait for a more frightening statistic before appreciating the danger.

Political competition is not supposed to be a contact sport in which supporters demonstrate loyalty by breaking heads, smashing windscreens or chasing opponents out of neighbourhoods. Campaigns are opportunities to persuade, debate, canvass and present alternatives. They are not territorial conquests. No political party owns a street, a community or a public space. No candidate has an exclusive right to campaign in a particular part of the country. And no citizen should need a security convoy to exercise the basic freedom of political association.

Unfortunately, Nigeria has a long and uncomfortable history of politicians cultivating the services of young men who are recruited, equipped or encouraged to intimidate opponents. Some are described as supporters, mobilisers or loyalists when their activities serve political interests, but conveniently become unknown hoodlums when violence attracts public condemnation. This convenient disowning must end. Those who recruit, finance, encourage or deploy violent enforcers cannot escape responsibility simply because the violence has become embarrassing.

Of course, allegations must be investigated and responsibility established on evidence. It would be irresponsible to attribute every attack to a particular party or political sponsor merely because an opposing camp makes the accusation. But it would be equally irresponsible for political leaders to hide behind the absence of immediate proof while refusing to condemn violence or cooperate with investigations. The standard must apply equally, whether the victims belong to the ruling party or the opposition.

The security agencies have an especially important responsibility. The police must protect the right of every lawful political gathering to take place without intimidation. Their duty is not to preserve the comfort of incumbents, frustrate opposition mobilisation or display greater enthusiasm for one political colour than another. Security deployment should be guided by credible intelligence and assessed risks, not political convenience. Those who attack campaign convoys, disrupt meetings, threaten candidates or assault supporters must be identified, investigated and prosecuted.

It is encouraging that police authorities have issued warnings and made arrests in some cases. The Inspector-General of Police has also spoken against the recruitment and mobilisation of young Nigerians for political violence. But warnings, however emphatic, cannot substitute for prevention and enforcement. The public must see investigations pursued to their logical conclusion, sponsors exposed where evidence establishes their involvement, and prosecutions conducted without selective application of the law. Otherwise, the familiar cycle of outrage, arrest announcements and eventual silence will continue.

The Independent National Electoral Commission also has a role beyond preparing ballot papers and organising polling arrangements. Its responsibility to protect the integrity of the electoral process must include sustained engagement with security agencies and political parties on the safety of campaigns and voters. The National Peace Committee, civil society organisations, traditional institutions and religious leaders can help promote restraint, but moral appeals must be matched by institutional action.

The danger is that violence at this stage could become a rehearsal for something worse as the election approaches. Political hostility can escalate. An attack on one group may provoke retaliation against another; a disrupted meeting may become an excuse for revenge; inflammatory statements may turn suspicion into collective hostility. Before long, ordinary supporters who have little or nothing to gain from political office may become casualties of battles fought on behalf of those seeking it.

And what happens to the undecided citizen in such an environment? The trader who wants to listen to competing candidates, the student curious about policy proposals, the elderly voter who wishes to attend a rally, or the resident who simply wants to observe the political process may decide that staying away is safer. Violence therefore does more than injure its immediate victims. It narrows democratic participation, silences public discussion and allows intimidation to determine who can be heard.

Political leaders must understand that democracy does not belong to the people who can assemble the largest crowds, hire the loudest musicians or deploy the most intimidating entourages. It belongs to citizens whose rights remain intact regardless of the party they support. A candidate’s popularity cannot be measured by the fear generated around a campaign, just as political strength cannot be established by the number of opponents prevented from speaking.

President Bola Tinubu, state governors, party chairmen, presidential aspirants and other political leaders must speak clearly and consistently against violence, including when the perpetrators appear to be associated with their own political interests. The temptation to condemn attacks only when one’s own camp is affected is part of the problem. Political restraint cannot be selective, and neither can accountability.

The coming election should be an opportunity for Nigerians to interrogate competing ideas, assess records and make choices without intimidation. That requires political parties to discipline their supporters, candidates to moderate their language, security agencies to demonstrate impartiality, and the justice system to ensure that offences do not disappear into the familiar fog of political influence.

Nigeria has enough insecurity to contend with without adding politically sponsored violence to the national burden. We should not allow the pursuit of political power to turn our streets into battlegrounds or make physical intimidation an accepted instrument of electoral competition.

The warning signs are already visible. We must not pretend otherwise, nor should we wait until campaign violence becomes election violence before treating it as a national emergency. The people who throw stones today may be carrying more dangerous weapons tomorrow; the political rival chased away from a meeting today may become the target of a more organised assault later. Prevention is not an act of pessimism. It is an obligation of responsible leadership.

The 2027 election must be decided by the votes of Nigerians, not by the fists, knives, guns or threats of political enforcers. Those seeking public office must understand that the mandate they desire can only be legitimate when citizens are free to choose without fear.

Stop the violence before it consumes the election. And, more importantly, before it consumes the very democratic freedoms the election is supposed to protect.

World.title: Danielle Adewusi: 35 Years On, I Am Stepping into My Mother’s Legacy
World.content:
Miss Universe Nigeria 2026, Danielle Adewusi, is following in her mother’s footsteps 35 years after she won the same title. Ahead of the 75th Miss Universe, she speaks with Tosin Clegg about legacy, empowerment and her ambitions.

How did this journey start out for you?

Thirty-five years ago, my mother held the same title, having been Miss Universe Nigeria in 1991, and I would like to say that I am stepping into a legacy. I am competing at Miss Universe International at the end of this week, as I resume camp on Sunday, and I am doing something that has never been seen in pageantry before. It is called the Legacy Reign, and nobody has ever done anything like it in pageantry.

It honours three legacies. The first, which I have already spoken about, is my mother’s achievement 35 years ago. The second is that Nigeria won the Miss World pageant 25 years ago, while the third is the 75th edition of the Miss Universe competition. The convergence of these timelines is very significant to me and speaks strongly of legacy.

When I compete, I want to represent Nigeria well and honour the different tribes and legacies of the country. You will see this reflected in the wardrobe I will be bringing to camp. These are outfits I designed myself, which have been brought to life by my amazing stylists.

What has your pageantry journey been like up to this point?

I was always aware of pageantry because of my mum, and the thought that I would compete one day had always been at the back of my mind. In my fifth year of medical school, I was already doing a lot, as I am someone who multitasks, although I am doing even more now than I was doing then.

At some point, people started telling me that once I qualified as a doctor, I would have to give up all these other interests because I could only be a doctor. That did not sit right with me. I do not believe we have to diminish one aspect of our mission for another to be celebrated.

So, one day, I sat down and decided how I wanted things to be. I listed all the things I enjoyed and was good at, then took a step back to work out how to achieve them. I eventually decided that 2026 would be the year, and that was how the journey began.

What makes this global showcase so special to you?

I believe we have a chance of winning, and I have seen how Nigerians have rallied behind and supported me. Many Nigerians did not know who I was before this competition. I had about 2,000 followers on Instagram, but that number has now grown to tens of thousands.

I have seen the love and support, and I know that people genuinely believe we can make it happen this year. I worked hard behind the scenes even before competing at Miss Universe Nigeria, becoming a finalist or applying for the competition. I had already travelled to Thailand to receive training from one of the best runway coaches because I genuinely believe we can win.

Winning would make history for several reasons. On a personal level, I would become the seventh Black Miss Universe in the competition’s 75-year history. I would also be the first Nigerian to win the crown, as Nigeria has never won the competition.

In recent years, Miss Universe has changed some of its requirements, allowing women of any age to compete. Previously, the age limit was 28, and I am now 29. So, I would be the first queen to compete beyond the previous age restriction.

Tell us about your aspirations and resolve ahead of the competition.

I am deeply prayerful, and I am a believer. Only God has brought me this far, and only God can bring the crown. As a country competing in pageantry, we face many challenges because we are up against queens who are pageant veterans and have built significant followings through their successful participation in competitions.

I trust in God and in the preparation that has brought me this far.

With so much on your plate, what has kept you going?

I keep going because I understand my purpose, which is to advocate for and empower women and girls. Perhaps this comes from my mum, who is a strong woman and has spent her life caring for others. It may also have come from my sisters, but I believe I have a strong sense of sisterhood and connection with women and girls.

How confident are you about winning the competition?

I am extremely confident. I trust in the preparation I have undertaken, the character I have developed, the strength of my purpose and the faith that God has placed me on this path for a reason.

I know I have what it takes, and I am doing this for the right reasons. This journey has been years in the making, and I know it is going to be exceptional.

What comes next for you if you win?

One of my main goals when I joined this pageant was to bring women’s health education to every state and every school in Nigeria. I believe women and girls need this education, and it is important that they receive it early because it can help prevent diseases.

I would love to travel to more states and expand the work we have already been doing in Lagos, Edo and a few other places.

World.title: APC and The Ides of January 2027
World.content:
Joseph Ushigiale

The concept of democracy, even with its obvious limitations is one of the best system of government if well managed and implemented.

The freedom it bestows on an individual represented by his vote to chose who govern him and to remove same individual when he messes up is sheer bliss. This is especially in circumstances and situations where you have the institutional structures that guarantee that exercising your right will not be taken for granted. In other words, your vote counts.

So voters wait patiently for their representatives for an election year to roll by usually every four years. If a representative is standing for election, he presents a manifesto telling them how much he knows about where it hurts them and how an incumbent has failed them.

If he is an incumbent seeking reelection he will present his score card to convince the people how well he has represented them by the dividends of democracy he has attracted for their comfort and welfare.

The day for stocktaking in America was last Tuesday when Americans held their midterm elections. The Americans were quite unequivocal in expressing their disapproval over how their country was been run by administration.

It was a referendum on tariff regime, wars in Iran and Ukraine, immigration policy and necessity for ICE, relations with other countries of the world, the economy and the cost of living in the homes of every average American.

It was a big gamble by the Republicans and it cost them an arm and leg most especially control of Congress where the Democrats’ tremendous push back flipped sizable and historically red leaning states to blue.

The last time Democrats controlled both the House of Representatives and the Senate was from 2021 to 2023 under President Joe Biden. Before him Bill Clinton and Barack Obama did in their first terms.

With the democrats securing control of both chambers of Congress in a major political upset in the just concluded midterm elections, politics in Washington would head in a new trajectory.

I’ve taken time to go this length because our election is barely 90 days away but it seems there is more confusion than certainly. Can you imagine a US Judge nullifying the candidacy of a frontliner at the 11th?

It’s even more curious when the while the campaign council of the ruling party is being pelted with stones in some parts of the north a mammoth crowd of supporters poured out en masse to receive the presumptive opposition leader in Sokoto.

We have a lot to learn from democracy as it is practices in America. We must put the people first in any policy being formulated. This is because ultimately it’s the people who wear the shoes that know where it pinch. It’s not the leaders because they feel nothing.

For instance, take Obama and Clinton for example who were on campaign trail. None of them was on the ballot but they were concerned about their party, people and country.They were concerned bringing people back together, black, whites, Hispanics to unify a broken country.

Both of them have been there, especially Barack Obama a person of colour with roots in Kenya who surmounted all hurdles to emerge the President of the US and he secured an unprecedented second term.

Both of them had pedigrees and were in a position to speak candidly to the American people.

They didn’t ask that anyone should be disqualified or an opposition party opponent be shot dead as a Senator in Osun did. They addressed issues that were fundamental to their country, people and government. They referred to their legacies US vs Iran deal, Obamacare etc that were abandoned setting off the trend of conflicts over the Suez of Homutz which is the source of higher oil prices today.

The American people listened attentively and waited for last Tuesday to deliver their verdict. There is a big lesson there for the APC to learn if they choose to and it’s the voice of the silent majority who decided in speaking last.

There were permutations and predictions from pollsters who polled voters from different backgrounds, spoke to different sets of respondents all in the hope of gauging where the election pendulum would swing. Regrettably, it sent them on a wrong direction handing the least favoured party, the Democrats a handsome win.

We have seen almost all the governors empty into the ruling party but no one asked Democrats Governors to decamp to Republican party and providing security to protect campaign billboard is an absurdity and a first in Nigeria.

President Tinubu has placed the people last in his election strategy and governors in the forefront. In January when Nigerians shall march to their polling booths to vote, there will only be 31 governors representing 31 voters cards perhaps with their family and friends to vote. This number will hardly guarantee a win for the President even if he adds all members of his family. So why the decampment? Are the governors possessing magical powers enabling them to multiply votes mysteriously? We shall see how that pans out.

These are questions that need answers and clarity ahead of 2027. It’s also worth noting that today’s politician has scant regards for the sanctity of a vote. If a vote that puts you in power doesn’t count, does democracy count anymore?

There’s a need for the political class to avoid winners takes all syndrome and embrace the multiparty system democracy provides to broaden participation. Danger looms when the political space is closed to the majority giving advantage to privileged or favoured few.

The anger in the system can be linked to this. While government is asking Nigerians to sacrifice even the little advantage of fuel subsidy for the masses, its removal has remained the cornerstone or main policy thrust of this administration.

Meanwhile, those asking for sacrifice are visibly displaying opulence, driving in convoys financed by tax payers, flying in private jets with their families and living in fanciful houses paid for by tax payers.

Yet, Nigerians are wallowing in hunger and poverty and still debating for salary increase from N70,000 to N300000 while waiting for January 2027.

World.title: Shiloh Godson Gives Netflix’s ‘Ordinary People’ Its Eerie Pulse
World.content:
Godson’s score gives ‘Ordinary People’ more than a soundtrack, creating atmosphere, deepening characterisation and heightening suspense, revelation, tension, action and loss. Sunday Okobi writes

There are sounds. There are movie sounds. And there are tension-building soundtracks that grip viewers and keep them on their seats from beginning to end with unwavering focus. They can shift from drama to chaos, from serenity to suspense, just to prepare movie enthusiasts for danger before it unfolds on screen.

This is the feeling that lingers when you watch ‘Ordinary People’, the 2026 Nollywood whodunit series on Netflix.

Directed by Moses Inwang, the adrenaline-fuelled thriller features a stellar ensemble cast, which includes Ramsey Nouah, Adunni Ade, Jackie Appiah, Uche Montana, Sharon Ooja, Lasisi Elenu, among others. Yet one of the series’ most distinctive contributions comes from behind the scenes: a score that gives its unsettling world an eerie, unpredictable pulse.

That is where Shiloh Godson comes in. As a music composer, Godson created the series’ original score, using a blend of modern electronic and traditional elements across its eight episodes.

From confrontations to shocking revelations, the music shifts seamlessly, preparing viewers for the danger and suspense ahead. Rather than relying on piercing sounds, he balances symphonic arrangements, slow strings, high-energy chaos, and carefully placed sound effects to build anxiety and suspense.

For Godson, the musical direction emerged from conversations with Inwang about the contradiction at the heart of Tornado, an upright, principled man by day and a cold-blooded murderer by night.

In his briefing, Godson enthusiastically said: “We wanted the score to hold that contradiction. The religious elements needed to feel different from what audiences might expect. We wanted the music to be able to move in unexpected directions while the choral voices still carried that sense of spirituality.”

The choral passages did not immediately sound the way they do in the finished series. Godson added: “We recorded the choristers wailing. It sounded rather strange and somewhat uncomfortable, and we reshaped them in the studio until we got the refined unsettling tone that suits the production.”

The score also gives Tornado, known as Jonas and played by Nouah, a distinct sonic identity. When he reveals himself to Ofege, the first victim viewers see him attack, a low, swelling bass motif begins to gather momentum. It suggests control and calculation, while the surrounding voices hint at the layers concealed beneath his composed exterior.

“Jonas is meticulous and strategic. He plans everything,” Godson said, adding: “He’s like an onion: you keep peeling back layers before you understand who he really is. We wanted the music to reflect that gradual reveal, with the sound building as those layers come off.”

Another carefully measured buildup occurs when Tornado finally reveals himself to his boys at the creek. The reworked version of Sound Sultan’s ‘Motherland (Area Oh)’ is followed swiftly by a symphonic arrangement that evokes Africa and stirs a sense of homecoming. The transition is both familiar and chilling, giving the moment a recognisable musical signature.

“That was the right feeling. We wanted viewers to reminisce about the importance of home and how it feels to be home. Moses Iwang and his team also contributed a lot to the soundtrack,” Godson disclosed to this journalist during a virtual coffee meeting.

In contrast, Emilia, played by Sharon Ooja, is associated with a different musical energy. Her impulsive nature comes through in sharp, forceful hits that give her scenes a distinct texture, evoking danger, hysteria, and the possibility of complete breakdown.

The contrast extends to the action sequences. During the school shootout and escape in Episode 8, electric guitars cut through the score, used sparingly but with considerable impact. Godson describes the music as a collaborative effort, crediting Inwang with playing a substantial role in shaping it during the editing process.

The result is a score built less around a single signature tune than around distinct sonic identities: choral voices that unsettle, bass that gathers like a threat, and guitars that drive the action forward. It is also the work of a wider team, including HS Choir PH, Sharon Imoukhuede, Miriam Shongotola, Olaonipekun Oluwafem, and Sneezemankind.

In a crime drama shrouded in secrets, the music does more than accompany the action. It gives viewers another way to sense what is coming and what remains concealed.

The series also demonstrates a notable level of sophistication in its sound design, particularly during its crime scenes. During gun battles between the police and Tornado’s criminal gang, for instance, viewers can almost feel their heart racing as the music tempo heightens when the armed officers stealthily make their way into the buildings without the soundtrack resorting to exaggerated, pounding effects. The restraint makes the tension more convincing, allowing silence and subtle sound cues to do some of the work.

Power, fame, lust, and wealth drive many of the characters’ actions, leading to domestic violence, kidnapping, financial disputes, murder, and confrontations with the police. Godson’s musical choices intensify these moments. They reinforce the characters’ motives and the consequences of their actions.

One striking example is when Detective Margaret enters the lair of Darey Laguda, played by Shawn Faqua. The soundscape shifts almost effortlessly as a chorus of female voices rises. It is difficult to tell whether the voices are wailing or singing, but it becomes clear that Laguda’s cover has been blown. Rather than relying on the more familiar use of songs in African screen storytelling, Godson transforms choral voices into an atmosphere suspended between the sacred and the sinister.

Through rising beats and carefully controlled shifts in tone, the score accompanies revelations about the secret lives of the rich and famous, as well as moments of trauma, celebration, deception, pain, anguish, and silence. These are no ordinary people – not simply because of their celebrity status or social standing, but because of the disturbing contrast between their respectable public personas and their sinister lives after dark.

Yet the soundtrack is not all crime, gunfire, and suspense. Romantic scenes offer brief departures from the explosive action, although even these moments can carry an undercurrent of impending doom. At times, the musical choices create an almost darkly comic effect, as though the soundtrack were warning a character to enjoy the romance now and face the consequences later.

By the final episode, Tornado’s meticulously constructed world begins to collapse when he sees the lifeless body of his wife and partner in crime, Chinelo (Dunni), on the floor. It is an unmistakable oh-oh moment. The pulse begins to dwindle, growing slower and slower, as the music holds viewers in the aftermath of the revelation.

Then the tension surges again! Through guitars and synths, Godson sustains the unease as Tornado reacts to Dunni’s death and the firebomb unleashes destruction. The sound intensifies the moment, carrying the emotional weight of the scene while driving the series towards its explosive conclusion.

Undoubtedly, Godson’s work gives Ordinary People more than a soundtrack. It creates an atmosphere, deepens characterisation, and shapes how viewers experience suspense, revelation, and loss. In the entire series, although appearances are deceptive and secrets thrive, the sound gives them a pulse to follow – and a warning that something is never quite as ordinary as it seems. It was worth the time investment!

World.title: A Logistics Lesson for INEC from America’s Midterm Elections
World.content:
By Adeola Akinremi

I saw the FEDECO elections firsthand, and what I remember most is the endless waiting by voters at the polling stations. Voters waited. Officials waited. Whole communities waited for election materials that were always on their way and never seemed to arrive. The frustration was real, and it had little to do with politics. It was about logistics.

More than four decades later, Nigeria has repeatedly rebranded its electoral management institution – from FEC to FEDECO, NEC, NECON and eventually INEC. Yet, despite the changes in names, structures and administrations, the underlying problems of electoral credibility, transparency and integrity remain stubbornly persistent. The name has changed; the problem has not.

Today, Nigeria is a far larger country. It has more than 176,000 polling units, and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it plans to deploy about 1.4 million ad hoc staff for the next general election. Yet the old complaint has outlived the old commission. Election materials still arrive late in too many places, and every late arrival raises the same uncomfortable question: whose vote was lost to the clock?

To his credit, the INEC chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, has said as much. In October, he inaugurated an Electoral Logistics Committee for the 2027 elections and declared that no Nigerian should be disenfranchised because materials came late. He has also argued that an election is only as strong as its logistics. With the polls less than three months away, the commission has time to answer one more serious question. It is the one I want to put this week.

How can an election management body guarantee that every vote is collected, protected, transported and counted on time, regardless of how remote or difficult the community is to reach?

That is the burning question on my mind for this edition. Riverine communities in the Niger Delta, island settlements, rural roads that fail in the rains, insecurity and sheer distance all complicate the movement of people and materials. An answer, or at least the outline of one, came from an unlikely place on November 3, during the American midterm elections.

In Los Angeles County, the Sheriff’s Department deployed eight helicopters, landing at seven helipads, to collect sealed ballot containers from places such as Lancaster, Palmdale and Van Nuys and fly them to the county’s central processing facility in the City of Industry. LAist, a news organization in Los Angeles reported that officials wanted to cut transport delays and to avoid giving communities closer to the centre an advantage in the timing of early results.

The helicopters are the visible part of a partnership between the Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, which runs elections, and the Sheriff’s Department, which supplies transport and security. The relationship itself is an old partnership. A 2012 report by electionline Weekly quoted a Registrar’s official saying the Sheriff’s Department had supported ballot transport from Catalina Island for more than 30 years, by boat or by aircraft depending on the weather. The election office chose the method. The Sheriff confirmed it three weeks before polling day.

The custody rules matter as much as the aircraft. Ballot containers are sealed and their contents recorded before they move. Departure times and container numbers are communicated ahead to the processing centre, and the numbers are checked again on arrival. No one is left alone with ballots or equipment.

Two things stand out. First, the election authority never surrendered its authority. The Sheriff provides a capability; the Registrar keeps the ballots, the process and the count. Second, the system does not depend on one mode of transport. Fog has diverted ballot helicopters in past Los Angeles elections, and ground routes carried on. Redundancy is part of the design. I found no evidence of a single countywide agreement governing all of this. What is documented is a long-running operational partnership with clearly defined roles, which is a more useful thing to copy than a document.

Los Angeles is not an outlier. In Hawaii, Maui County arranged charter flights with Kamaka Air to bring ballots from Molokai and Lnai, with sealed containers, signed handovers and election officials on board. The flights are procured in advance, not improvised on election night. In Arizona, Coconino County moved ballots out of Supai, the Havasupai village at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, by mule train, with riders from both major parties. In Ohio, the Erie County elections board, the Sheriff’s Office and the US Coast Guard share the job of bringing ballots back from Kelleys Island on Lake Erie, with seals checked and each transfer recorded in the presence of representatives of both parties.

Sky, canyon and lake. Three geographies, three different vehicles, one design: standing relationships with other public agencies, specialised transport planned in advance, and documented custody at every handover. That is the principle, and it travels. Nigeria no more needs helicopters for the Niger Delta than Arizona needed them for the Grand Canyon. It needs the architecture, with the transport matched to the terrain.

Here is what I am not saying. I am not asking INEC to learn from America. I am asking it to finish what it has already started.

INEC’s own review of the 2023 general election identified transportation, procurement, reverse logistics and security as areas needing improvement. The commission brought the National Union of Road Transport Workers, the National Association of Road Transport Owners and the Maritime Workers’ Union of Nigeria into the conversation. Its recommendations were specific: revise the memoranda of understanding with transport unions to deal with vehicle condition, driver control and the return of materials; work with the Federal Road Safety Corps on roadworthiness checks; enforce contractual penalties when providers fail; and strengthen supervision of transport agreements at the local government level. European Union observers, for their part, listed late deployment among the weaknesses of 2023.

These are not an outsider’s suggestions. They are INEC’s own findings. The question is whether they have become standing practice or remained entries in a report. A recommendation is not a reform, and a reform is not a practice until it has been budgeted, assigned and tested under pressure.

The new Electoral Logistics Committee and the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security give INEC a natural home for the work. What is missing is a formal framework that makes cooperation predictable. Call it an Election Logistics Partnership Framework, resting on four requirements.

First, written agreements that define who does what: INEC for planning and custody of materials; the Police for protection; the Road Safety Corps for roadworthiness; maritime agencies and boat operators for waterways; transport unions and operators for vehicles and drivers; emergency agencies for contingencies. Second, advance planning. Classify every polling unit by accessibility, match transport to terrain, contract it early and rehearse it.

Third, a standard chain-of-custody record for every movement of sensitive materials, with a unique reference number, container count, seal numbers, times of departure and arrival, and the names and signatures of the releasing and receiving officials, plus a formal incident report for any broken seal or unexplained delay. Fourth, public reporting and an independent post-election review, so that failures are counted as carefully as votes.

A word of caution. In Nigeria, the involvement of security agencies in handling election materials will always raise questions of neutrality, and rightly so. The American examples must not be read as an argument for giving security agencies more power over elections. In Los Angeles, the Sheriff moves the ballots; he does not count them. In Nigeria, INEC officials must remain responsible for materials throughout. Security personnel must protect without taking independent custody. Party agents and accredited observers should be able to witness the relevant handovers. And faster transport is no substitute for transparent collation and timely publication of results.

INEC does not need to buy helicopters or import American procedures. It needs to take its own findings, give them budgets, owners and deadlines, and build the partnerships that make them routine.

At the end of the day, democracy is measured not only by the right to cast a vote, but by a country’s ability to protect that vote and bring it home.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: adeola@hintells.com

World.title: Comparative Analysis of Nigeria’s Foreign Investment Dynamics
World.content:
Omoniyi Akinsiju

Nigeria’s external trade and payment position since 2024 has shifted from years of volatile, oil-dependent deficits to a multi-year streak of robust current account and trade surpluses.

Historical economic data from 2000 to 2026, sourced from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), and CEIC Data, validate the long-term structural evolution of Nigeria’s external balance. This trajectory demonstrates a shift from volatile, single-commodity dependence into a sustained multi-year streak of robust current account and merchandise trade surpluses.Between the years 2000 and 2014, a period described as the global commodity super-cycle, Nigeria maintained large external surpluses driven almost entirely by crude oil exports. Current account surpluses routinely averaged between 5% and 15% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). It reached a historical quarterly high of +$10.38 billion in Q2 2008 and peaked at over $29 billion annually in full year 2008. Sustained high global crude oil prices drove the surplus. We estimate that the accumulation of these surpluses between 2001 and 2008 was enough to prompt new developmental curves in a diversified Nigerian economy.

Where the Surplus Funds Went

Rather than direct the entirety of the commodity windfall into long-term industrial infrastructure and enable a diversified non-oil-based economy, the surplus capital was deployed by the administrations of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umar Musa Yar’adua and Goodluck Jonathan (1999 to 2015) into consumption-focused foreign reserve accumulation and a sovereign debt clearance, while developmental opportunities and advantages were ignored.

For context, we tracked the growth of Nigeria’s current accounts and reserves. Gross foreign reserves expanded from under $8 billion in 2000 to an all-time peak of $62 billion in September 2008; this provided short-term external shock absorption while Obasanjo’s administration, between 2005 and 2006, used approximately $12 billion of its accumulated reserves to clear a total of $30 billion in external debt owed to Paris Club creditors. This significantly lowered the sovereign debt burden.

To take advantage of the increased federation revenue, the Excess Crude Account (ECA) was established in 2004. The account peaked at $22 billion in 2008. In 2011, $1 billion was transferred from the ECA to set up the Nigeria Infrastructure Advisory Fund, Future Generations Fund, and Stabilisation Fund, all components of the Nigeria Sovereign Wealth Fund.

On the surface, the savings and debt clearance policies looked good, but the economy soon unravelled. Because the ECA lacked firm constitutional backing, State Governors frequently challenged the central government’s right to withhold oil revenues. Between 2008 and 2014, regular distributions to federal, state, and local government council areas slashed the ECA from $22 billion down to under $3 billion. The money so shared was utilised primarily for recurrent expenditure (public sector salaries, administrative overheads) rather than capital investments.

The then management of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) also used the surplus foreign exchange inflows to peg, or artificially support, the exchange rate, funding cheap dollars for non-oil consumer goods imports while rerouting billions of dollars in foreign exchange to subsidise imported Premium Motor Spirit (petrol). The trade surplus was effectively spent on imported fuel consumption rather than domestic refining.

Impact on the Larger Economy

While the windfall generated temporary GDP expansion, which averaged 6% to 8% growth annually, and expanded the country’s urban service sector like banking, telecommunications, and trade, it failed to alter Nigeria’s fundamental economic structure. Oil and gas continued to account for over 90% of export receipts and over 70% of government revenue throughout the super-cycle.

During that same period, crucial economic enablers such as national grid power, intermodal freight rail, critical roads and deep-sea ports remained severely underfunded. This drove up operational costs and constrained domestic manufacturing. Domestic refineries were left in disrepair. As a result, Nigeria spent a massive portion of its oil receipts importing refined petroleum products back into the country.

Because surpluses were spent or distributed rather than converted into self-sustaining infrastructure and industrial assets, the economy remained fully exposed to global oil price volatility. Thus, when crude prices crashed in late 2014, Nigeria immediately slid into a currency crisis and, by 2016, its first major recession in decades.

In summary, the windfall created short-term liquidity, but no effort was made to convert it into long-term capital assets, industrial output, or export diversification.

By the end of 2014, estimates of the population living in poverty in Nigeria ranged from 45% to 53%. This put the total number of extremely poor Nigerians between 80 million and 93 million in 2014.

Structural Volatility and Multi-Year Deficits (2015–2021)

Beginning in the last quarter of 2014, a combination of global crude price crashes, oil production disruptions, currency overvaluation, and soaring fuel import costs plunged Nigeria’s external balance into structural deficits. The country recorded consecutive annual current account deficits between 2019 and 2021. According to CBN Balance of Payments (BoP) data, the current account fell to -$17.0 billion (~-4.0% of GDP) in 2019 and -$15.8 billion in 2020. The quarter ending December 2019 recorded an all-time-low current account deficit of -$6.12 billion.

2023 – Present: Years of Reforms, Structural Turnaround & Multi-Year Streak:

Beginning in 2022 and accelerating through 2024 to 2026, FX market realignments, domestic refiner integration, and aggressive non-oil export expansion converted the external position into a multi-year surplus streak.

Our analysis found that the near four years of the Federal administration mark a record of consistent current account surpluses, underpinned by an aggressive strategy to not only drive FDI but also link it to domestic macroeconomic stability with a medium- to long-term microeconomic impact.

This structural pivot stems from bold, yet painful market corrections initiated in 2023. The corrections were driven primarily by the unification of the foreign exchange market and the elimination of the costly petrol subsidy.

While these policies initially triggered significant domestic inflation and currency depreciation, they successfully re-engineered Nigeria’s external balance sheets and attracted renewed global investor attention.

To understand the full scope of Nigeria’s capital recovery, it is crucial to analyse both where the money is flowing (Sector Breakdown) and the nature of the capital itself (Foreign Direct Investment – FDI vs Foreign Portfolio Investment- FPI).

Macro-Level FDI Inflows (Actualised Capital)

According to tracking data from the UNCTAD World Investment Report 2026, Nigeria’s actualised physical FDI flows experienced a sharp drop initially due to transitional volatility, followed by a substantial recovery. In 2023, actualised FDI settled at $1.87 billion. While this was technically an improvement from the historic low of 2022, the economy remained heavily constrained by active multinational divestments (such as exits by GSK and Unilever).

Again, in 2024, actualised inflows dipped slightly to $1.61 billion because investors adopted a “wait-and-see” approach while navigating intense Naira depreciation and early structural FX backlog clearance.

However, by 2025, inflows surged 148.1% to $4.01 billion. Backed by massive project-finance deals in the energy sector, this rebound returned Nigeria to Africa’s top five FDI destinations, major evidence of the success of the economic reforms.

When you combine FDI with portfolio equity and money market instruments, Nigeria’s total capital importation skyrocketed from $3.9 billion in 2023 to $23.22 billion in 2025.

Sector Breakdown: Where the Capital is Flowing to

Since 2023, foreign capital has shifted dramatically. While the oil sector is rebounding, non-oil sectors like digital infrastructure and manufacturing are attracting substantial shares of actualised inflows. The oil and gas sector, the rebound leader, accounts for roughly 42% of total inflows between 2025 and 2026. A major facilitating factor is the presidential directives that slashed contracting timelines from 36 months to less than 6 months, unlocking massive project financing such as the $2.4 billion Renaissance-Shell onshore acquisition.

The Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector accounted for 24% of inflows. Cross-border expansions in telecommunications, digital infrastructure, and data centres (e.g., Airtel Africa’s data centre expansions) dominated this segment. The manufacturing and industrial sector, meanwhile, accounted for about 18% of inflows. Key references include major cross-border manufacturing deals like the acquisition of Lafarge Cement by China’s Huaxin Cement and the multi-billion-dollar expansion of Indorama Petrochemicals.

The banking and finance sector, which is credited with 11% of the inflow, recorded an influx of foreign capital as Nigerian banks engaged in recapitalisation exercises to meet new CBN thresholds.

The visual breakdown of Nigeria’s total $23.22 billion overall capital importation by 2025 shows that, while portfolio investments and short-term debt instruments provided most of the immediate liquidity used to stabilise the Naira, physical FDI served as the slower, long-term foundation, as we observe a clear restructuring of the current account to surplus.

Restructuring the Current Account to Constant Surplus

The CBN’s strategy under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration has been clear: use high-yielding FPI to aggressively clear FX backlogs and defend the Naira in the short term, while structural reforms steadily rebuild investor trust for long-term FDI. While the surge in portfolio investment successfully boosted foreign reserves to over $55 billion, it came at the cost of high domestic borrowing rates for local businesses. But from our standpoint, as inflation begins to moderate, the focus is shifting toward converting these temporary portfolio flows into permanent, factory-to-market FDI.

Moving Capital from FPI into FDI

For nearly two years, foreign capital prioritised government debt and Treasury bills (FPI) over physical infrastructure (FDI) because short-term paper yielded safely above 25%. As yields on fixed-income securities compress in alignment with the 23% Monetary Policy Rate (MPR), the relative attractiveness of letting cash sit passively in bonds decreases.

Institutional capital and cross-border private equity firms will naturally begin migrating their asset allocations away from volatile money markets and into higher-yielding physical equity investments, infrastructure concessions, and greenfield corporate projects.

The Realignment of Domestic Venture Capital

During the high-interest cycle (where the MPR sat at 27.5%), local high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) and institutional investors preferred to lock up capital in risk-free government securities and Treasury bills, which yielded historic returns, but as yields on fixed-income instruments drop in response to the 23% MPR, pass-through returns on safe assets will compress. This dynamic will compel local asset managers and family offices to diversify back into alternative asset classes. Local startup equity will become highly attractive again as investors hunt for double-digit growth opportunities that outperform falling fixed yields.

This stability restores foreign investor confidence. Because the rate cut reflects genuine macroeconomic easing rather than a desperate stimulus, global VCs can, as a result, project startup exit valuations and cash flows with a much greater predictability.

How Surpluses Continue to Impact the Larger Economy

The persistent net trade and current account inflows have expanded gross foreign reserves from $45 billion to $55 billion by the third quarter of 2026. This provides the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) with over 14 months of import cover. This is because surplus FX liquidity reduced structural demand pressures in the official foreign exchange market, stabilising the local currency without relying exclusively on defensive interventions by the CBN.

In addition, instead of spending export receipts to import finished fuels, domestic refining retained value locally, reducing the fiscal deficit and converting Nigeria from a net importer into a net exporter of refined products across West Africa. Meanwhile, non-oil export receipts have continued to surge, led by solid minerals (gold, lead), agricultural exports (cashew nuts, cocoa beans, sesame seeds), and industrial chemicals (urea fertiliser to North America). Exports to Africa have increased significantly, with exports to ECOWAS trading partners, Togo, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, leading regional trade and boosting non-oil foreign currency earnings for local exporters.

Investor Confidence and Sovereign Ratings

The structural rebalancing of external accounts has supported a historic run on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX), pushing market capitalisation past landmark high thresholds. Improved external liquidity and manageable short-term debt ratios have led rating agencies such as Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s, and Fitch to upgrade Nigeria’s credit Outlook/Rating, lowering sovereign borrowing risk in international financial markets.

JP Morgan and Nigeria’s FDI

JP Morgan Chase’s move to secure a national merchant banking license in Nigeria marks a significant shift in West Africa’s corporate finance landscape. Transitioning from a representative office to a fully licensed merchant bank allows JP Morgan to extend beyond institutional coverage into trade finance, corporate lending, cross-border underwriting, and balance-sheet execution.

Though the expansion provides a strong endorsement of the Tinubu administration’s market-oriented reforms, its structural impact on Nigeria’s Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) must be critically appraised through both strategic opportunities and practical risks.

A major institutional barrier to FDI in West Africa is the cost of capital and the complexity of structuring project risk. With direct merchant banking capabilities, JP Morgan can underwrite large-scale energy infrastructure, telecommunications, and industrial projects, sharing risk with international consortiums.

A fully operational merchant bank lowers execution drags for multinational corporations entering Nigeria. It offers direct cross-border trade lines, structured commodity hedging, and syndicated offshore/onshore financing without relying on domestic intermediary banks.

Sovereign and corporate debt issuers in Nigeria gain direct access to global capital markets. This is just as the presence of the world’s largest investment bank validates Nigeria’s macro-stability narrative to global pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and private equity firms.

Current Account & Trade Surpluses

We note, however, that while macro-level metrics such as trade balances, external reserves, and current account balances have strengthened, the federal administration has continued, through policies and multiple interventions, to transmit improved macroeconomic stability to the real economy.

Indeed, corporate exporters and capital markets have benefited directly from FX availability. Local consumers and micro-enterprises continue to navigate the elevated cost of living associated with broader structural reforms. Nonetheless, we believe the national economy is closer than ever to breaking into micro-impact attributions.

-Akinsiju, PhD is the Chairman, ‎Independent Media and Policy Initiative (IMPI)

World.title: Spring tides tomorrow: Check the coastal tide times
World.content:
High and low tide times for South Africa’s coastal cities on Saturday. Image: Pexels

If you’re heading to the coast on Saturday, check the tide times before planning your activities.

Water levels change throughout the day, while wind, waves, swell and the shape of the seabed also affect conditions along the shore and at sea.

When will high and low tides occur on Saturday?

According to the South African Weather Service, spring tides bring higher high tides and lower low tides than usual.



These changes can affect swimming, surfing and fishing along the coast.

Higher tides may cover rocks and reefs, while lower tides expose more of the shoreline.

Beachgoers, anglers and other coastal visitors should check tide times and sea conditions before heading out.



New moon brings spring tides to the coast

Spring tides occur when the Sun, Moon and Earth align during a new moon or full moon.

The next new moon is expected on Monday, 9 November 2026.

As the Sun and Moon’s gravitational pulls combine, they create a greater difference between high and low tides, resulting in higher high tides and lower low tides than usual



Beachgoers should also watch out for:

Strong currents: Rip currents can pull swimmers away from the shore, even when the sea looks calm.

Rip currents can pull swimmers away from the shore, even when the sea looks calm. Unexpected waves: Larger waves can catch people off guard, particularly near rocks and tidal pools.

Larger waves can catch people off guard, particularly near rocks and tidal pools. Rising water levels: The incoming tide can quickly reduce the amount of beach available for walking or fishing.

The incoming tide can quickly reduce the amount of beach available for walking or fishing. Slippery rocks: Wet rocks and exposed reefs can make walking along the shoreline dangerous.

Check the latest weather and marine warnings before you head to the coast.

World.title: Johannesburg’s first family? Meet Helen Zille’s husband and kids
World.content:
Helen Zille is leading the Johannesburg mayoral race, as the Democratic Alliance (DA) has emerged as a frontrunner after this week’s local government elections.

The 75-year-old has previously helmed control of Cape Town, winning the 2008 World Mayor Award, which honoured her leadership and efforts to improve service delivery in the city.

IS HELEN ZILLE JOHANNESBURG’S NEXT MAYOR?

As it stands with the voter count, the DA is in a strong position to take control of Johannesburg. However, Helen Zille is not guaranteed the mayoralty.



After the IEC finalises the election results, the newly elected councillors will then vote for the mayor. For Helen to get the keys to the city, the DA will likely need to rally support from other parties, such as Action SA, to secure a majority in the council.

She will then need the majority of councillors’ votes to become Johannesburg’s next mayor.

MEET HER HUSBAND AND KIDS…

Helen Zille has spoken of receiving the support from her family, including husband, and two sons, in her bid to become Johannesburg mayor.



Helen is married to retired professor Johann Maree, who has a PhD in sociology from the University of Cape Town. The couple married in 1982.

ThrowbackThursday — my husband and I on honeymoon in 1982 pic.twitter.com/vLJ4JOJSRy — Helen Zille (@helenzille) October 9, 2025

They have two sons together: Paul and Thomas.



Paul, who married Gretl Visser in 2014, is a mathematics teacher and founder of Paper Video, an organisation that distributes educational resources to students around the country.

He’s also a member of Beams, a music band that has played at several of Cape Town’s hot spots. Paul gave his mother the nickname “GodZille” over her strict parenting style.

Thomas is a digital marketing manager and has worked for Showmax and CNBC Africa. He bears a striking resemblance to his mother.

Helen Zille is also a grandmother to Mila and Francois, the daughter and son of Paul and Gretl.

She is also a foster grandmother to children she took in from her domestic worker.

World.title: Thai national who tried to smuggle parrot eggs through OR Tambo gets hefty sentence
World.content:
Preliminary investigations indicated the eggs belonged to a parrot species protected under CITES. Image: PASA

In August, a 50-year-old man from Thailand was arrested at OR Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg for attempting to smuggle 50 protected parrot eggs out of South Africa.

The man was convicted and sentenced in the Kempton Park Regional Court this week. It followed a joint operation by the Green Scorpions and police.

Under a plea agreement, he was sentenced to a R500 000 fine or five years’ imprisonment.



The sentence was suspended for five years. This is subject to R300 000 being paid to the South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI).

The money will contribute towards the care of animals seized during law enforcement operations.

Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE), David Maynier, welcomed the conviction.

“This case is an example of what can be achieved with cooperation and coordination across law enforcement agencies,” he said.

Parrot eggs rescued after smuggling attempt

The suspect was arrested at OR Tambo airport in August this year after attempting to smuggle 50 endangered parrot eggs out of the country.

Customs officials discovered the eggs concealed inside a homemade incubator bag carried as hand luggage.



The arrest followed an intelligence-driven operation involving the DFFE, SAPS Crime Intelligence and Border Police.

SANBI staff subsequently stepped in to care for the seized eggs. Despite the conditions in which they were transported, many successfully hatched. The chicks received intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival.

Preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs may belong to parrot species protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

Maynier said the institute’s expertise had also been vital in securing the conviction.

“The Court’s ruling that funds must be paid to SANBI is welcomed, and the DFFE will be pursuing similar requests in other cases where wildlife is confiscated,” he added.

Arrest warrant issued in separate case

The case came just weeks after another Thai national was arrested at the same airport in connection with an even larger suspected parrot egg smuggling operation.

In July, a 23-year-old Thai national was detained at OR Tambo after authorities discovered 418 parrot eggs in his possession.

The two incidents have heightened concerns about South Africa’s role in international wildlife trafficking.

“These arrests highlight the growing sophistication of transnational wildlife trafficking networks,” the environment ministry said.

According to the DFFE, the Green Scorpions will continue the investigation into the wider trafficking network with the support of other countries and international organisations.

World.title: NASA looks to NSRI for future astronaut rescue operations
World.content:
The NSRI could one day play a vital role in rescuing astronauts off the Cape coast. Image via Facebook @SeaRescue

For the first time in the National Sea Rescue Institute (NSRI)’s 59-year existence, the organisation could potentially play a vital role in rescuing NASA astronauts.

According to the NSRI, NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) is developing contingency plans for emergency situations – such as a launch abort – when astronauts return from future Artemis missions to the Moon.

As such, the famed space agency is assessing several potential recovery areas worldwide – including Cape Town.



NSRI MEETS NASA REPS

NASA representatives recently paid a “surprise” visit to Cape Town, whereby they made contact with the NSRI at very short notice, explained Charlz Maritz, NSRI Head of Operations.

“Our understanding is that the NASA team had heard about the NSRI as a potential maritime rescue resource while in South Africa and wanted to learn more about our capabilities,” he said. “It is encouraging to know that the NSRI remains highly regarded when it comes to maritime rescue and safety around our coast.

“At the heart of it, it is still about saving lives in difficult conditions and coordinating an effective response.”

The reps also took the opportunity to meet with local trauma facilities. In doing so, they assessed their emergency medical capabilities on their visit to the Mother City.

WHAT NSRI RESCUE WOULD ENTAIL

The meeting between the NSRI and NASA’s representatives saw the parties discussing the former’s “potential role in locating, reaching and recovering astronauts and specialist rescue personnel at sea.”

In several emergency scenarios, if an Orion spacecraft were to abort eight minutes from launching from the state of Florida, it could splash down off the Cape coast.



A launch abort could see a spacecraft splashing down on the Cape coast, one of many potential recovery areas worldwide. Image: Pexels

Should astronauts get injured and cannot await a response from NASA or the US Department of Defence recovery teams, the NSRI – so long as the location is within operational capabilities – could initiate an immediate rescue. Moreover, they could assist in transporting astronauts and specialist rescuers back to shore to receive medical attention.

However, said Maritz, logistical issues – specifically, the distance between the splashdown and the coast – could severely limit the NSRI’s range and time at sea.

Additionally, astronaut recovery involves specialised medical, technical, safety and security procedures. As such, the NSRI’s primary role would be carrying out maritime rescue, while NASA’s specialist teams would oversee spacecraft-specific requirements.

OTHER FACTORS TO CONSIDER

NASA representatives also briefed the NSRI about other factors, including:

How the Orion spacecraft would behave in the event of an emergency abort.

Astronaut injuries that could occur following a harder-than-normal splashdown.

Providing responders with technical guidance regarding potential hazards and safe access to the capsule, along with relevant medical information for hospitals.

What’s more, they assessed the medical and rescue support available in the highly unlikely event of spacecraft ditching occurring shortly after launch.

This assessment entails visiting Cape Town and several other countries situated along the West African seaboard.

A NEW FRONTIER IN MARITIME RESCUE

All in all, it sounds like the visit was productive. This could give South African organisations like the NSRI a chance to contribute to space-related matters in the future. Plus, as Maritz noted, it also shows how highly they’re valued by the likes of NASA for their maritime rescue operations.

In other news, over 17 000 rooibos plant seeds are being primed for an upcoming space mission to the International Space Station.

World.title: Gayton open to DA coalition: ‘We are vying for power’
World.content:
Gayton McKenzie has expressed interest in forming a coalition with the DA. Images via Facebook

Patriotic Alliance president Gayton McKenzie has expressed interest in working with the Democratic Alliance in a coalition government, despite claiming that he “despises” the political party.

The PA has gained significant ground in the Western Cape and Northern Cape and has emerged as the largest party in Prince Albert, securing 5 out of 10 council seats.

The outspoken leader has also called on his party members to “accept defeat graciously”, after losing two wards in Eldorado Park, Johannesburg



GAYTON MCKENZIE OPEN TO DA COALITION

Speaking at a media briefing at the IEC national results centre, Gayton McKenzie revealed that the PA’s next agenda was to discuss the way forward on coalition talks, particularly in Prince Albert in the Western Cape, where the party won 5 out of 10 council seats.

The PA’s mayoral candidate for Prince Albert Municipality is Arnold MacKay.

Results revealed that the DA won 4 seats, while the ANC secured just one.



He said: “We don’t like the DA, let me be frank. I despise them. But we will work with them because it’s not about me; it’s about the leadership of the PA

“What the leadership decides on Monday, we will work with anyone. If the AWB still existed, we would have worked with them. It’s about our people”.

Gayton responded to claims that both he and PA Deputy-President were after political power, even at the expense of their personal feelings.



He continued: “We are vying for power. Don’t let people lie to you; politicians love power. People say McKenzie loves power, yes, of course. I’m a retired businessman; I’ve made my money. If I didnt love and want power, why would I put myself in politics”

Apart from Prince Albert, the PA emerged as the second-largest party in George, behind the DA, and third in Kannaland, behind the DA and ICOSA.

WATCH: PA leader Gayton McKenzie says he is willing to consider working with the DA in coalition arrangements for the benefit of society, despite admitting that he hates the party.



McKenzie says he is prepared to ensure a smooth working relationship in metros where the two… pic.twitter.com/C8KlrdtaUo  November 6, 2026

‘ACCEPT DEFEAT GRACIOUSLY’

Meanwhile, Gayton McKenzie has called on PA members to “accept defeat graciously”, after losing wards 17 and 18 in Eldorado Park.

The 51-year-old claimed that he had been “inundated with conspiracy theories and allegations” about the party’s “shocking loss of both wards”.

He shared in a Facebook post: “I hereby wanna make it public that we accept defeat in both Wards and wanna congratulate the DA. We should not be sore losers.



“The people made their choice, and instead of blaming the people, we should go and do some introspection. The numbers we had were totally wrong.”

World.title: City bemoans cable theft near ‘unlawfully-occupied’ land in trendy Cape Town suburb
World.content:
The vandalism and theft has also impacted MyCiTi bus operations in the area. Image: CoCT

The City of Cape Town says repeated cable theft and vandalism has cost taxpayers around R8 million in Lower Woodstock.

The damage has targeted electrical infrastructure in and around the Tide Street Substation. Some of the equipment was brand new.

The City says the incidents are linked to criminal activity near the “unlawful occupation” of Transnet-owned land, on the fringes of Lower Woodstock.



The neighbourhood has undergone significant gentrification in recent years. It is now home to coffee shops, bars, restaurants, supermarkets, art galleries and the popular Old Biscuit Mill market.

The City warns that the damage poses a threat to electricity supplies for residential and commercial customers in the area. The latest incident was reported on 2 November 2026.

Some damaged medium-voltage cables also remain unfixed. This is because shacks have been built over them, making repairs difficult.



“This situation is unacceptable, dangerous to the perpetrators and surrounding communities and a complete waste of public funds, as the damage has to be fixed repeatedly at great cost,” the City of Cape Town said in a statement.

Cable theft impacts electricity infrastructure and MyCiTi services

The targeted infrastructure includes substations, cables, switchgear, control panels and transformers.

Both low- and medium-voltage equipment have been affected.



Cable theft and vandalism has also impacted MyCiTi operations and infrastructure in the area.

The City noted that streetlights along the MyCiTi route from the Culemborg Safe Spaces Shelter to Paarden Eiland remain out of order as a result of the damage.

The municipality says the situation is “completely unsustainable,” with the estimated R8 million in damage excluding labour and other repair-related costs.



City monitoring area amid ongoing eviction battle

All recent and historical incidents have been reported to SAPS for investigation.

City law enforcement is also monitoring the area. Meanwhile, officials are exploring ways to better protect electrical infrastructure.

The land occupation has also become the subject of an ongoing legal battle.



Transnet secured an eviction order, but occupants appealed the ruling to the Supreme Court of Appeal. This has suspended the execution of the order.

The City and Transnet are appealing the ruling, citing risks to public safety, service delivery and electricity supplies to residential and commercial customers.

The City says it will continue exploring anti-theft and vandalism measures across the metro.
