World.title: Hajduk’s Perfect Conference League Start Ends With 1-0 Loss to Lincoln
World.content:
Hajduk suffered their first European defeat of the season on Thursday night, beaten 1-0 by Gibraltar champions Lincoln Red Imps in the third round of the Conference League league phase. The only goal came in the 89th minute, when a header struck the post and rebounded into the net off Dennis Hadžikadunić.

It was a jarring result after Hajduk’s perfect start, with wins over Ajax and Thun. Lincoln, who had yet to take a point in the competition, won without registering a single shot on target.

Lineups

Lincoln Red Imps: Hankins; Nano, Rutjens, Cardozo, Eersteling; García, Mandi, Lopes, Torrilla, Toledano; Gómez

Hajduk: Silić; Hrgović, Hadžikadunić, Van Hoorenbeeck, Acapandié; Fayad, Del Moral; Šotiček, Dalisson, Bamba; Šego

Hajduk were without Adrion Pajaziti, Ivica Ivušić, Leander Dendoncker and Roko Brajković, while Lincoln had a full squad.

Match report

Hajduk quickly took control with a high press that forced plenty of errors from the hosts. The fast pitch caught Hajduk out at times. In the 10th minute, Bamba tried to send Šotiček through, but the pass ran away from the winger. Three minutes later, Bamba won the ball and charged towards goal, only for his attempted pass across to Šotiček to be blocked.

Dalisson went close in the 17th minute with a shot from around 20 meters that flew just past the bar. Lincoln’s first chance forward came in the 22nd minute, when Silić comfortably gathered Nano’s cross. Šego then tried one of his trademark free kicks from a tight angle in the 27th minute, but sent it over.

By the half-hour mark, the game was being played almost entirely in Lincoln’s half, and Rutjens was booked in the 30th minute. The hosts’ first real counter-attack came a minute later, but Acapandié reacted well to clear in his own box.

Hajduk’s best move of the half came in the 40th minute. Šego headed down a long ball, and Dalisson met it with a good volley, but again it went over. Just before the break, a run from Bamba through the Lincoln defense ended with a Fayad shot that was blocked. Hajduk dominated the half but went in at 0-0 without a single shot on target.

Neither side made changes at the break. Kike Gómez was booked in the 49th minute for another heavy challenge, and two minutes later, Lincoln right-back Eersteling landed awkwardly on his shoulder and needed treatment. He eventually made way for Álvarez.

Lincoln began to find openings. In the 53rd minute, Toledano was well placed around ten meters out, but Fayad nicked the ball off him before he could shoot. Šotiček was booked for diving in the 58th minute, and Bamba followed five minutes later for a foul on Gómez. In the 64th minute, Hajduk survived two dangerous moments. First, a Lincoln player missed the target from close range, then Silić came off his line in time to cut out a dangerous pass.

García made a double change in the 68th minute, bringing on Martin for Šego and Marešić for Van Hoorenbeeck. Dalisson tried his luck from distance again in the 72nd minute without hitting the target, and three minutes later, Hajduk wasted their clearest chance yet. Šotiček was left alone ten meters out after a rebound, with time to pick his spot, but failed to find the target.

Livaja replaced Dalisson in the 76th minute, and Hadžikadunić sent an overhead kick high over the crossbar two minutes later. In the 80th minute, Torrilla was booked for stopping Šotiček on a three-on-two counter, and Marešić put the resulting free kick over.

Hajduk’s only shot on target came in the 85th minute. Livaja chested down a ball from a corner and struck it at goal. García then sent on Huram and Šutalo for Šotiček and Bamba.

Then came the blow. In the 89th minute, Nano swung in a free kick, and Christian Rutjens rose highest in the Hajduk box. His header came back off the post, struck Hadžikadunić and went in. Six minutes of stoppage time were added, and Hajduk threw everything forward, but there was no way back.

It was Lincoln’s first win of the Conference League campaign, played in front of 1,309 spectators. Hajduk stay on six points, and in both previous seasons under the new format, seven points have been enough to finish in the top 24. They host Sint-Truiden on November 26 and Nordsjælland on December 10, before closing the league phase away to Midtjylland on December 17.

World.title: British Arrivals in Croatia Set to Increase in 2027 Following WTM London
World.content:
November the 5th, 2026 – British arrivals in Croatia are looking very likely to increase throughout 2027 as the country wows at the WTM in London.

The World Travel Market (WTM) is traditionally held in London at the beginning of November, and it’s one of the largest and most important tourism fairs in the world. Naturally, the Croatian National Tourist Board presented the overall Croatian tourism offer, and Slobodna Dalmacija reports that the delegation was led by the Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina and HTZ director Kristjan Staničić. The Croatian stand’s offer was presented by 32 co-exhibitors.

the uk is one of croatia’s most important source markets

“The signals from the British market are extremely positive for Croatia; the UK is one of the country’s most important source markets, from which we continuously achieve very good results, and British guests are among those with the highest average daily spending in Croatia.

Precisely for that reason, we’re using this appearance at the WTM also for a series of meetings with leading British tour operators, airlines and other partners, with special emphasis on strengthening air connectivity, further growth of tourist traffic and development of cooperation in 2027. Research of the British market shows that guests are paying more and more attention to the quality of the offer and value for money, and are looking for trips outside the main summer months, shorter city breaks and authentic experiences.

It’s exactly these trends that are fully in line with the direction in which we’re developing Croatian tourism – towards higher quality and competitiveness, a more diverse offer and more even tourist activity throughout the whole year. Our goal is to additionally strengthen Croatia’s position on the British market, but also to ensure that the further development of tourism brings greater value to our destinations, the economy and local communities,” Minister Glavina stated.

from huge airlines to travel agencies

During the first day of the fair meetings were held with representatives of partners and organisations such as Jet2.com & Jet2Holidays, EasyJet Holidays, British Airways, TravelZoo, Love Holidays, the British Association of Travel Agents (ABTA), CBS travel, Travel Weekly and others. Key topics were previous activities and results, and certain partners are also announcing additional expansions in their programmes towards Croatian destinations. The above is best confirmed by the latest ABTA trends research, according to which demand for travel on the British market is still strong despite the rise in the cost of living, geopolitical uncertainties, disruptions in air traffic and climate change.

As many as 88 percent of respondents went on at least one holiday during the previous 12 months, which is one percentage point more than the year before and equal to the result from 2019. An important indicator of the research is the position of Croatia, which is in 13th place on the list of world destinations that British travellers plan to visit in the next 12 months, which confirms the competitive position of our country on the important UK market.

research conducted by tomas

“The British market is extremely important for Croatian tourism given that it is a country that enters the top 10 markets from which Croatia achieves the highest tourist traffic, and the recently published results of the TOMAS research show that Brits are the second guests by spending.

On the UK market, we’re also observing an interesting change, which opens additional potentials for Croatia as well, and that is city break tourism, which has become the most popular form of holiday for British guests. Croatia is an interesting destination for them in that context due to its proximity, so we will carry out investments and activities with the aim of further strengthening air traffic towards Croatian destinations also during 2027, and the priority remains the further strengthening of the quality of the overall tourism offer,” director Staničić stated, adding that Croatia has a stable position on the market, which was also confirmed by numerous partners during the talks.

top destinations

Positive trends from the UK market are also indicated by the results of tourist traffic, that is, data from the eVisitor system, according to which from this market in our country during the first 10 months 841 thousand arrivals (+2%) and 4.1 million overnight stays (+1%) were achieved. In this, Britons achieved the most overnight stays in Dubrovnik-Neretva and Split-Dalmatia counties, and looking by destinations, in Dubrovnik, Split, Konavle, Župa Dubrovačka, Rovinj and Zadar.

“Our partners on the British market recognise Croatia not only as a summer destination, but as somewhere that carries high value, authenticity and exceptional diversity. We’re particularly pleased by the fact that British travel organisers are actively expanding their programmes, which directly affects the extension of the main part of the tourist year. British travellers today more than ever are looking for authentic experiences, top gastronomy, preserved nature and rich cultural heritage. Our focus on the promotion of sustainable tourism and the offer outside the summer season perfectly resonates with the trends on the UK market, where younger generations and experienced travellers are paying more and more attention to the ecological and social responsibility of the destination,” believes Bisera Fabrio, director of the HTZ Representative Office in London.

croatia’s incredible food and wine scene

The complete presentation of Croatian eno-gastronomy was complemented by a presentation and tasting of Croatian wines, held as part of the Croatian stand in cooperation between the Croatian National Tourist Board and the Croatian Chamber of Economy. Croatia presented itself within the exhibition stand with a recognisable visual identity, whose panels and video walls will be decorated with multimedia content connected with the new promotional video “Croatia – I hear it’s beautiful” with the one and only John Malkovich taking the main role.

World.title: Court upholds school's request for an earlier start to the day against parents' wishes
World.content:
The start time for school classes is set by a government regulation, under which classes generally begin at 9 a.m. or later. The regulation allows schools to make exceptions and start classes earlier, but not before 8 a.m.

Classes at Kõrveküla Basic School have started at 8 a.m. in previous years and the school continued this practice during the current academic year.

The central issue in the court dispute was whether Kõrveküla Basic School had grounds to justify starting classes earlier than the time stipulated in the government regulation and whether the school had weighed the relevant interests when making its decision.

The parents who filed the complaint emphasized the importance of children's well-being and mental health, arguing that an earlier start to the school day would make it impossible to ensure students got enough sleep. They maintained that there were no circumstances justifying an exception and that the school's decision was primarily based on transportation arrangements and budget considerations.

Tartu Administrative Court disagreed with these arguments. According to the court, whether exceptional circumstances exist must be assessed based on the specific characteristics of the school and the surrounding area, taking into account factors such as transportation arrangements, differences between sparsely and densely populated areas, the size of the school, its distance from a major regional center and local infrastructure.

The court found that any decision to start the school day before 9 a.m. as an exception to the general rule must take into account the specific characteristics of the school and the surrounding area, transportation options and the size of the school.

In the case of Kõrveküla Basic School, the court considered it important to take into account the interests of students living both near the school and farther away in sparsely populated areas, as well as families' differing transportation options. The court also noted that starting the school day later would mean ending it later, potentially affecting students' opportunities to participate in extracurricular activities and reducing the time available in the evening to spend with family and friends, do homework and rest.

The administrative court found that circumstances justifying an earlier start to classes existed in the case of Kõrveküla Basic School.

According to the court, the local government's obligation to arrange transportation to and from school for basic school students also had to be taken into account. The court found that an earlier start time could be justified by the need to provide school transportation and equal access to education for children living farther away, while avoiding unreasonable and costly duplication of public transportation routes.

The court also considered the need to use local government budget funds efficiently to be an exceptional circumstance.

The court found that the school had not overlooked students' mental health when making its decision. It noted that, in addition to getting enough sleep, students' mental health is significantly affected by the structure of the school day and their families' overall daily routines.

World.title: Ukrainian citizen sentenced to prison in Estonia for migrant smuggling
World.content:
A Pärnu court sentenced a 37-year-old Ukrainian citizen to a year and ten months in prison for smuggling migrants into Estonia, with expulsion and an entry ban to follow.

On October 4, police detained Oleksandr Suvorov in Mäeküla, Järva County, where four people who had entered Estonia illegally were found in his vehicle: one Algerian citizen and three Somali citizens.

Under an expedited procedure, Pärnu District Court sentenced Suvorov to one year and ten months in prison, with two months to be served immediately.

The remaining sentence was suspended for a probationary period of two and a half years, provided he commits no further intentional crimes.

Estonian police stopped Oleksandr Suvorov's car in Järva County. October 2026. Source: PPA

After serving his term, Suvorov will be ordered to leave the country and barred from reentering Estonia for five years.

Under Estonian law, anyone bringing a foreign national across the border illegally can face up to three years in prison, or up to seven years if the foreigner's health or life is put at serious risk.

World.title: Estonia mulls additional support as competition for EU research grants intensifies
World.content:
Estonian Research Council is considering expanding support for applicants who narrowly miss out on EU funding as, under current funding plans, only about one in 20 applicants would receive a European Research Council Starting Grant.

The European Research Council (ERC) received 7,710 applications in its Starting Grant call, which closed in October, up 60 percent from a year earlier. At the same time, the planned budget for the call fell from €705 million to €594 million. While 421 projects were selected for funding in the previous round, under current plans there would be enough money for approximately 373 grants next summer.

ERC grants are among the most prestigious research funding instruments and are also considered a mark of international recognition for scientific excellence. Starting Grants, for example, generally provide researchers with up to €1.5 million over five years to launch independent research projects or establish their own research groups.

However, eligibility for Starting Grants was expanded this year. Previously, researchers could apply between two and seven years after completing their doctorates, but for the 2027 call, applications were accepted immediately after doctoral graduation and for up to 10 years afterward.

According to Kristiina Tõnnisson, head of the Estonian Research Council (ETAg), such a low success rate raises questions for researchers about whether the time and money spent preparing applications are worth the investment.

"When we look at the system as a whole and consider how much time and energy is spent across Europe, there is a systemic problem. However, it is important to clarify that this is currently a preliminary budget and evaluations are underway. The final budget for the call could still increase," she explained.

Tõnnisson said Estonian researchers have been successful in securing prestigious grants, particularly considering Estonia's small population in the European context. The success rate for applications across all ERC grant categories under the current Horizon Europe research framework program has been approximately 7 percent. There are currently 17 active ERC-funded research projects in Estonia. She therefore encourages Estonian researchers to continue applying for ERC grants while also considering other European funding opportunities.

Mari Moora, vice rector for research at the University of Tartu and a former member of an ERC evaluation panel, also believes researchers with strong ideas should apply for Starting Grants. "If you have a good, original idea, please put it in writing and apply, despite the increase in the number of applications," she said.

According to Moora, the rise in application numbers has not been accompanied by an increase in their average scientific quality. For example, during the recently concluded Starting Grant evaluation round, she had to review significantly more applications than before that, in her assessment, may have been largely written by artificial intelligence. She believes AI is also a major factor behind the sharp increase in applications.

"The reason I would say that 60 percent was AI-generated text is that the material was very uninteresting, of poor quality and lacked original ideas. So my argument would be that a good, original idea presented in a well-written application has roughly the same chance of securing funding as in previous years," she explained from an evaluator's perspective.

Burden on evaluators

The workload faced by evaluators was already a concern for the ERC in the spring, when the council planned to extend the waiting period before applicants who received lower scores could apply again. However, following opposition from the research community, the ERC decided to retain the existing restrictions on resubmissions for Starting, Consolidator and Advanced Grants for the 2027 calls.

"The issue is broader because it affects not only the ERC, but the Estonian Research Council is facing the same challenge. The number of applications we receive is also constantly growing and we are trying to maintain quality. If the application success rate falls below 15 percent, something in the system needs to change. We are relatively close to that threshold and are already looking at the best approach and whether anything can be changed," Kristiina Tõnnisson said.

"At the Estonian Research Council, every project has three evaluators, which requires an enormous amount of resources," Tõnnisson added. She said research funding organizations are discussing, among other things, whether fewer expert reviews could be required for each application. They are also considering whether interviews in the final round contribute enough to the decision-making process to justify the time they take.

One option described by Tõnnisson would be to have AI rank applications and leave the bottom third of the rankings without expert review. Another possibility would be to introduce a lottery system: Evaluators would select the strongest applications, and funding recipients would then be chosen by lottery from among projects that are difficult to distinguish on merit. "All these different options are being considered by research funding organizations across Europe," Tõnnisson said.

To reduce the workload of evaluators, Mari Moora suggested checking whether applications contain accurate references and whether the cited sources actually exist before proceeding to a substantive evaluation. She had also encountered references to nonexistent sources in applications she reviewed.

However, Moora sees a risk in entrusting AI with evaluating the scientific merits of applications, warning that it could favor familiar ideas over novel ones. "AI can only evaluate what it knows. It might start discriminating against original ideas," she said.

Additional support for researchers

The Estonian Research Council already provides support to Estonian researchers who narrowly miss out on prestigious European grants. For example, researchers who reach the second evaluation stage of the ERC Starting Grant competition, receive an A grade but fail to secure funding can apply for bridge funding for up to 18 months.

According to Tõnnisson, increased competition has prompted ETAg to consider extending this support to researchers who receive a B grade. The agency is assessing how much the expansion would cost and whether it could be financed through the state budget or European Union structural funds. No decision has yet been made. "This still needs to be discussed at the political level and with the relevant stakeholders," Tõnnisson said.

She said bridge funding can determine whether a researcher disappointed by a funding decision remains in academia at all. "One researcher specifically told us that without the ERC bridge grant, they would definitely have left academia and taken another job," Tõnnisson said.

Moora believes a greater risk for Estonia than competition for Starting Grants is the possibility that access to European funding measures designed to strengthen research capacity could be reduced in the next budget period. She is also concerned about how much structural funding Estonia will allocate to research and higher education in the future.

"Research funding around the world is declining somewhat due to various political and social factors. Under current plans, research funding in Estonia is also set to decline. We still have a couple of years to change those plans, as no final decisions have been made, but the risk is there," Moora explained.

The Starting Grant call that closed in October still falls under the European Union's current budget period. EU member states are aiming to reach a political agreement on the next long-term budget by the end of 2026. If they succeed, the budget for the next Horizon Europe research program should become clear during 2027, along with more details about funding for the European Research Council. The new budget period begins January 1, 2028.

World.title: Estonia allows banks to suspend suspicious payments to combat internet fraud
World.content:
Banks recently gained the right to temporarily suspend suspicious payments and intend to start exercising that right. Meanwhile, fraud involving cash withdrawals has increased.

Last year, people in Estonia lost nearly €30 million to scammers. Only a few percent of victims managed to recover the money they lost. The Riigikogu has now passed a law allowing banks to temporarily suspend suspicious payments, communicate with the police and share information with other financial institutions.

Sandra Horma, head of fraud prevention at the Estonian Banking Association, said the change may not initially be welcomed by all customers, as people are generally convinced they want to go through with their transactions. She explained that banks want to protect people in precisely those situations where it is clear to the bank that a customer is communicating with a scammer.

Unusually large amounts

A bank can intervene, for example, when an unusually large sum is being transferred to a new recipient. However, banks cannot intervene in every situation.

For example, cash withdrawals and the use of cash began increasing significantly in 2026. "It was very difficult to do anything at bank branches," Horma acknowledged. She said there have also been cases where people have claimed they need to sell their apartments because they are moving to Russia to receive medical treatment.

In October, the European Court of Justice ruled that if a scammer makes a money transfer without the victim's consent, the bank must also bear responsibility and refund the money to its customer. Although the ruling is considered a landmark decision, legal experts do not expect it to lead to an increase in compensation payments in Estonia.

Banks not responsible if customer trusts scammers

Attorney Ksenia Kravtšenko said that if a customer receives a phone call, enters their security credentials and hands them over to a scammer, the bank does not consider the transaction an unauthorized payment because the customer has placed their trust in someone they should not have trusted.

Just a few months ago, Estonia was considering a measure to better prevent fraud that would stop people from entering Smart-ID PIN codes while on a phone call. Although the solution is now ready, the plan was abandoned because customers prefer convenience over security.

Kalev Pihl, the creator of Smart-ID, explained that when a group of friends gets together and decides to buy tickets, they need to make or authorize payments. "If they were on a WhatsApp or Messenger call at the same time, the call would be disconnected. They wouldn't be able to use those same calling services to carry out the transactions," he explained.

Pihl acknowledged that he had identified more such use cases than he initially expected.

World.title: Defense official: Russia is stepping up attacks on civilian infrastructure
World.content:
With front lines largely unchanged, Russia is intensifying long-range strikes on civilian infrastructure, Estonian Defense Ministry official Gert Kaju said Friday.

Both Ukraine and Russia are preparing for talks in Abu Dhabi, but Kaju, director of the Defense Readiness Department at the Ministry of Defense, said statements made by both sides leave little reason to expect a major breakthrough.

He noted that the results of this Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S., in which Democrats flipped both the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives, are unlikely to change American diplomatic efforts either.

"If anything, we can expect the U.S. to increase pressure on both sides to make concessions and show at least some progress in negotiations," Kaju continued. "But neither side looks to be ready to do so."

On the battlefield, Russian forces have made little progress and fighting along the front has largely stabilized. Russian casualties remain high, however, and Moscow has stepped up long-range strikes to compensate for its lack of success on the ground.

"It's primarily civilian sites that have been targeted," Kaju said, adding that a recent ceasefire in Oleshky had ended and Russian forces had resumed hostilities in the Kherson region.

The past week has seen around 200 clashes a day, with Russian troops facing around 2,000 losses a day.

"At one point last week, Russian losses were estimated at more than 2,500 in a single day, making it one of the deadliest days, if not the deadliest, for Russian forces in recent months," Kaju said.

Ukraine disrupting Russian combat prep

Weekly losses are estimated at around 15,000. The front line, however, has barely budged.

The defense official attributed the high casualties in part to Ukraine's effective use of medium-range unmanned systems, which have allowed it to strike deeper into Russian rear areas in occupied territory and disrupt preparations for combat as well as operations near the front.

"So Ukraine has managed to somewhat blunt Russia's offensive capabilities with its medium-range strikes," Kaju noted.

Russia's main offensive efforts, meanwhile, remain focused on the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, with attacks continuing toward Huliaipole as well.

Kaju said Russia has intensified its long-range strikes, targeting anything they deem necessary, including civilian, social, medical, energy, logistics and transport facilities and infrastructure.

He cited a November 2 Russian airstrike on a school in Zaporizhzhia Oblast where humanitarian aid was being distributed. The attack killed 42 people and left 33 missing.

"This is one of the highest single death tolls the Russians have caused with such a bombing," the official noted.

The strike involved a 1,000-kilogram aerial bomb with a blast radius of up to 250 meters. Russian forces then dropped nine more bombs on a shelter where people had taken refuge from the initial attack, killing and injuring several people, including rescuers responding to the first strike.

Sights set on energy infrastructure

The following day, Russian aircraft bombed general hospitals in Kharkiv and Dnipro, damaging both facilities and forcing patients to be evacuated to other hospitals. Kaju said dozens of people were injured as a result as well.

"Russia is continuing to deliberately target civilian infrastructure," he said.

In addition to hospitals and similar facilities, however, Russia is also targeting energy infrastructure ahead of winter in an apparent effort to break Ukraine's resolve.

"Fortunately, it's seemingly had no such significant effect so far," Kaju added.

The Estonian defense official expects Ukraine to retaliate against Russian energy infrastructure this winter, noting that Ukraine's long-range strike capabilities have improved considerably.

"So this coming winter will certainly be significant, if not decisive, in determining how well each side manages to withstand these attacks," Kaju said.

World.title: Maritime Museum orders €1 million research vessel from Latvia
World.content:
The Estonian Maritime Museum is purchasing a new research vessel, with construction set to take place in Latvia. The catamaran will be the first research vessel built specifically to the museum's requirements.

The museum signed a contract Tuesday with Latvian shipbuilder Invessel to build the new vessel. The catamaran will feature a spacious aft deck for diving operations as well as a crane. The museum's former research vessel, Mare, has stood as an exhibit at Seaplane Harbour since 2018.

Estonian Maritime Museum board member Urmas Dresen noted that 2028 will mark 50 years of the museum's underwater archaeology activities.

Mare was used for more than marine archaeology. In August 2005, under the command of Vello Mäss, the vessel transported Estonian divers to the wreck of the Copterline Sikorsky helicopter that crashed into the sea near Aegna.

Mare served the Maritime Museum from 1982 onward.

Construction of the new catamaran is expected to begin with a keel-laying ceremony in February. The vessel will cost about €1 million and is scheduled for completion in 2028.

According to Dresen, the project will be funded entirely from the Estonian Maritime Museum's budget.

"We do not have any support funds," he said.

Once the vessel is completed, a naming competition will be held.

Dresen noted that, unlike the Navy and the State Fleet, which often wait years for new ships and have struggled to secure funding for an icebreaker, the Maritime Museum benefits from purchasing smaller vessels.

World.title: Justice chancellor flags concern over conscripts' dental care access
World.content:
Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) conscripts serving in a Tallinn-based unit have been facing difficulties getting dentist appointments, the acting chancellor of justice found.

The Office of the Chancellor of Justice inspected the Strategic Communications Center of the EDF's Cyber Command on August 11 to review conscripts' service conditions and assess whether their rights were being protected.

During the inspection, officials toured the unit's Filtri tee facilities and spoke with active duty servicemembers and conscripts.

In a letter to the center's commander, Capt. Raiko Jäärats, Deputy Chancellor of Justice and adviser Olari Koppel, serving as acting chancellor of justice, said conscripts are legally entitled to see a doctor and dentist, but accessing dental care has proved difficult. One conscript told inspectors that reaching the dentist had been difficult.

Under the current system, conscripts must call the dental office at their place of service or ask their squad leader for help arranging an appointment; those experiencing pain should go to the medical center.

If the dentist can't take the conscript's call, they call back once they can — but conscripts themselves may be unavailable to answer.

"As a result, more than ten weeks may pass between contacting the dentist and getting an appointment," Koppel wrote.

Timely care a must

Citing the chief dentist, Koppel noted that a new patient registration system has been in development since September which should make it easier for conscripts to contact the dentist's office and get seen sooner.

Until the new system is in place, however, the Office of the Chancellor of Justice has asked the Cyber Command's Strategic Communications Center to ensure conscripts can get dental care promptly when needed.

The office's inspection also found too few toilets in the unit's conscripts' barracks and no suitable space for them to spend their leisure time.

The indoor gym was also found to be too small to accommodate everyone interested in working out, with no schedule in place for allocating its use.

World.title: PÖFF artistic director: We're a discovery festival for new voices in cinema
World.content:
As PÖFF celebrates its 30th anniversary, new artistic director Triin Tramberg discusses the festival's place in an increasingly competitive international film landscape and the challenges of selecting films.

The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) has developed a strong identity over 30 years. As the festival's new artistic director, how do you balance that identity with the need for change?

PÖFF has definitely changed. The very first PÖFF had 25 films in its program; today, we have around 183 feature-length films. So, of course, times have changed considerably and I think it's extremely important for a festival to keep up with developments around the world while maintaining its identity. Over those 30 years, PÖFF has really established its identity among filmmakers, within the industry and with audiences. We have grown into a respected brand associated with quality, both internationally and locally.

Who are PÖFF's main competitors at this time of year?

Of course we have competitors, considering how extensive the film festival landscape is, and it's very difficult to stand out. From August through November, there are about 20 festivals that require world premieres, so there is a lot of competition for new films.

But at the same time, now that I've really gone through the submissions, having previously focused more on debut films, I can see a pattern. For filmmakers, we are definitely a very serious Plan B if they can't get into Venice.

I think that's completely normal within the festival landscape. The big five — Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Toronto and Sundance — are the festivals where filmmakers want to premiere their films. We have to acknowledge that this is often because these festivals are where major deals, particularly film sales, are made.

So I understand why filmmakers want to go there. But I'm very happy to see that they submit their films to us at the same time. And when we look at the festivals around us, I can't say that we've lost a significant number of films. We are one of the last festivals of the year, so there is an important distinction between us and other festivals.

One of PÖFF's advantages is its very large film industry event, Industry@PÖFF & Baltic Event.

Indeed, I think this is also one of the reasons we're attractive, because we present all kinds of projects — new projects in development or in postproduction.

I think our industry section can be compared with the one in Cannes. When it comes to panels and discussions, we're quite innovative, I'd say, and we're bold in addressing certain subjects.

We really do tackle the issues facing the industry, and we also try to bring leading industry representatives here to discuss these questions and find answers.

So I think our industry section really complements the festival, and vice versa.

PÖFF now has seven competition programs, alongside the competitions at Just Film and PÖFF Shorts. How many competition programs does the festival need and how often should they change?

That's a very good question and it's something I've started looking into closely. But I've said that I won't make any changes in my first year. First, I want to see how this year's festival goes.

I think adding the documentary competition was essential, considering the volume of submissions we received. It just felt unfair to ask filmmakers to pay a submission fee for films we couldn't include in our programs. We were seeing documentaries that had real value, but there was nowhere to put them. So this was essential.

As for the number of films, I reduced the number in all the competition programs, simply because otherwise it would have been impossible to navigate the competitions.

And I think when these competitions were established, the film industry was different. There was a very clear distinction between a major art-house film and a smaller art-house film.

Now, I would say everyone is looking for audience-friendly films with artistic value. So finding a way to distinguish between them is definitely this year's challenge.

For now, let's see whether there will be changes to the competitions in the coming years.

Despite taking place at the end of the festival year, PÖFF still attracts a considerable number of new films. With so many films being produced, should the festival become more selective?

I think there's definitely an overproduction of films, especially here in Europe. I believe more than 2,500 films are produced each year, which is definitely too many. That's also why it's possible to select excellent European films, because not all of them can go to Berlin, Venice, Cannes or Locarno.

So yes, I do believe there's an overproduction of films and we have to be very selective. That's also one of the reasons I decided to reduce the size of the competitions.

As a festival, we have an obligation to showcase new films that will travel around the world and highlight directors who deserve recognition within the film industry. So we have to be selective and think carefully about whom we give the spotlight to.

How do you approach politically charged films?

I think the question is also about how they are politically charged. I'm not someone who usually rejects a different point of view.

In general, I think film is political — it's a platform for different voices to be heard. But at the same time, the film has to be good. That's my main requirement for including a film in our program.

I've taken risks at this festival, of course. You can't ignore the fact that if someone wants to find problems, they will find them. But for me, these films represent voices we've given a platform to because they needed one.

Would PÖFF screen films made in present-day Russia with state or regime funding?

No. I would say that, for me, Russian and Israeli films made with state or regime support are not something we should screen under those circumstances.

But at the same time, I do feel we need to look for filmmakers who may not share the beliefs of their home countries, who have fled, for example, and we shouldn't punish them.

And again, the question is: What are their films about?

I think it's always a slippery slope when you make such a decision and there will certainly be people who are strongly opposed to supporting anyone from these countries.

As an end-of-year festival, does PÖFF feel obligated to present the best films from other major festivals, including titles that already have distribution deals?

I would say that right now, with seven competition programs and up to 185 films in the program, 60 percent are in the noncompetition sections and 40 percent are new titles.

And of course, as an end-of-year festival, creating a Best of the Fest program is one of the highlights for film lovers who want to catch up on films from all the major festivals.

But I also think our noncompetition program is very important for our audience. It helps provide context for our competition programs and, ultimately, it also helps us generate the box office revenue we need as a festival.

If we didn't bring these films to the screen and didn't have this relationship with the box office, with revenue that we also share with cinemas, we simply couldn't manage.

But again, I see some questions emerging. Previously, perhaps a couple of years ago, local distributors focused mainly on award-winning titles. Now they're acquiring more films throughout the festival circuit, which also complicates our ability to meet expectations.

So we have to address the question of what role the festival should play for films that are going to be released in theaters anyway.

And, as I said earlier, there's an overproduction of films. So maybe we should reconsider our approach to showcasing the best films from other festivals. That's probably a question I'll need to address in the coming years.

Yet many PÖFF competition winners never reach Estonian cinemas afterward. Of course, that's also a question for distributors.

I still think we have to take it step by step.

First of all, we've now found that distributors are acquiring films they previously wouldn't have considered when PÖFF really wants to screen them. So we have to negotiate.

I think distributors are also trying to find their way. And let's see, over the coming years, what kinds of films I'll select for the competitions as the festival's artistic director. I can't predict that.

Hopefully that will change, so winning films can have a life in Estonia beyond the festival.

Hopefully. And I think it would be quite a boost for the festival if we could distribute these films ourselves, but that's a completely different business strategy.

So you haven't worked on that?

No, we've always considered the idea, but it requires a different approach.

Again, I come back to the issue of film overproduction. If distributors see what works in Tallinn, perhaps they'll start taking these risks as well.

We do have a lot of sales agents who pick up films and our films go on to travel around the world, to different festivals and also to local audiences.

Some of them have been quite successful. Many directors made their debuts here and launched their careers at PÖFF.

Indeed, their second films have already been screened in Berlin, Cannes and other festivals. That's one of the things about us — we're something of a discovery festival.

As the festival's new artistic director, how would you define PÖFF's identity? It brings together three groups — audiences, filmmakers and the industry. Which is most important to you?

All of them are important, because that's how the program comes together.

Personally, I always think about the audience, so for me, I guess that's the most important part.

For me, the most fascinating thing is to discover something and create an emotional response.

Throughout history, cinema has been one of the easiest and most accessible forms of entertainment. Even when times are tough, going to the movies with your family is still an event.

You go to the movies and experience a new culture, a new point of view, a new emotion. That's the most important thing for me.

I always say that no story is unique — the question is how the story is told.

I think PÖFF today offers a guarantee of quality for everyone looking for something new in cinema.

For filmmakers, I think Tallinn is a platform that allows them to present daring stories.

Our mission is to discover new voices, new stories and new approaches to the language of cinema.

As I can also see from this year's submissions, we have a lot of debut films. In fact, we received around 400 submissions for first feature films alone.

So Tallinn is a place where filmmakers can establish their careers.

And for the industry, it's a place for discovery. Companies find new people to work with and develop new projects.

Restored classics are becoming increasingly prominent at film festivals. Is this something PÖFF wants to develop as well?

Yes. First of all, I'm young, so I still have so much to see myself.

I mean, there are so many films and so many references and there's an entire generation that hasn't seen certain important films at all, myself included.

Therefore, I think it's also our mission as a film festival to bring these films back to the big screen.

That's why I'm very happy about the "PÖFF Celebrates" program, which features films from our very first festival.

We would have brought many more of these films to Tallinn if they had been digitized, because the main problem nowadays is that they exist on 35-millimeter film prints and aren't available in Digital Cinema Package (DCP) format.

But it was fantastic to revisit these films and this is definitely something we'll continue doing in the future.

Is this also how film festivals can adapt to the growing importance of streaming services such as Netflix?

Definitely. Of course, it's great to watch Netflix on a rainy Sunday — we just watched "The Sixth Sense" with my daughter. It was a great experience.

But at the same time, nothing beats watching a film on the big screen with all those heightened emotions, especially if you have guests present and a Q&A or if you're seeing something for the very first time.

You feel part of something special and unique, hearing all those live reactions to a scene and realizing there are so many like-minded people — or the opposite, when you find yourself wondering, "Why are they laughing?"

So I think nothing compares to the collective emotional experience that cinema provides.

Naturally, all these platforms have their place, but they'll never match the experience of watching a film in a movie theater.

Because cinema and the moviegoing experience are alive.

Exactly.

The interview was first published in the Baltic Film Magazine.

World.title: Iraq and UAE dismantle drug smuggling network, arrest 20 suspects
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Ministry of Interior cooperated with UAE authorities to destroy an international drug smuggling network, resulting in the arrest of 20 individuals of Gulf, Arab, African, and Asian nationality.

The operation resulted in the confiscation of 200,000 Captagon tablets and more than 30 kilos of narcotics, including cocaine, crystal methamphetamine, marijuana, hashish, and synthetic substances known as spice.

According to UAE police, the network sought to transport the narcotics across a border region in Ras Al Khaimah with the intention of distributing them throughout the nation.

Iraq’s General Directorate for Narcotics and Psychotropic Substances, the UAE’s National Drug Enforcement Authority (NDEA), and Ras Al Khaimah Police were all engaged in the operation, which was judicially coordinated by the UAE’s Federal Public Prosecution.

Iraqi and Emirati officials shared intelligence, which helped them identify the network, thwart the smuggling effort, and arrest individuals involved.

The operation demonstrates Iraq and the UAE’s continuous security collaboration in the fight against worldwide narcotics trafficking and organized crime.

World.title: Jude’s brother Jobe Bellingham gets England call-up
World.content:
London – Jobe Bellingham was named alongside older brother Jude in Thomas Tuchel’s England squad for the first time on Friday as Chelsea’s Cole Palmer missed out.

Fulham teenager Josh King is also handed his first call-up ahead of Nations League games against Croatia and Spain later this month.

Tuchel said Palmer “misses too many opportunities” to impress at international level after pulling out of England’s last squad due to injury.

The Chelsea star, who was not included for the World Cup, has been left out as Tuchel takes the chance to look at younger options with a place in the quarter-finals of the Nations League almost guaranteed

Jobe Bellingham has been rewarded for a strong start to his second season at Borussia Dortmund, where Jude also played for three seasons before moving to Real Madrid.

King has impressed despite Fulham’s struggles in the Premier League, while Liverpool’s 18-year-old winger Rio Ngumoha is also included.

England are second in group A3 after four games, with three wins and a defeat, against Spain at Wembley.

The Three Lions host Croatia, who they beat 7-0 last month, on Thursday before travelling to take on Spain with just one point needed to qualify for the knockout rounds in March.

Newly-crowned Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane is set to surpass Peter Shilton as England’s most capped male player after moving level with the former goalkeeper on 125 appearances against the Czech Republic last time out.

Squad in full:

Goalkeepers: Jordan Pickford (Everton), Jason Steele (Brighton), James Trafford (Leeds)

Defenders: Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid/ESP), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guehi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle), Ezri Konsa, Ben White (both Arsenal), Djed Spence (Inter Milan/ITA), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen/GER)

Midfielders: Elliot Anderson (Manchester City), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid/ESP), Jobe Bellingham (Borussia Dortmund/GER), James Garner (Everton), Josh King (Fulham), Myles Lewis-Skelly, Declan Rice, Eberechi Eze (all Arsenal)

Forwards: Harry Kane (Bayern Munich/GER), Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona/ESP), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest)

World.title: Auto sector propels growth in German factory output
World.content:
Frankfurt – A rebound in car production gave German factory output a bigger boost than expected in September, official data showed Friday, the latest sign Europe’s largest economy was gaining strength.

Auto sector production jumped around 17 percent from a month earlier following a sluggish period caused largely by factory holidays and plant maintenance over the summer.

It was nevertheless some rare good news from an industry that has been hard hit by fierce Chinese competition, falling demand and rising costs.

This helped lift overall industrial production by 0.7 percent for the month, said statistics agency Destatis, above analyst expectations of a far smaller increase.

The economy ministry said the data “helped offset the declines in industrial production seen in the middle of the year,” caused by factors like higher energy costs linked to the Middle East war and low water levels on rivers.

Germany’s economy is struggling to pull itself out of long decline driven by weakening demand for its exports, Chinese competition and a range of deep-rooted problems.

But the manufacturing powerhouse is expected to notch up its fastest growth for several years in 2026, in large part due to a public spending blitz on defence and infrastructure.

September’s factory data was also helped by the pharmaceutical sector, which registered eight percent growth.

But there were falls in the construction sector and in manufacturing of machinery and equipment, Destatis said.

Despite September’s positive data, Dirk Schumacher, chief economist at German public lender KfW, cautioned that the economy continued to face headwinds.

“There remains a long list of risk factors that could bring the industrial recovery to an end before it has even really got going,” he said.

“The nervousness in the financial markets regarding the further expansion of AI infrastructure is just one example of this.”

World.title: Iran exempts Iraq from Strait of Hormuz restrictions as oil exports rise
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iran has confirmed that Iraqi ships are free from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, enabling them to transit through the crucial waterway despite the continuous interruptions caused by the regional strife.

On Tuesday, Amir Moqaddam, Deputy Head of the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, stated that Iraq, China, India, and Qatar had been given exemptions, enabling their vessels to pass the strait.

The exemption is especially important for Iraq, which depends significantly on oil exports for government income and has had enormous difficulty since the Strait of Hormuz was essentially blocked with the commencement of the US-Israel war with Iran in February 2026.

According to maritime analytics company Kpler, Iraq’s crude oil exports via the strait surged from 1.69 million barrels per day in August to 2.65 million barrels per day in October, showing that export volumes had recovered despite the continuing violence.

Iran had earlier issued an exception for Iraqi vessels in April, citing Iraq as a neighboring nation with strong relations to Tehran. The most recent statement maintains that agreement.

While Iran intends to collect transit fees from some nations, it is unclear if Iraqi vessels would be obliged to pay.

The exception might bring significant relief to Iraq’s oil industry, allowing it to continue export profits while reducing economic pressures.

However, there is still concern about maritime security in the area, since the US maintains a separate naval embargo targeting boats entering or departing Iranian ports.

Although the Iranian exception permits Iraqi ships to pass through Tehran’s limitations, it does not guarantee safe passage in light of ongoing military tensions and assaults on commercial boats in the Gulf.

World.title: Beijing seeks to bolster AI shares
World.content:
Tokyo – After recent sharp drops for some Chinese tech stocks, Beijing is trying to prop them up — seeing the sector, and in particular AI, as a central strategic priority.

In August, buzzy Chinese startup Unitree, whose walking, dancing humanoids are often used by AI researchers trying to make robots act autonomously, went public.

Its shares skyrocketed on its Shanghai debut in August — but almost three months later they are down 40 percent from their peak that day.

Chinese chipmakers Moore Threads and MetaX — touted as challengers to US behemoth Nvidia — have both plunged by around 50 percent over the past six months.

Similar steep falls can be seen across Shanghai’s tech-focused Star50 index, China’s answer to Wall Street’s Nasdaq, which is down only around six percent over the same period.

Volatility on Wall Street hasn’t helped — the Nasdaq plunged 5.5 percent on Thursday — with fears that the vast sums spent on AI infrastructure will not translate into big profits.

However, the Chinese government is taking steps.

Officials this week reactivated liquidity-injection tools aimed at encouraging share purchases while boosting the trading volume of state-backed investment funds, according to local media reports.

On Tuesday, net capital inflows into nine exchange-traded funds (ETFs), commonly used by Beijing to prop up the market, reached 120 billion yuan ($18 billion) — a near-record, according to Bloomberg data, targeting tech stocks in particular.

The Financial Times also reported this week that Chinese regulators had told banks to halt company listings in an attempt to boost market liquidity.

“Chinese technology shares have been under significant pressure, with investors concerned about weak domestic demand, intense competition and disappointing earnings,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets.

However, now “fresh policy support, lower valuations and hopes of improving sentiment are encouraging investors to revisit a sector that has struggled for much of the year”, she added.

– Packed to the rafters –

Overall, tech investors in China remain optimistic, said Ajin Jin, partner at Shanghai-based investment firm Kunquan.

“In both Beijing and Shanghai, weekly roadshows are still taking place, and every single one is packed to the rafters, with people even sitting in the aisles,” he said.

Li Daxiao, one of China’s most prominent investment gurus, also said “the burgeoning development of the industry is unstoppable” and should be clearly distinguished from “share price fluctuations”.

“Technology shares have been affected by external risks and have fallen in tandem with their counterparts in the US, Japan and South Korea,” he told AFP.

Stephen Inness of SPI Asset Management said that “a state-backed effort would add to steps taken by China last month to stabilise its equity market”.

However, he warned the measures “have so far proved insufficient against the backdrop of a weak domestic economy and doubts over AI earnings”.

World.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ set for blockbuster return after 13 years
World.content:
Paris – Fans of the violent “Grand Theft Auto” video game franchise are just two weeks away from getting their hands on the latest edition, which has taken almost a decade to make and has become the most expensive title in history.

The franchise allows players to act out gangster fantasies — shooting up bars, crashing cars — in fictional renderings of US cities where the soundtrack piped through in-game radio is almost as important as the cutting-edge visuals.

GTA VI, which comes 13 years after its predecessor, is expected to break sales records when it lands on November 19 thanks in part to a monumental marketing campaign that kicked off in late 2023 with the first official trailer.

“It is going to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time,” Chris Dring of The Game Business outlet told AFP.

The previous edition, GTA V, is still the second-biggest selling game ever — it took just three days to rack up $1 billion in sales, two days less than the movie “Avengers: Endgame”.

The budget of GTA VI has reportedly ballooned to over $1 billion — far higher than any other game or film — and projections have it on track to make several billion in its first week, which would smash all records for any cultural product.

– ‘Top creators’ –

‘GTA VI’ has two main protagonists, former drug-runner Jason and newly released ex-con Lucia, who try to survive in Vice City, a reimagining of Miami.

Lucia is the first playable woman character in a main edition of the almost 30-year history of a franchise.

During the 1990s and 2000s the game’s graphic depictions of sex, violence and misogyny became notorious — tabloid media outrage boosting the title’s notoriety and helping sales to skyrocket.

Rockstar Games has spent eight years developing the sixth edition, a process beset by difficulties including the leak of development footage and code for the game online in 2022.

But expectations are sky-high.

“They’ve spent a long time on this game, but they are probably the top game entertainment creators in the world,” said Dring.

Analysts expect the game to have an impact on the entire video game sector, including on console sales and accessories.

Several other studios delayed the release of new games to avoid being caught in the hype cycle around GTA VI.

Analysis firm Sensor Tower said the game had already generated around $750 million from pre-sales.

Surveys suggested almost one-third of the 49 million people who use PS5 and Xbox Series consoles in the United States intended to buy the game.

“The purchase intent that we’re seeing on ‘Grand Theft Auto’ is far away above any other game we’ve ever tracked,” said Mat Piscatella of consultancy Circana.

“For me, it’s the game of the decade,” Jocelin Lebeau, 39, a gamer who works for the French military, told AFP at a recent event in Paris. “I’m ready to buy it sight unseen.”

World.title: Carrick fights for Man Utd job ahead of international break
World.content:
London – Michael Carrick takes charge of Manchester United for what could be the last time against Aston Villa this weekend as he battles to save his job despite a morale-boosting midweek victory over Roma.

United’s dramatic win in the Champions League gave the coach breathing space but he remains under intense pressure ahead of the international break.

Elsewhere in the Premier League, Manchester City will be seeking to avoid a rare third straight league defeat when they face Nottingham Forest as they try to keep pace with leaders Arsenal.

AFP Sport looks at three talking points ahead of the action:

Carrick’s last chance?

When Manchester United’s players trudged off at half-time against Roma on Tuesday, 2-0 down and seemingly out of ideas, Michael Carrick’s fate appeared to be sealed.

Instead, his underperforming team somehow turned things around, with Matheus Cunha scoring two late goals in a 3-2 win at a feverish Old Trafford.

It ended a run of nine games without a victory — United’s longest winless run since the 1988/89 season.

Defender Diogo Dalot said he hopes the Roma result can kickstart their season.

“Nights like this can change momentum, can change seasons, and I think this win is going to give us confidence for the next games,” he said.

But the brutal reality is that United could be bottom of the Premier League when they kick off on Sunday if results go against them.

Whatever the outcome, the international break will give the club’s hierarchy an opportunity to consider their long-term options.

Villa’s Spanish manager, Unai Emery, was tipped as a potential candidate for the Old Trafford hot seat but reports suggest he is close to signing a new deal with the Birmingham club.

Two-way title race?

Manchester City know that even if they keep pace with Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal, it might ultimately all be in vain.

The Etihad club are still waiting to discover their fate after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules — with a huge points deduction one potential punishment.

Arsenal appear to be the only other serious contender for the title, having the happy knack of winning even when below par.

On paper, both clubs face a straightforward task this weekend, though City’s trip to Nottingham Forest could be trickier than it looks.

Opta’s “expected points” table, which orders the Premier League based on expected goals for and against, has Oliver Glasner’s team in third — a remarkable 16 places higher than they are in the real table.

Arsenal, who host struggling Hull, have won 18 of their past 19 Premier League games against promoted sides.

Things looking up for Spurs

The doom and gloom around Tottenham has lifted after a three-game winning streak in the Premier League under manager Roberto De Zerbi.

Less than three weeks ago Spurs, without a single win, propped up the division. They are now comfortably placed in mid-table.

Defender Archie Gray credits the spirit of the squad for the turnaround, which has the club just four points behind fourth-placed Chelsea.

“We all get on really well and you can see that out there on the pitch,” he told SpursPlay. “Even with the celebration(s), all the subs are running to the players and they are little things that mean so much to us. That’s the most important thing and why we’ve been improving.”

Daniel Farke’s Leeds are winless in their past five Premier League games and have scored just twice during that run, slipping to 12th in the table.

Friday

Saturday

Leeds v Tottenham (1230), Arsenal v Hull, Fulham v Newcastle, Nottingham Forest v Manchester City (1730)

Sunday

Brighton v Brentford, Crystal Palace v Liverpool, Ipswich v Bournemouth, Sunderland v Chelsea (all 1400), Manchester United v Aston Villa (1630)

World.title: Israel faces new era of sinking US support after election
World.content:
Jerusalem – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s brash campaign posters are still up on Israeli public buses — images of him, US President Donald Trump and soaring warjets that laud the two leaders attacking Iran together.

Neither is now advertising the state of the two countries’ alliance.

A week after an inconclusive election for Netanyahu, Americans overwhelmingly rejected Trump and chose a Congress led by Democrats who want a tougher approach to Israel, whether on Iran, Gaza or settler violence in the occupied West Bank.

The back-to-back elections look to many observers like a turning point, with Israel no longer able to take for granted the cover of the world’s most powerful country.

“This is a new era. The confluence of the Gaza war and the war with Iran have really changed how mainstream Americans — not people particularly concerned with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict — see Israel,” said Yael Sternhell, an expert on the United States at Tel Aviv University.

Vice President JD Vance, assessing why his Republicans fared poorly, listed four ways to bring voters back, including ending the Iran war and changing “our relationship with Israel”.

Trump did not disagree. Just as voting was underway Tuesday, Trump said he had agreed with Netanyahu to end the $3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel by the end of this year, explicitly tying the decision to the US political mood.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has served on and off for nearly two decades, had eagerly sought Trump’s endorsement but also acknowledged his country’s growing isolation.

In the final days of the campaign, he suggested Israel turn to cryptocurrencies to circumvent international sanctions he expected would intensify.

Netanyahu has not commented on the US election or Trump’s aid remarks.

Amit Segal, a journalist known for his proximity to Netanyahu, posted that the political situation in the United States marked a “catastrophe” for Israel.

– Can Eisenkot restore the alliance? –

Opposition contender Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to cobble together a coalition to oust Netanyahu, has cast himself as capable of repairing relations.

In an English-language statement, the former military chief said he believed in “liberal values” and also wanted to work “closely and constructively” with Trump.

Yair Golan, the main left-wing leader inside Eisenkot’s bloc, called for Israel to restore a bipartisan approach destroyed by Netanyahu who he said promoted a “destructive Israeli narrative of eternal war and authoritarian rule”.

Netanyahu boasted in his campaign about standing up to Democratic presidents including Barack Obama, who remains a hero for many Democrats. Netanyahu openly aligned with Republicans a decade ago to attack Obama’s diplomacy on Iran.

“Netanyahu certainly rubs Democrats the wrong way and has made every effort to alienate them,” Sternhell said.

“But Eisenkot can’t just be a nicer man to receive a softer approach from this new Congress,” she added. “He’s going to need new policies.”

She said Eisenkot would likely enjoy Israeli public support for cracking down on extremist settlers, who have attacked Palestinians in the West Bank with virtual impunity.

But Israel has shifted to the right, with wide initial support for the Gaza war.

– Broadening criticism of Israel –

The new Congress will include progressive Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate, who describe the devastation in Gaza as genocide, an assertion rejected by Israel.

Netanyahu “made a bet not only on the Republicans but almost personally on Trump”, said Eli Kowaz, senior policy director of the Economic Cooperation Foundation, an Israeli think tank that backs a two-state solution with the Palestinians.

“These results show that bet had an expiry date,” Kowaz said. “Also, for the first time, really, I think there’s a realisation that it isn’t only about the Democrats. It’s a problem with the relationship with America.”

Without US assistance, Israel still has its own major arms industry and retains a clear edge fighting non-state actors such as Hamas and Hezbollah, said Ehud Eilam, a former researcher for the Israeli defence ministry.

But he said Israel would need to rely more on cheaper artillery or non-sophisticated bombs, further increasing risks of civilian casualties that have enraged international opinion.

“Israel can adjust to a new strategic reality of losing much and even all US military aid, but it will be tough for Israel. It will require Israel to consider hard choices such as taking huge loans or raising taxes,” Eilam said.

Kowaz said that Eisenkot, aware of politics in Washington, was trying to show he is interested in regional stability and strategic agreements and not just “an indefinite state of war”.

“He is definitely laying out a different vision for Israel’s relationship with the United States.”

World.title: Manipur rebel arrested from Delhi hotel
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In an intelligence-backed operation, RK Regan Singh aka Gandhi, a wanted militant belonging to People's Liberation Army, Manipur, has been arrested from a hotel in south Delhi.

PLA is a separatist militant group fighting for the creation of an independent and socialist Manipur.

Confirming the arrest, special commissioner HGS Dhaliwal said that Gandhi's family members were the founders of the outfit. He was questioned about his presence in the capital before being handed over to Manipur Police.

Acting on a tip-off, the crime branch set up technical surveillance and local intelligence gathering. The initial trail pointed toward the AIIMS area but it yielded nothing.

Officers faced a major problem as they didn't have a photograph of militant. However, they managed to zero in on him in Yusuf Sarai.

NEW DELHI: Observing that the Constitution is supreme and that no individual or political organisation stands above it, Supreme Court Friday issued notice to office-bearers of Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC), including its president, seeking their response on why contempt proceedings should not be initiated against them over a now-deleted social media post on CJI Surya Kant.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi was hearing a petition filed by advocate Vineet Jindal seeking suo motu action regarding the post published on the official X account of Indian National Congress's Keralam unit.KPCC submitted that the post was uploaded without office-bearers' approval, and was immediately taken down after it came to the notice of the party. It said an unconditional apology had also been issued.The bench, however, said SC would examine "whether it has come from the pen or your heart" and agreed to hear the petition. "...Independence of the judiciary is not a matter of political convenience," the court said.It said while judgements are always open to criticism, "freedom of expression cannot be a shield for intimidation or interference with the administration of justice" and "judicial restraint must never be mistaken for institutional weakness".

World.title: With working strength of just 2, Sikkim HC unable to hear intra-court appeals
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Sikkim HC, with a sanctioned strength of three judges but a working strength of two, is unable to hear intra-court appeals against judgements rendered by two single-judge benches headed by the chief justice and the other judge.Pendency of appeals against single-judge bench's orders has forced Sikkim CJ A Muhammed Mustaque to write to CJI Surya Kant for issuance of appropriate orders "for facilitating transfer of five pending writ appeals to another high court or making such other suitable arrangement in the interest of justice".A bench of CJI Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana Friday treated the Sikkim CJ's letter on the administrative side as a suo motu writ petition and sought response from the Centre.Sikkim CJ, in his letter, said, "The continued pendency of these matters, owing to the aforesaid institutional constraint, may adversely affect the timely dispensation of justice and legitimate expectations of the litigants. The situation, therefore, calls for appropriate consideration so that the appeals may be heard and adjudicated upon without undue delay."Justice Mustaque became CJ of Sikkim HC on Jan 4. In June, the HC's first woman judge Meenakshi M Rai became CJ of Patna HC, reducing Sikkim's working strength to two, the other judge in the HC being Justice Bhaskar Raj Pradhan.

World.content:

NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has allowed a complainant to submit additional documents in a case alleging that Congress MP Sonia Gandhi was included in poll rolls before acquiring Indian citizenship.The ACJM court has scheduled the next hearing for Nov 18 after the complainant's counsel sought more time to place further evidence on record.The complaint by advocate Vikas Tripathi alleges that Italian-origin Sonia's name appeared on the voter list of New Delhi parliamentary constituency in 1980, before she acquired Indian citizenship on April 30, 1983. Her name was allegedly deleted in 1982 and reinstated in 1983, also before she became an Indian citizen.A sessions court had in Sept this year set aside an order by the ACJM refusing to order an FIR against Sonia. Judge Vishal Gogne allowed the appeal by Tripathi saying the ACJM's rejection was based on an unverified photocopy of a record and constituted a "non-speaking (unreasoned)" order.Gogne emphasised that electoral rolls were meant exclusively for citizens and rejected the ACJM court's observations on the roles of the Centre and Election Commission as "improper".

World.title: HC judge vacancies at decade-low 26%, but pendency keeps piling up
World.content:
With 64 lakh cases, backlog refuses to ease

NEW DELHI: After hovering between 36% and 40% over the past decade, vacancies in HC judges have shown a significant decline, falling to 26%, this despite sanctioned strength of judges in HCs increasing from 906 in 2014 to 1,122.

The largest HC, Allahabad, has brought down its vacancies to 56 against a sanctioned strength of 160 judges, as of Nov 1.

The other HCs with bigger benches and usually large vacancies - Bombay, Punjab and Haryana, Madras, Calcutta, Karnataka and Delhi - too, have increased their working strength, bringing down vacancies.

The last time judges' vacancies were this low (at 26%) was in July 2009, when there were 234 judges posts to be filled against a sanctioned strength of 886 in 21 HCs then.



Vacancies in HCs started gradually climbing thereafter, which coincided with the friction between higher judiciary and govt over an attempt to bring a judicial accountability bill and passage of National Judicial Appointments Commission Act by Parliament. NJAC Act was later struck down by Supreme Court.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

In Nov 2014, vacancies were at 36% (in 24 HCs), with 353 judges posts vacant against a sanctioned strength of 984.





These vacancies remained at 35% in March 2022 with 387 posts vacant, though the sanctioned strength was increased to 1,104 judges.

Large vacancies are a prime factor behind backlog of cases. Though SC historically never had large vacancies, case pendency in SC has increased from 52,000 in 2009 to more than 92,000 at present.

The situation is worse in HCs and much worse in district and lower judiciary, deteriorating every month. In 2009, total pendency of cases in HCs was at 39.5 lakh, which climbed to 45 lakh in 2013, and is at 64 lakh at present.

The pendency in lower judiciary is similarly getting worse while the large number of vacancies remain static at around 5,000 against a sanctioned strength of 25,894 judicial officers.

World.title: NMC adds 9,783 PG medical seats, takes total to 68,305
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India's postgraduate medical education system is set for a major expansion, with 9,783 seats being added for the 2026-27 academic year. The increase takes the total approved PG intake to 68,305, up from 58,522, with govt medical colleges accounting for the largest share of the new seats.

Of the additional seats, 4,373 have been added in govt colleges, 4,148 in private colleges and 1,262 in deemed universities, Dr M K Ramesh, president of NMC's Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), told TOI.

PG medical seats are spread across several states, with five accounting for a little over half of the national intake. Karnataka has the highest number, with 8,998 approved seats for 2026-27, followed by Maharashtra with 7,682. Uttar Pradesh has 6,983 seats, Tamil Nadu 6,819 and Telangana 4,417. Together, these five states account for 34,899 seats, or around 51% of the total.

NEW DELHI: Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) Friday released date sheets for the Class X and XII board examinations for 2027, with both scheduled to begin on Feb 16.The schedules were announced 101 days before the start of the examinations, giving students more than three months to prepare.According to a circular issued by CBSE controller of examinations Sanyam Bhardwaj, over 46.3 lakh students have registered for the 2027 examinations - more than 26.5 lakh from Class X and over 19.8 lakh from Class XII. World.title: More than 30% ethanol in E20, says Karnataka minister
World.content:
Karnataka minister Rizwan Arshad Friday alleged that tests at state-authorised labs found "excess" mixing of ethanol in E20 fuel, as high as 31.2% in some cases. Samples were collected from 63 petrol bunks across the state and 14 of them had ethanol above the prescribed limit, he said.

PSUs denied the claim, saying it was not supported by tests conducted under statutory and technical procedures. Fuel retailers said 56 samples from Karnataka, tested in a nationwide drive, were found to contain ethanol in the prescribed 19-21% range.

World.title: Paraguayan President Pena impeached over banking crisis
World.content:
Paraguayan Senators on Friday (November 6, 2026) voted to impeach President Santiago Pena over the collapse of a major bank that locked almost half the population out of their accounts and triggered widespread protests.

Mr. Pena had offered his resignation over the disaster, but lawmakers pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings that would strip him of immunity granted to former Presidents.

He did not attend the trial in the Senate despite earlier pledging to defend himself.

The President “is declared guilty of poor performance in his duties,” Senate President Basilio Nunez declared after a vote of 44 in favor of impeachment and one absence out of 45 senators.

Around three million people have been unable to access their money since the Central Bank took control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday and froze its accounts over concerns about its solvency.

A Central Bank official told AFP that advance payments to some affected depositors had begun on Thursday (November 5, 2026) afternoon.

The bank’s demise brought thousands of people onto the streets demanding repercussions for U.S.-backed Mr. Pena, who until last year had a stake in Grupo Vazquez, which controlled Ueno.
