World.title: Azerbaijan and Bulgaria hold sixth round of political consultations (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. The sixth round of political consultations between the Ministries of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan and Bulgaria was held in Sofia.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan said in a report.

According to the ministry, the delegations were headed by Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov and Bulgarian Deputy Foreign Minister Ivanka Tasheva, respectively.

During the political consultations, the current state of strategic partnership relations between the two countries and prospects for their development were discussed in detail, along with issues of cooperation in the political, economic and energy sectors, including green energy corridors, transport and logistics, and other areas.

The sides also held a detailed exchange of views on diversifying trade turnover and promoting mutual investments. The importance of continuing mutual support and coordination within international organizations was emphasized at the meeting.

In addition, opportunities to expand ties in the humanitarian, cultural, scientific and educational fields were considered. It was noted that cooperation in these areas constitutes an important component of bilateral relations.

As part of the visit, Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova met with Elnur Mammadov. The meeting focused on issues of mutual interest.

The Deputy Minister also met with Rusi Ivanov, Adviser to the Prime Minister of Bulgaria on Foreign Policy. The sides exchanged views on expanding bilateral ties and prospects for developing cooperation.

Subsequently, the Azerbaijani delegation held a meeting at the National Assembly of Bulgaria with members of the Bulgaria-Azerbaijan Interparliamentary Friendship Group and its Chairman, Hamid Hamid, as well as members of the Foreign Policy Committee and the committee's Deputy Chairman, Slavi Vasilev. During the discussions, the important role of interparliamentary relations in promoting parliamentary diplomacy, intensifying contacts between legislative bodies and developing bilateral ties was emphasized.

During the visit, Elnur Mammadov also delivered a lecture to attendees of the Diplomatic Institute of the Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and members of the Student Diplomatic Club of Sofia University St. Kliment Ohridski.

World.title: Woodside to cut over 500 jobs globally as part of cost reduction drive
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 6. Woodside Energy plans to reduce its global workforce by more than 500 positions as part of its structural cost reduction program, according to the company's Capital Markets Day 2026 presentation.

The workforce reduction is one of the measures the company listed for reaching its target of cutting $400 million in annual structural costs from 2028. The others are AI-enabled maintenance planning, supply chain optimisation, and risk-based contracting processes.

Woodside said that $130 million of the targeted savings will come from streamlined processes, $170 million from external spending and $100 million from portfolio optimisation.

Woodside Energy, headquartered in Perth, is Australia's largest independent oil and gas company and is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange. Its portfolio includes LNG and domestic gas operations in Australia, deepwater oil in the US Gulf of America, the Sangomar oil field in Senegal, and the Trion project under development in Mexico. Woodside said its enablers include a 'One Team' culture, digital and AI innovation, and critical capabilities. The structural cost reduction target excludes contractor spending on major capital projects such as Scarborough, Trion, Louisiana LNG and Beaumont New Ammonia. Woodside held its Capital Markets Day 2026 in Sydney on November 5 and will hold a second event in New York on November 12. At last year's Capital Markets Day, in November 2025, the company set out its growth plans to 2032.

World.title: Moving house seven times in 18 months the reality for many renters
World.content:
Frances Thiele has moved seven times in the past 18 months.

Bouncing between share houses, the 61-year-old disability support worker has struggled to find an affordable rental in the regional city of Albany, about 450 kilometres south of Perth.

"There just isn't anything," she said.

"The cheapest place I found for one person was $500, and that's half of my week's wages."

In Western Australia, rent inflation is at record levels, with new research from Anglicare showing essential workers are essentially locked out of the private rental market.

Renters in Albany are being priced out of the housing market. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Just one property across WA's two most populous regions, the Great Southern and South West, was within budget for key workers in health and childcare sectors, according to the charity's annual rental affordability snapshot.

Ms Thiele's precarious housing situation comes despite working full time.

"The job I do doesn't make money from people — it's not a job that'll ever be highly paid," she said.

" I do it because I feel useful, and I feel like I'm helping the community. "

Rising costs have forced her into shared housing, where she splits $850 a week in rent with a housemate.

The 61-year-old splits $850 a week in rent with another housemate. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

"It's easier to get a big house because these are hard to rent out as no-one can afford them," she said.

"With two wages, it just makes it much cheaper for us."

No room to grow in the Pilbara

Further north in WA's Pilbara, employers say they are now forced to compete with mining and energy giants to find staff somewhere to live.

Clark Smith says lack of accommodation means he cannot expand. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Clark Smith runs a small mechanical workshop in Karratha, 1,530 kilometres north of Perth and said accommodation shortages were stopping his business from growing.

"I could put three guys on tomorrow and not even make a dent in the work we've got," he said.

" I would expand in a second, but I just can't. "

Mr Smith used any available option to house workers.

"I've put people in mates' houses … we've had people staying at the yard in caravans," he said.

"I've had staff houses, three or four guys in it, which at the end of the day, living and working together is not healthy either."

Clark Smith (right), with employees Brad Wild and Jayden Crute at his Karratha workshop. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Karratha has been Mr Smith's home for 17 years and accommodation had always been a challenge.

"We lived in a van with no air con through a couple of months of the summer, wherever you could get," he said.

"In five years, we lived in 10 different houses."

Small businesses struggle to compete

Many roles offered in Karratha included housing and a car, something small business owners found difficult to match.

"All of them know that, at the drop of a hat tomorrow, they could go work for a company and earn twice as much and have a roof over their head," Mr Smith said.

"I can't compete; it's physically impossible to compete."

Clark Smith has turned to multiple methods to house staff amid Karratha's accommodation shortage. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

One employee of Mr Smith's was living in affordable housing, as part of a scheme supported by the City of Karratha and industry partners.

Mr Smith said the scheme was helpful, but it came with limitations.

"You're only allowed one per business, and if she gets a pay rise, they get kicked out of their housing because you have to earn under [a certain] amount," he said.

Loading...

Other employees have had to move between houses or relied on relatives to stay in Karratha.

"I've got a 22-year-old who still lives at home … he doesn't have a choice," Mr Smith said.

"It's very hard to make this place a home because of the accommodation situation."

World.title: NT government accused of cherrypicking data to support crime claims
World.content:
A report has found the Northern Territory government is cherrypicking data to back its narrative that crime is down, with one legal expert saying the government is "intentionally misleading" the public.

In their Tough On Crime report released this week, researchers at the Jumbunna Institute for Indigenous Education and Research say the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government has relied on incomplete and unverified data as evidence that its law and order measures are working.

The CLP ran a tough-on-crime campaign leading up to the 2024 NT election, promising to reduce offending, rebuild the economy and restore the Territory lifestyle.

Data from NT Courts reveals more criminal offences have been recorded annually in recent years. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

After winning office, the party introduced a raft of new policies to curb crime, including bail reform, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and reinstating spit hoods in youth detention.

Last month, Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said two years after the "centrepiece" crime reforms were introduced, bail refusals were up by 55 per cent, crimes involving edged weapons were down by 12 per cent and 300 offences allegedly committed by 10 to 11-year-olds were before the courts.

But the Jumbunna Institute report's authors say Ms Finocchiaro's "numerous claims" that the government's legislative and policy reforms had reduced crime "cannot be supported by existing data".

The report identifies what the researchers say are several core problems with the government's "over-reliance on policing data" and contend that multiple independent sources are needed to create a complete picture.

NT chief minister Lia Finocchiaro has made numerous claims that the government's legislative and policy reforms have reduced crime. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

They say figures from NT Police's SerPro crime data IT system, introduced in late 2023, cannot be reliably compared with data from before then and that SerPro data is published with a delay of up to five months.

Crime surge threatens CLP's law and order agenda Two years after the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government came to power on a tough-on-crime platform, official crime data shows a mixed bag of results.

"So when [the government] stands up there in front of the community and uses that data to make claims about reductions in crime, that data is not reliable and shouldn't be used," co-author Tatiana Corrales said.

"Claims that the government is addressing the crime crisis [created under] Labor, we can't even test that.

"Despite what some of the more popular messaging may be, there's actually no clear trend."

The report's authors also say different time frames can produce "stark" differences in data outcomes.

"There is a misrepresentation of crime rates and a presentation of crime data that is overly simplistic," Ms Corrales said.

"There is definitely a lot of spin, [the government] is not being transparent about the limitations of the data.

"I'm not convinced that that's unique to the NT government … but I think it's particularly problematic in the NT because [the government has] pushed through such punitive legislation that is really having a negative impact on communities across the NT."

Ms Corrales said the NT government was "cherry-picking" favourable data to support its claims.

In one example, the report highlighted NT Police data showing the number of family and domestic violence offences in the Territory had decreased between 2024 and 2025, while court finalisation data showed a "marked increase".

In another, the government issued a media release in May, highlighting a 24 per cent drop in house break-ins without mentioning property offending across the NT was up by 5.8 per cent.

Drawing on other sources of data, including court statistics, the Australian Bureau of Statistics and the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency (NAAJA), which the authors say provide a "more complete picture", the report found victimisation rates had increased, imprisonment rates and court listings were up and demand for legal services had surged since 2024.

Ben Grimes says the data suggests CLP claims regarding crime rates are misleading. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

NAAJA chief executive Ben Grimes said it was difficult to conclude anything other than that the government was being "intentionally misleading".

"Either they're incompetent, and they don't understand the data and the systems that they're meant to be administering, or they're deliberately painting an inaccurate picture to Territorians," he said.

He pointed to NAAJA's own data, included in the report, which tracks the average number of daily arrests in the NT.

"What we would have expected was to see a surge in arrests after the change of government under the CLP's new laws and policies, followed by a dramatic decrease in arrests as crime was supposedly decreasing," he said.

"But what we really clearly see is over two years of elevated daily arrest rates.

" We now have to be sceptical — every time the government talks about crime, we have to question whether or not they're actually intentionally misleading or hiding pieces of the story from us. "

In response to questions about the report's findings, a Northern Territory government spokesperson said crime and court statistics were publicly available.

"Territorians can see for themselves that their record investment in police and strong law and order measures are beginning to deliver results," they said.

"NT crime statistics are independently compiled by the Department of the Attorney-General and Justice from offences recorded by NT Police.

"Crime statistics in the NT show that the Finocchiaro CLP government is reversing Labor's crime crisis."

World.title: Indigenous people 'very rarely' sit on a jury in SA, report finds
World.content:
Indigenous people "very rarely" sit on a jury in South Australia despite being over-represented in the criminal justice system, a report has found.

Research led by the South Australian Law Reform Institute (SALRI) considered the "complex" and "multi-faceted" reasons behind an "acute lack" of indigenous jurors.

In the report, published by the Australian Institute of Judicial Administration Limited, SALRI made 34 recommendations to improve participation for the state's Attorney-General to consider.

The report found the key issues included electoral enrolment, criminal history disqualifications and cultural safety.

"Indigenous people in South Australia [and indeed nationally] are not being offered the same opportunity to serve on a jury, whether they in fact do so or not," the report found.

"Even potential Indigenous jurors are 'very rare' in Port Augusta, despite the fact that about a quarter of the local community are Indigenous."

John Williams (left) and David Plater (right) contributed to the report. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

SALRI director John Williams said being judged by a jury of your peers was a crucial facet of the justice system.

"Experienced criminal lawyers, experienced judicial officers, experienced members of the Aboriginal community say that they cannot recall moments where anybody is being called … that should give us concern," he said.

Scope for change

Mr Williams said the current practice of solely using the electoral role to summon people for jury duty was problematic, given the under-enrolment of Indigenous voters.

The report raised the idea of using enrolment data from SA's First Nations Voice to Parliament as a supplementary source for future juror selections.

The most recent Voice election was held in March to elect an indigenous advisory body to parliament but was beset with organisational issues, including reports of voters being turned away.

"This is unique in the country and the opportunity to use the electoral role of the Voice as part of a general role for choosing the people for jury, that's an initiative that no other state has," Mr Williams said.

The report considered the idea of using enrolment data from SA's Voice to Parliament as an extra source for future juror selections. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

SALRI cited criminal history as a significant reason for why Indigenous people were disqualified from jury duty, and said the grounds for exclusions in SA were "too broad and lack a coherent basis."

"There are fewer disqualifications to be a Member of Parliament than there are to be on a jury, this leads to a very strange set of circumstances," Mr Williams said.

"It's not clear to me that if someone has a bad driving record, they wouldn't be able to turn their mind to sophisticated questions about whether someone's innocent or not."

SALRI's report made 34 recommendations to improve access for Indigenous people to sit on a jury in SA. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

SALRI deputy director David Plater said the style and content of a jury summons was seen as "formal" and "threatening" and needed to be revised.

"Many people, not just Aboriginal people, when you receive a jury summons, ask yourself, am I in trouble?" he said.

The report also recommended criminal District Court circuits be extended beyond Port Augusta and Mount Gambier to include areas with a significant Indigenous populations such as Port Lincoln and Berri, subject to financial and infrastructure constraints.

Consultation needed

Chief executive of the Aboriginal Legal Rights Movement Klyton Wanganeen said the under-representation impacted Indigenous people standing trial.

"The first thing is that they're not sure of the system, they look at all the faces and there's nothing there that they would make them feel at ease," he said.

" You have non-Aboriginal people standing and sitting making judgements based on the evidence, but they already have preconceived ideas about Aboriginal people, many of which are wrong. "

Klyton Wanganeen is the chief executive of the Aboriginal Legal Rights Movement. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Mr Wanganeen said he would like to see Indigenous jury representation bolstered, but only if it was a free choice and that any law changes must be accompanied with consultation in communities.

"I wouldn't like Aboriginal people to be forced to sit on a jury. I'd like them to make up their own mind because there's a number of risks associated with Aboriginal people who may be on a jury," he said.

Mr Wanganeen said cultural issues could arise around judging someone from a different indigenous cultural group.

"Having people judged by a jury that an Aboriginal person is on, it's not hard to find their identity, their address and those types of things."

"Our people would feel uncomfortable making a decision that leads to a really hefty penalty for an Aboriginal person, bearing in mind they [the jury] don't impose the penalty."

SA Attorney-General Kyam Maher will consider the report's findings and recommendations. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

In a statement, Attorney-General Kyam Maher said the government would carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations and respond "in due course".

"Juries should be representative of the communities they serve and we know that there are barriers to Indigenous participation in juries in SA," he said.

World.title: 'Forgotten' veterans conscripted for Vietnam return to army barracks
World.content:
Former national servicemen conscripted during the Vietnam War have returned to the barracks where they completed training half a century ago.

About 63,000 men were drafted into national service between 1965 and 1972 using a lottery system based on their birthdays.

Nearly a third of the national servicemen, known as nashos, served in Vietnam.

But the rest did not and spent their 18 to 24 months of service in non-combat roles.

Bob Gilligan was forced to leave behind his life in Port Macquarie when he received his conscription letter in 1968.

"You're a little bit trepidant, waiting to see what was going to happen. We didn't know exactly what was going on," he said.

" All of a sudden, you just left your family, friends, work. "

Bob Gilligan, 77, says he has mixed emotions remembering his time as a national serviceman. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

Conscription 'culture shock'

Mr Gilligan spent his first 12 weeks completing initial training at the Singleton Training Area in NSW's Hunter Valley.

"It was a bit of a culture shock. You soon realised it was cold and you were going to be yelled at a lot," he said.

"It was hard. I left a good job for two years; I got engaged while I was still in the national service."

Fellow nasho Ross Durham remembered arriving at Singleton in 1966 with a "fear of the unknown".

"You thought, 'I wonder where I'm going to go, wonder where I'm going to end up,'" he said.

"You live with this nervousness and you get pulled out of your current lifestyle."

Ross Durham and Bob Gilligan worked with Nasho Fair Go to organise the reunion. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

Advocacy organisation Nasho Fair Go arranged for close to 100 nashos to return to Singleton, which is now home to the Australian Army's School of Infantry.

Executive officer at the School of Infantry, Major James Weaver, said it was an honour to host the nashos and show them how the facility had changed.

Major James Weaver says the next generation of soldiers are inspired by the spirit of the nashos. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

"These guys would have been doing all the same stuff back then," he said.

"We're still teaching them to be fit, strong, healthy, work as a team, be good shots and work with the weapon of the day."

'Forgotten' veterans

Nashos who did not serve in Vietnam have struggled to get the same recognition and benefits as other veterans.

Mr Gilligan said the mission of Nasho Fair Go, to be "a voice for the men Australia forgot", resonated with him.

"Vietnam veterans, because it was war service, they came back and they got looked after … they got a bit of recognition," he said.

Nasho Fair Go says it has had to fight to get the same recognition for the national servicemen as other veterans. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

Mr Durham took pride in his contribution to the war effort, despite not having served on the ground in Vietnam.

"I [spent two years] looking after the vehicles going to Vietnam, which I took pretty seriously," he said.

"Those poor guys over there on the front line, the last thing they wanted to have happen is a vehicle breakdown with a Viet Cong running at them."

Mr Durham said he was concerned the stories of many nashos would soon be lost.

"I'd like to see more recognition … but unfortunately, as we all age, our numbers are diminishing," he said.

Nashos toured the Australian Army Infantry Museum in the Singleton Military Area. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

Equal health benefits

On July 1, nashos became eligible to receive the same health benefits as other veterans after a decades-long fight.

Before the change, the group had fewer entitlements to make health-related compensation claims.

"We're able to get treatment for injuries that came from our services," Mr Gilligan said.

Mr Durham said despite the struggle for recognition, he was grateful for his time in the national service.

"I think I became a lot more sensible [from my time] in the army … it didn't do me any harm."

Mr Gilligan said it was a day of mixed emotions.

World.title: Artwork memorialises long-gone 'Tin Town' settlement in western NSW
World.content:
Standing tall on two large monolithic slates in Western NSW are the names of 31 families who once lived in a long-gone town camp.

May Welsh raised seven of her children in what was called "Tin Town" and was one of the last residents to move out.

Now her family's name is etched into a remembrance site for the largely Aboriginal town camp, near Warrena Creek outside Coonamble.

"It means a lot [to me] because my mum and dad used to live here and a lot of friends and relations and that," Ms Welch said.

The slates are part of a regional art trail to commemorate the beauty of the shire's nature and Indigenous history.

May Welsh still fondly remembers her time in Tin Town. (ABC Western Plains: Lily Plass)

"It recognises that this part of Coonamble was once part of the community," Coonamble Regional Art Trail project coordinator Andrew Hull said.

" There's nothing here now but there's a historical marker that will forever tell the story of Tin Town. "

Marking the former settlement

The town camp was one of many reserves outside regional towns in the 1900s.

It was established around the 1940s, with the name Tin Town coming from the materials people used to create homes.

Tin shanties were found in the reserves across regional Australia in the 1900s. (ABC)

"People created their homes from bits of corrugated iron and tin and what they could," Mr Hull said.

"Over the years, more substantial homes were built."

The site was eventually decommissioned in the late 1970s and the homes bulldozed.

Andrew Hull has been the project coordinator since 2025. (ABC Western Plains: Lily Plass)

Following community consultations, the decision was made to place the slates at the empty former site of the settlement.

"It's the site it needs to be at," Mr Hull said.

Despite the settlement not having running water or electricity, Ms Welsh said she preferred the life in Tin Town.

"I still would have rather been back here though; too much going on in town," she said.

Former residents including Ms Welsh and their descendants gathered to mark the unveiling of the slates.

Former Tin Town residents Boon Hamilton and May Welsh gather for the opening of the site. (Supplied: Andrew Hull)

Ms Welsh said she thought the slate would encourage future generations to come and ask questions about the settlement.

"Especially with the young kids that come down and read them," she said.

Using art to remember

The slate is part of Coonamble's Regional Art Trail with other projects in the surrounding towns of Gulargambone and Quambone.

The artwork was created by Ian Marr, who spent his childhood on a station near Wilcannia.

Ian Marr said he made sure to check for any typos before engraving the names. (ABC Western Plains: Lily Plass)

"It's about remembering and it's about where we have lived and loved and had their wonderful lives like this old community here," Marr said.

"Inscription in stone like this is a way of making a readable history, especially in this case for the families.

"It's about giving descendants somewhere to come and somewhere to mark the lives of their ancestors."

Other projects include two galahs made of chicken wire at the entrance to Gulargambone, a mural in Coonamble's Smith Park and a Wailwan contemplation area.

Brian Campbell's galah guards the entrance to Gulargambone. (Supplied: Andrew Hull )

Marr said he hoped the slate will remain there for generations to come.

"I think it'll be here for a very long time.

"I do give a 500-year warranty on my work."

World.title: Call for funding for 'lifesaving' community music programs
World.content:
For Campbell Nicholson, playing an instrument is a way to leave the world behind for a while.

"It's like you're in a zone. Everything else just goes away," he said.

"You don't worry about anything else outside of that room."

He has always been around music.

He remembers being "dragged along" to rehearsals when his mother was the conductor of his local community band at Warragul, in Victoria's east.

But one day, he decided to give an instrument a go.

"I asked her if I could play, and she said she had a spare trombone spot," he said.

"I ended up picking up trombone, and to be honest, I loved it from the beginning."

Campbell Nicholson says playing an instrument lets him leave the world behind. (Supplied: Emma Nicholson)

But he admits that if he had not had a family connection to the band, he might not have found his love for the instrument.

"There's not too many music programs in the community," Campbell said.

A musical culture

Growing up in Canada, music teacher Malcolm McCaffery said music was embedded in schools, which helped foster his passion.

Now living in Gippsland, he is trying to recapture that and pass it on to the next generation.

Mr McCaffery works in school and community settings teaching instruments, and runs bands and jam sessions to connect music makers.

Malcolm McCaffery wants to create a musical culture in Gippsland. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

He believes regional music education is fragmented, with many schools unable to devote teaching hours to the subject, and students facing high costs for private tuition.

He said there was, however, no lack of enthusiasm from young people.

" That's the thing that I think is amazing, how much kids respond to music. "

Mr McCaffery said learning an instrument fostered creativity, resilience and problem-solving skills that kids could apply to other areas of life.

It also gets people off screens and could have a positive impact on mental health.

He said community groups were "filling the gap somewhat" for those young people keen to make music.

Importance of community music

Senior lecturer in music education at Edith Cowan University Jason Goopy said community music programs, those run by local community members beyond formal institutions like schools, could connect regional young people with music in safe settings.

Jason Goopy says community music education programs provide safe spaces for youngsters. (Supplied: Edith Cowan University)

Earlier this year, Dr Goopy led research into the positive impact of community music programs in regional Australia for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, including by promoting mental wellbeing.

"It's something that is saving lives," he said.

He found the programs could also help vulnerable young people develop life skills such as budgeting or looking for work.

"Building confidence and competence in music is setting these young kids up that perhaps have been let down in other areas of life," he said.

Dr Goopy said his study highlighted that young people were highly interested in music and motivated by it, so it could be harnessed as a resource to make a difference.

But he cautioned that programs required funding and support to keep them going.

"The evidence is clear, not only from my research, but from across the field, that arts and cultural education is making a difference and the only way that it can continue to reach further is through funding support," he said.

'An incredible thing'

Community Music Victoria program manager Nicki Johnson said it was difficult to know how many community music programs existed around Victoria.

"We know that there are many people making their music in quiet little niches and nooks around the state," she said.

Nicki Johnson says it's difficult to know how many community music groups exist. (Supplied: Nicki Johnson)

The peak body connects groups with each other to help grow the sector and provides advice on funding opportunities, mostly in the form of sporadic grants.

Ms Johnson said more opportunities need to be provided for people to give music a go, and steady government funding was important to facilitate it.

"If you can break down the barrier to having a go, you get a very quick return on your investment — you can see people's eyes light up," she said.

Campbell said the power of playing an instrument and the connection it brings has helped his mental health.

The VCE student said he had noticed himself becoming more stressed in recent years as school got harder, making it more difficult to stay positive.

He said the band has acted as a buffer against the negativity.

"Having those players and playing music with them, working together, cooperating and making friendships in that group, is such an incredible thing," he said.

Headspace clinical adviser Cat McKenzie said music programs could help young people in regional areas facing mental health issues and feelings of disconnection.

She said music could act as a "vehicle for connection" when shared with others.

"Music … can help us express emotions and process experiences and sometimes communicate things that are hard to put into words," she said.

Cat McKenzie says music supports young people's mental health. (Supplied: Headspace)

Minister for Creative Industries Vicki Ward said creative experiences benefit people of all ages.

"This year alone we're investing more than $1 billion to support our artists, from grassroots programs through to major cultural institutions," she said.

"We fund a range of organisations that support people of all ages to participate in creative activities — from music and dance to circus and theatre."

World.title: Tradies down tools to save man's life with makeshift tourniquet
World.content:
Carpenter Josh Sander and apprentice Gary Tunbridge are being called heroes after downing tools to save a man's life.

They were working on a pergola at a quiet Gracemere cul-de-sac in central Queensland just before 8am on Monday.

"We were just about to jump up on the roof, and we heard a lady across the road start yelling out," Mr Sander said.

The pair rushed to help, finding 93-year-old Ian Barton lying on his back patio, surrounded by blood, having tripped on the lip of a small ramp.

"He's had a bowl of porridge in his hand, and he's landed on it, and it sliced the artery in his wrist … straight away we knew it was an artery," Mr Sander said.

"Going out there, seeing the blood … I sort of stopped for a second and then realised, 'This is life or death now, so I'm going to have to think of something quickly here.'

" We just ripped in and weren't afraid to get a bit bloody and it's turned out for the best. "

Mr Sander said he grabbed a tea towel and wrapped Mr Barton's wrist tightly, but it did not slow the bleeding enough.

"So, I sent Gary over to grab some tape [from the truck], and I ran inside and grabbed one of her [Ms Barton's] dresses and managed to get a lot tighter of a wrap, and then Gary very tightly wrapped the tape around it."

The pair put further pressure on the wound and makeshift tourniquet.

Josh Sander used a dress from the house and tape from his truck to tightly tape the wound and slow the bleeding. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

Mr Sander said the elderly man "faded off" a few times, and the pair had to "wake him up" while they waited 40 minutes for an ambulance.

When they noticed Mr Barton seemed to be choking, Mr Tunbridge spotted false teeth lodged in his mouth.

"He's reached in and pulled them out just to keep the airflow happening," Mr Sander said.

Joy Barton, 89, says the two young tradesmen are heroes in her eyes. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

Mr Barton was taken to Rockhampton hospital, where he remained in a stable condition.

His family are hopeful he could return home in the coming days.

In response to the more than 30-minute wait, a Queensland Ambulance Service spokesperson said the local Gracemere crew was experiencing significant demand at the time.

"But [they] responded as quickly as possible to treat and then transport the patient to hospital," the spokesperson said.

"We want to thank the members of the community for their quick thinking and providing care prior to our crew's arrival."

Joy Barton (right) says her husband, Ian (left), will have a few months of recovery at home when he leaves hospital. (Supplied: Joy Barton)

'It means the world'

Mr Barton's wife, Joy, said she was beyond grateful for the two men's help and considered them both heroes.

"They saved my husband's life … I thought he was going to die," she said.

"When they took him out on the ambulance chair, I kissed him. He looked so terrible."

Ian Barton's family are hopeful he can return home from hospital in the coming days. (Supplied: Joy Barton)

But Ms Barton was relieved to see her husband looking a lot better after an operation that afternoon.

"I said to him, 'Ian, darling, that bloke saved your life,'" she said.

"It means the world to me, what they did."

The couple's granddaughter posted to social media the next day, thanking the two tradesmen for their work. The pair were quickly tracked down and identified.

Ms Barton said she was still trying to work out how to repay them.

But the men said they were just relieved Mr Barton was recovering.

Ian and Joy Barton have been married for more than six decades. (Supplied: Joy Barton)

Mr Sander said it had been a few years since his last first aid course, but this had prompted him to consider booking in for a refresher.

For Mr Tunbridge, who only began his apprenticeship four months ago, it had been an eventful start to his career.

"They never said anything about being a paramedic," he said, firm that there would be no career change anytime soon.

World.title: Stricter regulation on the cards for controversial combat sports
World.content:
A NSW parliamentary inquiry has heard that controversial emerging combat sports, notorious for head-injury risks, are prepared to accept regulation, despite some medical experts calling for them to be blacklisted entirely.

NSW Sport Minister Steve Kamper referred activities like collision running, bare-knuckle boxing, and competitive slapping to a committee to investigate if they should be brought further under the control of the state's Combat Sport Authority (CSA).

On Friday, CSA chair Darren Kane told a hearing that the sports should be subject to stronger controls.

"These sports are dangerous, there's no way of hiding behind that … but rugby league's dangerous, and cricket's dangerous, thoroughbred racing is dangerous," he said.

"There's a very good reason why an ambulance follows every race around the inside of a racetrack, to make sure that they're on hand if a jockey falls off.

" It's a balancing act. "

Darren Kane says the sports should be subject to stronger controls. (Supplied: NSW parliament)

Under heavy scrutiny at the hearing was collision running — where two athletes run at each other and collide.

Neurologist Rowena Mobbs urged the committee to ban the sports being investigated, due to risks of brain injury like concussion, especially in collision running.

"I cannot see that it's a fundamental activity of a human to run at a brick wall, let alone a brick wall coming at you," Dr Mobbs said.

"I just can't see any sense in that."

Rowena Mobbs told the inquiry that the sports carry the risk of traumatic brain injury. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Organisers from the Run Nation Championship (RNC), a prominent collision running event, did not participate in the inquiry, nor did power slap organisers.

Mr Kane noted in his evidence that RNC had been working collaboratively with the CSA for an upcoming planned event in Sydney.

Boxing offshoot

The organisers of two fight groups gave evidence at the hearing — GTG Fight Club and Bare Knuckle Australia (BKA).

BKA spokesman Michael McConnell said there was reluctance in the community around regulation, but that it would be necessary to continue growing the sport.

"We can do this safely, and everyone can be looked after in the best way possible," he said.

" I think having these regulations is essential for this sport to not just survive but thrive and transcend and elevate to the next level. "

Michael McConnell hopes that any regulations are developed fairly and collaboratively. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

BKA said their bouts included vetted fighters, who were matched up by weight class and had their abilities assessed through gloved-up test fights.

The fighters were then paired up and fought without traditional boxing gloves.

BKA co-founder Randall Rayment said he was hesitant about regulation and wanted governments to "back off".

But he said he wanted the government to understand the positive outlet that bare-knuckle-style boxing could be for men who wanted a controlled environment to express themselves.

Harm minimisation

Organisers of the sports being examined have claimed the presence of medical staff at events was a harm-prevention strategy.

But in her evidence, Dr Mobbs refuted that argument.

"I state that no doctor on the sideline will be able to modify the risk of traumatic brain injury in either collision sports or power slap," she said.

" It is window dressing as far as prevention. "

'Do not try this at home': Controversial contact sport on the rise The Run Nation Championship will see two athletes run at each other, in a sport criticised for its head injury risks. Organisers argue the championship has been professionalised, and will grow to be as big as boxing.

In a written submission, the Australian Medical Association's (AMA) NSW branch said it did not endorse any of the sports in question, but it believed regulations were needed.

"Emerging activities typically magnify the most violent aspects of established sports, and thus present a significant public health concern," the AMA submission said.

"The NSW government should invest in evidence-based public education campaigns to increase awareness of the short-term and long-term health consequences of concussion, repetitive head impacts and traumatic brain injury associated with emerging combat sports and comparable activities."

Dr Mobbs and other medical bodies that made submissions agreed that education was crucial.

Social benefit

Sione Tongia and Stephen Gardiner have faced off in a BKA fight, but consider themselves close mates.

"I feel like at the end of the day, we're boxing; we just don't have gloves on," Mr Gardiner said.

Randall Rayment (centre), with fighters Sione Tongia (left) and Stephen Gardiner. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

Mr Tongia said he felt bare-knuckle events should remain to provide a place for young men to channel aggression and differences.

The fight club concept gaining traction in only unregulated Australian state The organiser of this fight club says it saves lives. But critics say it is putting young men at serious risk.

"I guarantee you that two people who have beef, after they fight each other, they feel good, they feel better," he said.

"When I fight, I don't fight for beef.

" I just fight because I feel like I better myself by doing it. "

The parliamentary committee will hand down its findings in a report by the end of 2026.

World.content:

The Duke of Sussex is appealing against his High Court defeat in a £50 million ($97.2 million) phone-hacking case against the publishers of the Daily Mail. Prince Harry, together with five co-claimants, has applied to the Court of Appeal for a new hearing after losing the privacy action against Associated Newspapers in July. Specific threats have been cited in a report prepared by Prince Harry’s team. Getty Images Sir Elton John, his husband David Furnish, Elizabeth Hurley, Sadie Frost and Baroness Lawrence are also appealing. Simon Hughes, the former Liberal Democrat MP, is the only one of the original claimants choosing not to appeal.



In a statement, Callum Galbraith, their lawyer, said: “We confirm that the claimants have today filed applications with the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal the judgments of Mr Justice Nicklin in respect of his dismissal of their claims and the indemnity costs order. Related Article Updated

Royal family Prince Harry holds back tears as he tells court Daily Mail made Meghan’s life ‘an absolute misery’ “The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed.” The group sued Associated Newspapers Limited in relation to allegations of phone hacking, blagging private medical records and other alleged illegal information gathering. Associated strongly denied the claims, which were heard at an 11-week trial in London earlier this year, with Justice Nicklin dismissing all 97 claims made by the original seven claimants in a judgment on July 7.



He said their entire case was based on inference rather than evidence, and accepted the journalists’ “lawful explanations” for how their stories were obtained. Elton John, Prince Harry and Elizabeth Hurley accused the Daily Mail of using illegal ploys such as phone hacking. Getty Images In a decision in August the judge ruled that the group had to pay £9.5 million within seven days as an initial contribution to the publisher’s costs before further hearings to determine the total sum. He also granted a rare indemnity order, which lifts the cap on how much the claimants must contribute towards the publisher’s costs. Such orders are only granted in cases where there has been “unreasonable” conduct or behaviour that takes it “out of the norm”. Prince Harry and the other claimants are also appealing against this order. They have an insurance policy that covers them for £16.2 million, creating a potential shortfall of £18.3 million to pay the total legal costs.



It will now be up to the Court of Appeal to decide whether to grant a new hearing. Prince Harry and his co-claimants will need to convince the court there are reasonable grounds to believe that Justice Nicklin’s decision was wrong. The decision on granting a full appeal hearing will be down to a single Court of Appeal judge, basing his or her decision on written submissions from the claimants’ legal team. If permission to appeal were to be granted, a full hearing would take place in front of three judges. The Duke criticised the judge’s decision at the time, describing the 426-page ruling as a “whitewash”. Loading In a joint statement after the ruling, the Duke and Baroness Lawrence said: “It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected. However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted.



“It feels here like one rule for the newspapers and another for the claimants. While the claimants presented evidence, Mail journalists simply gave denials, and the court chose uncritically to believe them, even in the face of inconsistencies, contradictions and blatant untruths that were obvious to neutral observers in court when compared to the documents.” Related Article Analysis

Royal family Here’s how it all went wrong in Harry’s ‘creepy’ hacking case. No wonder he’s furious Paul Dacre, the editor-in-chief of Associated, condemned the “confused and angry” Duke for bringing the failed claim, saying it formed part of a “conspiracy against the free press”. He said Prince Harry had been persuaded by campaigners to launch a “trumped-up action” that should “never” have reached trial. The London Telegraph revealed last month that the law firm at the heart of the failed claim had gone bankrupt.



Mark Thomson, who founded the company Thomson Heath & Associates in 2009 and owned 100 per cent of the shares, served as a co-ordinating solicitor for the whole group and personally represented Frost and Hughes. In total, seven lawyers from the firm worked on the case. Telegraph, London Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket Cricket Australia responds to explosive Khawaja claims Tom Decent November 7, 2026 — 10:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Cricket Australia says it remains comfortable with the findings of its investigation into the 2018 sandpaper scandal despite explosive new claims from Usman Khawaja that the entire Australian team knew about the ball-tampering plot. In its first response to Khawaja’s revelations, published in this masthead on Saturday, Cricket Australia defended its integrity process and insisted all relevant information provided to the governing body had been properly considered. Australia’s Test captain Pat Cummins and retired cricketer Usman Khawaja. Getty Images “There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month’s series in South Africa,” read a CA statement. “During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.



“All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process.” Former Test batsman Cameron Bancroft, who received a nine-month suspension for his role in the scandal, has read Saturday’s article. He received a call from Khawaja giving him a heads-up regarding his latest claims in an interview ahead of his book launch next week. Cameron Bancroft (left) and Steve Smith face the media after the Cape Town cheating scandal in 2018. Getty Bancroft has largely remained silent about the events of 2018, although he suggested in a 2021 interview that it was “self-explanatory” whether Australia’s bowlers knew about the ball tampering. Khawaja’s account directly challenges the findings of Cricket Australia’s investigation, which concluded that only David Warner, Steve Smith and Bancroft had prior knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper on the ball at Newlands.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows the whistle on more sandpaper use in South Africa in 2018 The retired Test batsman claims sandpaper was first discussed and used during the preceding Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, rather than Cape Town, where Bancroft was caught on camera concealing the material in his pants. “It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” Khawaja said. Khawaja, who compiled notes after the scandal erupted, also questioned why he was never interviewed by Cricket Australia despite sitting beside Bancroft in the Newlands dressing room. “I was sitting next to Cam Bancroft that whole Test match, and I didn’t get interviewed,” he said.



The revelations have renewed scrutiny of Australia’s bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, who issued a joint statement in 2021 denying knowledge of a foreign substance being taken onto the field in Cape Town to alter the condition of the ball. Khawaja believes Warner, Smith and Bancroft were unfairly singled out for punishment when the entire team should have accepted responsibility. World.title: Elon Musk pulls the plug on Cybertruck with all production to end next year
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaElon Musk Elon Musk pulls the plug on Cybertruck with all production to end next year Matt Sedensky November 7, 2026 — 10:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pick-up that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year. Elon Musk announced the model’s demise Friday with a curt post on X, his social media site, simply noting production of the vehicle “will be winding down” around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas. Musk said the move was to allow increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi. Elon Musk launched Tesla’s Cybertruck in 2019. AP For the Cybertruck, a pet project of Musk, who insisted it was Tesla’s best product, it marks an unceremonious end to one of the auto industry’s most ballyhooed debuts. “Few vehicles in history have generated as much attention,” said Armen Hareyan, whose Torque News site covers autos. “The Cybertruck became a cultural symbol – loved, mocked and impossible to ignore.”



View post on X The Cybertruck rolled onto the scene in a dramatic unveiling in 2019, when a Tesla designer hurled a metal ball at the vehicle to demonstrate its supposedly unbreakable glass, only to see it shatter. He repeated the stunt on another window of the truck only to shatter that one, too. Loading Even as some critics scoffed, Musk was steadfast. “I just wanted to make a futuristic battle tank — something that looks like it could come out of Blade Runner or Aliens or something like that but was also highly functional,” he told Automotive News. He called it “a better sports car than a Porsche 911” and “a better truck than an F-150”.



It struck some as the perfect vehicular reflection of the brash, convention-busting Musk. “A really controversial vehicle unveiled by a controversial individual into a market where none of the electric trucks have been able to really capture demand,” said Spencer Penn, a former Tesla executive who left the company before the Cybertruck’s launch and now heads software developer LightSource. Related Article Opinion

Elon Musk Musk turns away from Trump in bid to rescue Tesla Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Penn remembered watching the unveiling and feeling initially revolted by the sight of the Cybertruck, calling its appearance “madness.” But the more he looked at it, the more his opinion changed. He signed up for a pre-sale reservation, though ended up not getting a Cybertruck when Musk’s promises of a price tag under $US40,000 went unmet and the first trucks sold for double or more. Penn called the Cybertruck part of Tesla’s adventurous spirit that drives innovation. “Some of these bets work and some of these bets don’t,” he said.



While the decision to end Cybertruck production may be driven by sales realities, it’s also a reflection of Tesla’s shift to autonomous vehicles, on which Musk is betting the company’s future. The world’s wealthiest man has been appointed to a US committee on the future of warfare. Bloomberg Musk once forecast he’d make 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. US vehicle valuation and automotive research company Kelley Blue Book estimated Tesla sold just 20,237 of the vehicles last year, down about half from the year prior. Sales through the end of September this year were down another 28 per cent, according to Kelley. If the imposing, sharp-angled, dystopian appearance of the Cybertruck wasn’t enough to turn many potential buyers away, Musk did so himself by allying with a panoply of right-wing figures, most notably US President Donald Trump. He alienated some customers as his image morphed from eccentric innovator to polarising force trading his billions for political influence.



Once-passionate Tesla drivers rushed to sell off their cars, or slapped stickers on the bumper declaring, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.” Organisers staged demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms and urged investors to dump shares of the company’s stock. Anger spilled into violence, with Molotov cocktails hurled at Tesla vehicles, charging stations set ablaze, and dealerships covered in graffiti. Loading Lovers of the Cybertruck became targets, too, subjected to shouts of “Nazi!” and extended middle fingers. Ross Blankenship is one of them. When he first laid eyes on the Cybertruck, he felt transported to a world from his childhood, when he would play the sci-fi video game Halo. He had to have it. “I had that sort of child in me wanting to be part of something cool that would change the future of automotive,” Blankenship said in a call from his Cybertruck as he drove through Sunnyside, Colorado.



Even as Blankenship found he agreed with Musk on politics, he hated seeing a vehicle he loved turned into a political symbol. “I never bought it for any other reason than the fascination with the future technology of trucks … so that was a little heartbreaking.” He would buy another Cybertruck again in a heartbeat, calling its end “a sad moment.” AP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
Review Eating outMount Hawthorn A Perth neighbourhood bar branches into a new space that’s small in size yet big in ambition – and earns a hat in the process Max Veenhuyzen November 7, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. 1 / 3 Goat’s curd dumplings. Danica Zuks 2 / 3 Chocolate mousse with black banana at Bar Lyla. Danica Zuks 3 / 3 Shallot tarte tatin. Danica Zuks Previous Slide Next Slide Good Food hat 15 / 20 How we score Bar Lyla Contemporary$$$$ Imagine you’re out for dinner and drinks somewhere. How do you know that the people next to you work in hospitality? Don’t worry, they’ll tell you. Not in the same way that, as the joke goes, vegans and Crossfitters might, but via subtler means. They might, for instance, ask to dine at the bar: the best place, of course, to talk shop with bartenders. If a group orders a round of Negronis right away, odds are that they’re hospo folks having the night off.





But as far as lumens go, Lyla is as bright as its predecessor – so not bright at all – with tabletop mushroom lamps and the open kitchen among the space’s few light sources. You’ll notice the latter in the back corner behind the bar which is at least as big as the cooking area. If it wasn’t clear, drinks are a big deal at Bar Lyla: just as co-owner Jess Blyth hoped when she launched venue number two across the road from her Mount Hawthorn wine bar, Sonny’s. Yet as it turns, the food here is as notable as what’s being poured. As to be expected, I think, when you go into partnership with Lyla’s other owner, Sofika Boulton: a kitchen phenom who has been making noise over the past decade via stints at Wildflower, Bar Rogue and, of course, Sonny’s. Cocktails and wine represent the backbone of Bar Lyla. Danica Zuks I don’t know if it’s a change of scenery, a major career growth spurt since I last reviewed Sonny’s in 2024 or the excitement that comes with managing a tighter, more fluid blackboard menu, but if Boulton’s previous appointments denoted her as a talent to watch, then Lyla confirms that she has well and truly arrived.



Lyla’s menu might just be nine-dishes long, but clever thinking ensures each plate bangs. Lyla’s pickle plate, for example, might feature fleshy green olives, crisp hoops of fennel and spears of cucumber bathed in a performance-enhancing preserved lemon brine. These perky vegetables aren’t just a great start to dinner: they also make cameos throughout the night. That sharp vegetal edge in the house martini? Thanks vegetable brine! Bathing crunchy slices of underripe peach in the fennel’s pickling liquid gives them an intriguing anise flavour that pairs great with fatty salumi. As at Sonny’s, things cooked over charcoal are another highlight. Dense swordfish loin from Anthony Haslewood of Revolution Fisheries is slowly grilled to preserve its luscious, luxurious mouthfeel. You’d happily eat it as is but presented atop a zippy apple “dashi” and finely cut strips of veg, it’s a fish course for the ages. Related Article Built by hand, cooked by heart: The story behind Freo’s backyard supper club Baking remains one of Boulton’s strengths. Each day, she and offsider Nate McGuckin bake a dozen shallot tarte tatins that, topped with chunks of Cambray’s luscious Blackwood Blue, flip the French classic into a joyous new-age cheese course. (Also from the department of clever cheese change-ups: check out those golfball-sized “dumplings” of goat’s curd and ricotta – a gnudi by any other name – that are poached to order for maximum lightness!)



Fluffy milk buns are more pillowy and soft than brioche-rich. They get warmed in the oven and brushed with fermented honey while a creamy kefir-cultured butter quickly melts into the pull-apart bun’s lacquered crevices. For dessert, leftover buns – after being soaked in a syrup made with sake and passionfruit-like mountain marigold – get reborn as sake “babas” in one of the more inspired examples of upcycling day-old bread I’ve tasted lately. While you’re free to cherry-pick individual dishes, opting for the one-of-everything is the best way to appreciate Boulton’s quiet genius while locking up a great meal deal for two. (The set menu comes with a discounted buy-in compared to ordering everything individually.) Even better, it frees up your CPU for other key decisions, starting with what to drink. Daisy Case, sommelier across Lyla and Sonny’s, doesn’t just know their stuff: they know how to win guests’ confidence while playing matchmaker between drinker and the treasures of Lyla’s stockpile of booze. Ask Case about secret bottles that they’ve stashed away, and they might direct you towards a northern Italian red blend containing the lesser-seen variety, schiava.



Like Boulton – and Blyth and all of their colleagues at the bar – Case isn’t afraid to do things their way. As a result, Lyla and Perth’s dining scene is all the richer for it. The low-down Atmosphere: a cosy wining and dining destination proving – hallelujah! – there’s still room for venues with personality in our AI slop era. Go-to dishes: kefir milk buns with fermented honey ($12), shallot tarte tatin ($16), dark chocolate mousse ($8), “sake baba” ($10). Drinks: snappy cocktails from Jess Blyth, cool wines via Daisy Case, plus more temptation than thirsty guests will be able to refuse. Cost: about $140 for two people, excluding drinks. It took 10 years to plan and four years to build, and the budget blew out from $11 million to more than $100 million. But when the Museum of Old and New Art opened its two-level, subterranean Phrontisterion in June, the Hobart library became the only one of its kind in the world.

Thirty-thousand books line the shelves, but there is no Dewey Decimal System organising them. In fact, visitors don’t even need to return them to the spot they found them; if they want to put the book on a different shelf at the opposite end of another floor, they are more than welcome to.

The O, a custom app informed by cameras across the wing, will track down the book. It will also light up the spines of books related to whichever one you’re touching at that moment.

Watch the video below for a full tour of MONA’s Phrontisterion, where librarian Mary Lijnzaad explains how they allow visitors to flick through the pages of a rare, 403-year-old book that nobody is allowed to touch. You can also see the kids’ section, engulfed in a plywood design that makes you feel as though you’re sitting inside a book.

Raiders forward Hudson Young says the PNG Chiefs’ tax-free dollars will help wipe his mortgage and look after his family financially, while also conceding he wants to fulfil his final year at Canberra – provided coach Ricky Stuart will have him. Young touched down in Sydney late on Friday, just hours after Chiefs coach Willie Peters confirmed out-of-favour Rooster Sam Walker was a serious option as the club’s inaugural halfback if Walker was genuine about a move north. Hudson Young toured Port Moresby this week. The Chiefs flew Young to Port Moresby on Wednesday, and hope to nail down the representative forward, who is recovering from a season-ending Achilles injury, as signing #008. Young does not want to leave the Chiefs waiting, and said it was important he got the chance to inspect the country for himself so he was comfortable with any decision to commit.



The newcomers initially discussed a $900,000-a-season offer for Young, only for the NRL to confirm his market value under the salary cap would be $1 million. Tax-free third-party sponsors will also sweeten any deal for Young, who is regarded as one of the best second-rowers in rugby league. Hudson Young arrives back at Sydney airport after his trip to tour the PNG Chiefs facilities in Port Moresby. Christian Nicolussi/SMH The Raiders sensationally pulled their $4.4m four-year offer last week, and Stuart later told The Canberra Times he would entertain an early release for Young. Young has stayed quiet about his future – until now. “PNG will want a decision soon, and I need to go back and speak to my family,” Young told this masthead.



“One of the reasons why I’ve done this is because I’m 28 years old, I’m single, I don’t have any family in Canberra. It’s nothing against Canberra as to why I’ve gone up there and had a look. Raiders backrower Hudson Young suffered a season-ending injury in Canberra’s round 20 win over South Sydney. NRL Imagery “Canberra is a club I love. ‘Sticky’ [Stuart] has given me everything, and he still does. “But it is in the back of my mind I can do two or three years up there and come home and be mortgage free. “I haven’t come from money, so there are those benefits I can give my family and everyone around me. I also want to keep developing as a good footballer.



“I’m just doing what 170 other blokes [in the NRL] are doing and exploring my options. It’s not about exploring my value. Related Article NRL 2026 Parramatta set to welcome Addo-Carr back into the fold after false positive “There’s nothing there (in Canberra) holding me back from doing something like this. It’s about where do I want to be in the next stage of my life and career. “There’s a lot to take in. A lot has been said. I need to make a decision and back it.” Young said it had never entered his mind he would cut and run early from the Raiders in 2027.



“If I do move on in 2028, I don’t want to play for another club in 2027,” he said. “But it comes down to Sticky, it’s his team, if he doesn’t see fit for me to play at the club, I’d have to make a decision around that as well. “But it’s never crossed my mind for that to happen. I want to get back to 100 per cent with my leg and get back playing my best footy I can.” The Raiders offered Young the richest contract in the club’s history, and were even prepared to extend the deal to a fifth season. Club officials became frustrated when Young’s management asked for ratchet clauses to be included in any package to allow for the salary cap rising in future years, which could have seen the back-rower’s earning surge towards $1.3m a year, a figure the Raiders were never going to entertain.



Young ruptured his Achilles in the second half of the season, which cost him his Kangaroos jersey at the World Cup. It also paused his chance to tour Port Moresby earlier. He will return to pre-season training in the next fortnight, and said he would be back running before Christmas. The Chiefs have already signed Joey Manu, Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Zac Lomax, Brian To’o, Connor Watson and Matty Lees. The Duke of Sussex is appealing against his High Court defeat in a £50 million ($97.2 million) phone-hacking case against the publishers of the Daily Mail. Prince Harry, together with five co-claimants, has applied to the Court of Appeal for a new hearing after losing the privacy action against Associated Newspapers in July. Specific threats have been cited in a report prepared by Prince Harry’s team. Getty Images Sir Elton John, his husband David Furnish, Elizabeth Hurley, Sadie Frost and Baroness Lawrence are also appealing. Simon Hughes, the former Liberal Democrat MP, is the only one of the original claimants choosing not to appeal.



In a statement, Callum Galbraith, their lawyer, said: “We confirm that the claimants have today filed applications with the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal the judgments of Mr Justice Nicklin in respect of his dismissal of their claims and the indemnity costs order. Related Article Updated

Royal family Prince Harry holds back tears as he tells court Daily Mail made Meghan’s life ‘an absolute misery’ “The claimants respectfully disagree with those unprecedented decisions, which they consider to be legally and factually flawed.” The group sued Associated Newspapers Limited in relation to allegations of phone hacking, blagging private medical records and other alleged illegal information gathering. Associated strongly denied the claims, which were heard at an 11-week trial in London earlier this year, with Justice Nicklin dismissing all 97 claims made by the original seven claimants in a judgment on July 7.



He said their entire case was based on inference rather than evidence, and accepted the journalists’ “lawful explanations” for how their stories were obtained. Elton John, Prince Harry and Elizabeth Hurley accused the Daily Mail of using illegal ploys such as phone hacking. Getty Images In a decision in August the judge ruled that the group had to pay £9.5 million within seven days as an initial contribution to the publisher’s costs before further hearings to determine the total sum. He also granted a rare indemnity order, which lifts the cap on how much the claimants must contribute towards the publisher’s costs. Such orders are only granted in cases where there has been “unreasonable” conduct or behaviour that takes it “out of the norm”. Prince Harry and the other claimants are also appealing against this order. They have an insurance policy that covers them for £16.2 million, creating a potential shortfall of £18.3 million to pay the total legal costs.



It will now be up to the Court of Appeal to decide whether to grant a new hearing. Prince Harry and his co-claimants will need to convince the court there are reasonable grounds to believe that Justice Nicklin’s decision was wrong. The decision on granting a full appeal hearing will be down to a single Court of Appeal judge, basing his or her decision on written submissions from the claimants’ legal team. If permission to appeal were to be granted, a full hearing would take place in front of three judges. The Duke criticised the judge’s decision at the time, describing the 426-page ruling as a “whitewash”. Loading In a joint statement after the ruling, the Duke and Baroness Lawrence said: “It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected. However, the lengths to which the court has gone to exonerate the Mail is as shocking as it is totally unwarranted.



“It feels here like one rule for the newspapers and another for the claimants. While the claimants presented evidence, Mail journalists simply gave denials, and the court chose uncritically to believe them, even in the face of inconsistencies, contradictions and blatant untruths that were obvious to neutral observers in court when compared to the documents.” Related Article Analysis

Royal family Here’s how it all went wrong in Harry’s ‘creepy’ hacking case. No wonder he’s furious Paul Dacre, the editor-in-chief of Associated, condemned the “confused and angry” Duke for bringing the failed claim, saying it formed part of a “conspiracy against the free press”. He said Prince Harry had been persuaded by campaigners to launch a “trumped-up action” that should “never” have reached trial. The London Telegraph revealed last month that the law firm at the heart of the failed claim had gone bankrupt.



Mark Thomson, who founded the company Thomson Heath & Associates in 2009 and owned 100 per cent of the shares, served as a co-ordinating solicitor for the whole group and personally represented Frost and Hughes. In total, seven lawyers from the firm worked on the case. Telegraph, London Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Cricket Australia says it remains comfortable with the findings of its investigation into the 2018 sandpaper scandal despite explosive new claims from Usman Khawaja that the entire Australian team knew about the ball-tampering plot. In its first response to Khawaja’s revelations, published in this masthead on Saturday, Cricket Australia defended its integrity process and insisted all relevant information provided to the governing body had been properly considered. Australia’s Test captain Pat Cummins and retired cricketer Usman Khawaja. Getty Images “There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month’s series in South Africa,” read a CA statement. “During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.



“All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process.” Former Test batsman Cameron Bancroft, who received a nine-month suspension for his role in the scandal, has read Saturday’s article. He received a call from Khawaja giving him a heads-up regarding his latest claims in an interview ahead of his book launch next week. Cameron Bancroft (left) and Steve Smith face the media after the Cape Town cheating scandal in 2018. Getty Bancroft has largely remained silent about the events of 2018, although he suggested in a 2021 interview that it was “self-explanatory” whether Australia’s bowlers knew about the ball tampering. Khawaja’s account directly challenges the findings of Cricket Australia’s investigation, which concluded that only David Warner, Steve Smith and Bancroft had prior knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper on the ball at Newlands.

Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” Khawaja said. Khawaja, who compiled notes after the scandal erupted, also questioned why he was never interviewed by Cricket Australia despite sitting beside Bancroft in the Newlands dressing room. “I was sitting next to Cam Bancroft that whole Test match, and I didn’t get interviewed,” he said.



The revelations have renewed scrutiny of Australia’s bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, who issued a joint statement in 2021 denying knowledge of a foreign substance being taken onto the field in Cape Town to alter the condition of the ball. Khawaja believes Warner, Smith and Bancroft were unfairly singled out for punishment when the entire team should have accepted responsibility. World.title: Elon Musk pulls the plug on Cybertruck with all production to end next year
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaElon Musk Elon Musk pulls the plug on Cybertruck with all production to end next year Matt Sedensky November 7, 2026 — 10:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pick-up that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year. Elon Musk announced the model’s demise Friday with a curt post on X, his social media site, simply noting production of the vehicle “will be winding down” around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas. Musk said the move was to allow increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi. Elon Musk launched Tesla’s Cybertruck in 2019. AP For the Cybertruck, a pet project of Musk, who insisted it was Tesla’s best product, it marks an unceremonious end to one of the auto industry’s most ballyhooed debuts. “Few vehicles in history have generated as much attention,” said Armen Hareyan, whose Torque News site covers autos. “The Cybertruck became a cultural symbol – loved, mocked and impossible to ignore.”



View post on X The Cybertruck rolled onto the scene in a dramatic unveiling in 2019, when a Tesla designer hurled a metal ball at the vehicle to demonstrate its supposedly unbreakable glass, only to see it shatter. He repeated the stunt on another window of the truck only to shatter that one, too. Loading Even as some critics scoffed, Musk was steadfast. “I just wanted to make a futuristic battle tank — something that looks like it could come out of Blade Runner or Aliens or something like that but was also highly functional,” he told Automotive News. He called it “a better sports car than a Porsche 911” and “a better truck than an F-150”.



It struck some as the perfect vehicular reflection of the brash, convention-busting Musk. “A really controversial vehicle unveiled by a controversial individual into a market where none of the electric trucks have been able to really capture demand,” said Spencer Penn, a former Tesla executive who left the company before the Cybertruck’s launch and now heads software developer LightSource. Related Article Opinion

Elon Musk Musk turns away from Trump in bid to rescue Tesla Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Penn remembered watching the unveiling and feeling initially revolted by the sight of the Cybertruck, calling its appearance “madness.” But the more he looked at it, the more his opinion changed. He signed up for a pre-sale reservation, though ended up not getting a Cybertruck when Musk’s promises of a price tag under $US40,000 went unmet and the first trucks sold for double or more. Penn called the Cybertruck part of Tesla’s adventurous spirit that drives innovation. “Some of these bets work and some of these bets don’t,” he said.



While the decision to end Cybertruck production may be driven by sales realities, it’s also a reflection of Tesla’s shift to autonomous vehicles, on which Musk is betting the company’s future. The world’s wealthiest man has been appointed to a US committee on the future of warfare. Bloomberg Musk once forecast he’d make 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. US vehicle valuation and automotive research company Kelley Blue Book estimated Tesla sold just 20,237 of the vehicles last year, down about half from the year prior. Sales through the end of September this year were down another 28 per cent, according to Kelley. If the imposing, sharp-angled, dystopian appearance of the Cybertruck wasn’t enough to turn many potential buyers away, Musk did so himself by allying with a panoply of right-wing figures, most notably US President Donald Trump. He alienated some customers as his image morphed from eccentric innovator to polarising force trading his billions for political influence.



Once-passionate Tesla drivers rushed to sell off their cars, or slapped stickers on the bumper declaring, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.” Organisers staged demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms and urged investors to dump shares of the company’s stock. Anger spilled into violence, with Molotov cocktails hurled at Tesla vehicles, charging stations set ablaze, and dealerships covered in graffiti. Loading Lovers of the Cybertruck became targets, too, subjected to shouts of “Nazi!” and extended middle fingers. Ross Blankenship is one of them. When he first laid eyes on the Cybertruck, he felt transported to a world from his childhood, when he would play the sci-fi video game Halo. He had to have it. “I had that sort of child in me wanting to be part of something cool that would change the future of automotive,” Blankenship said in a call from his Cybertruck as he drove through Sunnyside, Colorado.



Even as Blankenship found he agreed with Musk on politics, he hated seeing a vehicle he loved turned into a political symbol. “I never bought it for any other reason than the fascination with the future technology of trucks … so that was a little heartbreaking.” He would buy another Cybertruck again in a heartbeat, calling its end “a sad moment.” AP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
