The O, a custom app informed by cameras across the wing, will track down the book. It will also light up the spines of books related to whichever one you’re touching at that moment.

Watch the video below for a full tour of MONA’s Phrontisterion, where librarian Mary Lijnzaad explains how they allow visitors to flick through the pages of a rare, 403-year-old book that nobody is allowed to touch. You can also see the kids’ section, engulfed in a plywood design that makes you feel as though you’re sitting inside a book.

World.title: ‘Nothing against Canberra’: Young breaks silence about his future
World.content:
Exclusive SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Nothing against Canberra’: Young breaks silence about his future Christian Nicolussi November 7, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Raiders forward Hudson Young says the PNG Chiefs’ tax-free dollars will help wipe his mortgage and look after his family financially, while also conceding he wants to fulfil his final year at Canberra – provided coach Ricky Stuart will have him. Young touched down in Sydney late on Friday, just hours after Chiefs coach Willie Peters confirmed out-of-favour Rooster Sam Walker was a serious option as the club’s inaugural halfback if Walker was genuine about a move north. Hudson Young toured Port Moresby this week. The Chiefs flew Young to Port Moresby on Wednesday, and hope to nail down the representative forward, who is recovering from a season-ending Achilles injury, as signing #008. Young does not want to leave the Chiefs waiting, and said it was important he got the chance to inspect the country for himself so he was comfortable with any decision to commit.



The newcomers initially discussed a $900,000-a-season offer for Young, only for the NRL to confirm his market value under the salary cap would be $1 million. Tax-free third-party sponsors will also sweeten any deal for Young, who is regarded as one of the best second-rowers in rugby league. Hudson Young arrives back at Sydney airport after his trip to tour the PNG Chiefs facilities in Port Moresby. Christian Nicolussi/SMH The Raiders sensationally pulled their $4.4m four-year offer last week, and Stuart later told The Canberra Times he would entertain an early release for Young. Young has stayed quiet about his future – until now. “PNG will want a decision soon, and I need to go back and speak to my family,” Young told this masthead.



“One of the reasons why I’ve done this is because I’m 28 years old, I’m single, I don’t have any family in Canberra. It’s nothing against Canberra as to why I’ve gone up there and had a look. Raiders backrower Hudson Young suffered a season-ending injury in Canberra’s round 20 win over South Sydney. NRL Imagery “Canberra is a club I love. ‘Sticky’ [Stuart] has given me everything, and he still does. “But it is in the back of my mind I can do two or three years up there and come home and be mortgage free. “I haven’t come from money, so there are those benefits I can give my family and everyone around me. I also want to keep developing as a good footballer.



“I’m just doing what 170 other blokes [in the NRL] are doing and exploring my options. It’s not about exploring my value. Related Article NRL 2026 Parramatta set to welcome Addo-Carr back into the fold after false positive “There’s nothing there (in Canberra) holding me back from doing something like this. It’s about where do I want to be in the next stage of my life and career. “There’s a lot to take in. A lot has been said. I need to make a decision and back it.” Young said it had never entered his mind he would cut and run early from the Raiders in 2027.



“If I do move on in 2028, I don’t want to play for another club in 2027,” he said. “But it comes down to Sticky, it’s his team, if he doesn’t see fit for me to play at the club, I’d have to make a decision around that as well. “But it’s never crossed my mind for that to happen. I want to get back to 100 per cent with my leg and get back playing my best footy I can.” The Raiders offered Young the richest contract in the club’s history, and were even prepared to extend the deal to a fifth season. Club officials became frustrated when Young’s management asked for ratchet clauses to be included in any package to allow for the salary cap rising in future years, which could have seen the back-rower’s earning surge towards $1.3m a year, a figure the Raiders were never going to entertain.



Young ruptured his Achilles in the second half of the season, which cost him his Kangaroos jersey at the World Cup. It also paused his chance to tour Port Moresby earlier. He will return to pre-season training in the next fortnight, and said he would be back running before Christmas. The Chiefs have already signed Joey Manu, Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Zac Lomax, Brian To’o, Connor Watson and Matty Lees. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Crews scramble to fix burst water main in Porirua
World.content:
Urgent repairs are under way as a burst water main interrupts supplies to residents in Titahi Bay in Porirua, north of Wellington City.

Crews have located the damaged section of pipe supplying the suburb and water is being used from local reservoirs, water provider Tiaki Wai says.

It warns that the reserve is likely to be depleted soon and Titahi Bay residents would then be without water.

Repairs should be completed by 2pm, a Tiaki Wai spokesperson said, although that timeline could change as the work progresses.

Water tankers have been requested to support residents during the outage and information on their locations should be available soon.

A statement from Tiaki Wai said it appreciated the community's patience while crews completed the repair and restored water services safely.

World.title: One dead, four injured in Wellington crash
World.content:
One person has died and four others injured after a crash in Wellington early Saturday morning.

Police got the call to the single-vehicle crash on Brandon Street about 2.10am.

"Sadly, one person was pronounced deceased and four others were injured and transported to hospital."

Police said the Serious Crash Unit had also been at the scene.

Road closures were put in place overnight at the meeting of Brandon Street and Customhouse Quay.

World.title: Could AI help save pilot whales from a stranding?
World.content:
Warning: Some readers may find the video in this story upsetting.

Audio player for " How AI could help prevent whale strandings " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2397552%2Fcould-ai-help-save-pilot-whales-from-a-stranding

How AI could help prevent whale strandings Saturday Morning Download MP3 20m

The death of pilot whales in Wairarapa after a stranding this week is not a sight anyone wants to see repeated and one project has been utilising AI to help the cause.

About 50 pilot whales were found trapped amongst rocks of the Ngawi coastline on Thursday, and despite efforts, none survived.

Pilot Pulse is a project prompted by concerned locals in Mohua Golden Bay, an area that sees an almost annual occurrence of mass pilot whale strandings.

Daren Grover from whale rescue group Project Jonah told Saturday Mornings the project has been trying to hear and track whales through echolocations before they are found on the beach.

"These animals live in a world of sound.

"Traditionally, acoustic buoys and acoustic monitors were something that you would put out in the ocean, you would hit record and then go back three to six months later, take the buoy back in, and then someone would have to sit and listen to hundreds and hundreds of hours of recordings."

But AI has meant the signals could be received in an instant.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407929786112

Grover said they were able to trial the technology last year with the goal of hearing the pilot whales.

"In a period from December last year through to May this year, we heard pilot whales twice... once on the day that there was a mass stranding, and we heard them once when there wasn't a mass stranding.

"So right now, we've gathered some data. It's not a lot of data, and we need to gather a lot more data before we can start to move forward with any future action."

Being able to get fast detection means response teams can mobilize in a high alert situation.

"We're looking at preparedness in one of the global stranding hotspots.

"The AI... it really has kind of turbocharged our ability to refine the notifications, and so when the buoy was launched last December on its first trial, we were getting notifications pretty much hourly."

People gather to assist in the pilot whale stranding near Wairarapa. Andrew Sim

Grover said this was different from preventing pilot whales from stranding in the first place as there was still an ethical debate to be had as to whether that should be done at all.

"We don't know why the pilot whales have stranded in the moment.

"We think about, well, let's stop them from stranding. And does that mean physical intervention? And any physical interaction they have with us is likely to cause stress."

Grover explained that heat stroke was the main cause of death for a stranded pilot whale, as they have a thick layer of blubber which helps them buoyancy.

But there is also the added stress of being surrounded by humans and separated from the rest of the pod.

Grover said the goal was now to get enough money and send a second buoy out to track the direction of the whales making the calls as they come through the bay.

World.title: Country Life: Calves, callouts and 75 years of country vetting
World.content:
Veterinarian Ben Mitchell has his work clothes lined up ready to jump into when the farmers call.

On a cold July morning he was heading out from his base at New Plymouth Vet Group to the Jordan dairy farm which was in the thick of calving.

"A thermal underneath, which is going to hopefully keep me warm out there, and then just some overalls and I've got some old school socks from many years ago and my gumboots."

He may have to help deliver a calf, but today it's a vet check and a natter about nutrition with fifth-generation dairy farmer Amanda Jordan.

Mitchell is eight years out of vet school but his connection with Jordan goes back a long way.

"I met Ben when he was just home from the hospital as a few-days-old baby. I got a cuddle," Jordan told Country Life.

Audio player for " 75 years of country calls and clinic care " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/country/2393365%2Fcountry-life-calves-callouts-and-75-years-of-country-vetting

75 years of country calls and clinic care Country Life Download MP3 22m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

New Plymouth Vet Group has many life-long clients like Jordan who have kept up the connection over generations.

"I was a little one at the cow shed when the vets were calling," she said.

Founded in 1951 by farmers, the group has expanded alongside New Plymouth into a mixed practice caring for livestock and pets.

The practice celebrated 75 years in November.

Farmers make up the board and there are about 75 to 80 dairy, sheep and beef official farm members of the "club".

The practice reinvests its small profit back into the clinic and aims to keep its prices as low as possible, catering for companion animals for urban clients as well these days.

Its central New Plymouth premises also cares for injured wild birds.

At the Jordan farm, Mitchell is gloved up with his stethoscope around his neck, checking on one of the heifer calves nestled in the calf shed.

Jordan told him calving had gone well so far with only a couple of bigger calves in the last couple of days.

Good spring weather had helped get their mum's colostrum into them, she said, upping the antibodies and guarding against sickness.

Jordan is one of the vet group's board members and praised the valuable service, particularly during busy times like calving.

Vet Ben Mitchell with days-old calves in the calf shed RNZ/Sally Round

"They drop and run and you can't really get any other professionals in any other industries to do that for you …you ring, the team triage you and where we're situated, you can have a vet on farm in 20 minutes if it's an emergency," she said.

With advances in genetics and more on-farm technology monitoring animal health, things have changed, even during Mitchell's time working as a vet.

"There's so much with genetics and with farm management plans and things," he said.

"I've only been out eight years, but I feel like even in that time, that we're calving [fewer] cows than we used to and so we are seeing some noticeable improvements."

He said work had moved more towards consultancy, education and guidance.

"We try to be very proactive and avoid problems before we see them."

Jordan said breeding for traits like easy calving and teat placement had created fewer problems which would necessitate a vet call-out.

"But you've still got to feed a cow well all year round to be able to get them in calf back in spring or whatever.

"There's no luck in farming. We've got to plan ahead and that's where the relationship with our vets comes in, whether that's nutrition or minerals, anything like that."

Vet Ben Mitchell and dairy farmer Amanda Jordan RNZ/Sally Round

Vets are also an important bulwark for farmers during tough times, Jordan said, such as during a tuberculosis outbreak in the herd.

"The well-being of your animals is so important [...] them standing beside us and talking us through what would be next, it was fantastic."

She said vets and a trusted vet-client relationship were a crucial part of rural communities.

"They can be some of the first people to notice that there might be an underlying issue on a farm. It might be skinny cows or calves aren't quite going well because they're not getting the time because [farmers are] overwhelmed."

Mitchell agreed a huge part of the job was building relationships over time with farmers who often work in isolation.

World.title: Election day weather turns sour with lightning, heavy rain and thunderstorms
World.content:
Most of the North Island and the upper South Island is under a severe thunderstorm watch as voters head to the polls on election day.

Overnight Friday, MetService recorded nearly 2000 lightning strikes throughout the top of the North Island, as well as heavy rainfall, with downpours reaching 33.5mm an hour in the Bay of Plenty.

About 1845 lightning strikes were recorded from midnight.

The MetService weather map for Election Day shows weather warnings in the North Island and upper South Island. MetService / Screenshot

Fire and Emergency responded to five weather-related callouts overnight, including flooding and reports of fallen trees.

In Auckland's Grey Lynn between Elgin and Northland streets, a billboard came down in strong winds. It knocked over fencing and is lying across the footpath and cycle lane and onto the road.

MetService is warning of a moderate risk that thunderstorms may become severe across a broad swath of the country, from Auckland and Coromandel Peninsula in the north to inland parts of the South Island north of Tekapo.

The watch is in place already for the northern areas and kicks in from 1pm in the south.

The watch also includes the Bay of Plenty, across the central high country to Taranaki, Whanganui southwards to northern and eastern parts of Wellington, and about the Tararua District and Wairarapa.

MetService is scheduled to update the watch at 6pm.

Severe thunderstorms would produce localised downpours of 25 to 40mm an hour, it said.

Rainfall of this intensity can cause surface and/or flash flooding, especially about low-lying areas such as streams, rivers or narrow valleys, and may also lead to slips.

World.title: I don’t have my ex-wife or daughter’s details, can I leave them my house? Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, No Stupid Questions, with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, Money with Susan Edmunds.

I divorced in my 50s, and had to rebuild and restructure my life. However, one thing has never changed - I still want my former wife and daughter to receive the benefit of what would have been theirs had we remained together.

Regardless of our circumstances, they are still my family. My concern relates to my estate and my will.

I have very limited information about their whereabouts. I know that they are no longer living in New Zealand, despite retaining New Zealand citizenship, and that they have migrated overseas.

I know the country in which they now live, but I do not have any current contact details for either of them.

I have a will with Public Trust and would like my estate to pass to them. I live alone, own a modest mortgage-free home and still have many possessions with sentimental value from earlier years.

My question is what ability do executors have to locate beneficiaries, when contact details are unavailable? My daughter, who is now 26 years old, still has a KiwiSaver account that I established for her in 2008, which may provide some evidence of her existence and identity.

I am concerned that attempts to locate beneficiaries could become a lengthy and expensive process, potentially creating significant legal costs and delaying the administration of the estate. I have acquaintances, but no close family or friends whom I could rely upon to assist, so I expect I would be largely dependent on the executors to manage everything.

I asked Justine Wood, who is a specialist trustee at Public Trust, what she would advise.

She said you were not alone in having a complex family situation, and your will should reflect your wishes and what is important to you, whatever form that takes.

"It's not clear whether you made your will before or after your divorce, which might change things, or if you've already included your ex-wife and daughter in your will, or just considering to do so," she said.

If your will was made before your divorce, your instructions for your ex-wife to inherit could be void, unless you specified you'd like her to inherit from you, despite a divorce, so it would be a good idea to review your will as a first step.

"Even if the will was made after your divorce, we'd still recommend a review, if you're feeling uncertain about how it communicates your wishes or want to clarify anything. Our team are always happy to help with any questions, so please give us a call."

She said not having your ex-wife or daughter's current contact details would not prevent your estate being left to them.

"It sounds like you may have named Public Trust the executor of your estate. When Public Trust is named executor, part of our role is to identify and work with the beneficiaries named in the will, and distribute the estate according to the willmaker's instructions.

"We regularly need to locate beneficiaries as part of this work. Even if you do not name Public Trust as your executor, whoever you name may be able to contact Public Trust for support.

"Where a beneficiary cannot be located, we have processes for trying to find them. The fact your ex-wife and daughter are New Zealand citizens is helpful, although them living overseas could make things trickier.

"Depending on the circumstances and the information available, this can involve carrying out online and public-record searches, and using specialist services, such as genealogists or private investigators.

"You are correct that locating a beneficiary can add time and expense to administering an estate. Sometimes, it can take months or years to settle these types of estates, if the people cannot be found - that's something for you to consider.

"A useful thing you could do is make the executor's job as straightforward as possible and give them a starting point. While you're able to do so, consider providing the executor with everything you currently know about your ex-wife and daughter, such as their full names, dates and places of birth, previous addresses, the country they are believed to be living in, any details of relatives or other people who may be able to help, and any other information that could assist in identifying or locating them.

"That information could really help further down the track."

I understand the gifting threshold is $8500 a year within five years of going into care [for people who are applying for the rest home subsidy]. Beyond that is $27,000 a year.

How far back can MSD go in assessing amounts for asset testing? Is it covered by the Limitations Act 2010?

A Ministry of Social Development spokesperson said there was no time limit on how far back it might consider assets that had been gifted.

"As you've stated, $27,000 is the threshold for gifting in any one year beyond the five-year gifting period."

I have been donating money to various organisations this year and have sent the relevant details to IRD in order to receive a small tax return next year.

Sounds simple... no, IRD staff have stated only particular organisations that we donate to can return New Zealanders a rebate. I tried for several months to obtain all relevant details to give to IRD staff, then gave up as being too difficult.

I am a pensioner, so do not have an expensive taxation adviser to work for me, so I now just donate money, without attempting to receive an IRD refund.

You are right that the 33.33 percent donation tax credit is only available for donations made to approved organisations. The list is quite long, but I have heard from people who have been caught out by the requirement that the charity is doing the bulk of its work in New Zealand.

World.title: Porirua farewells Deputy Mayor Kylie Wihapi after sudden death
World.content:
The mayor of Porirua says the councillors are working together to fill the gaps left by the sudden death of Deputy Mayor Kylie Wihapi.

Wihapi died after a fall at her home last weekend. She was 45 years old.

A funeral service was being held at Te Rauparaha Arena in Porirua on Saturday following her laying in state for two days of evening services and poroporoaki at Horouta Marae this week.

Intent focus on her community

Porirua Mayor Anita Baker said she was first struck by Wihapi's determination when she heard her speak about the impact of the construction of Transmission Gully in 2015.

"She came and spoke to council and it was like 'wow, who was this lady?'.

"She was so entrenched in what was right for her community, the safety for her kids, the noise for other residents and we went 'wow, she'd be a great councillor'," Baker said.

Wihapi would run and be elected to council the following year.

Baker said, even as she rose to deputy mayor, Wihapi's focus remained firmly on her community.

"She was so busy concentrating on everything else, she wasn't worried about herself.

"I'd say 'you have to wear the chains to this event because it's a civic thing that I need you to fill in for me' and it would be 'where'd she put them' because she never liked to wear them.

"She wasn't about the chains, it was about what she could do for people," Baker said.

Porirua Mayor Anita Baker. RNZ/Dom Thomas

Councillor Geoff Hayward was appointed to take over from Wihapi as deputy mayor on Thursday.

Baker said the decision to put Hayward forward came from discussions with Wihapi as she planned in advance for an overseas trip earlier in the year.

She said councillors were working together to fill the gaps left by Wihapi's absence at local events and meetings.

"We're all here for each other and we can say different things in the chambers, but when we leave, we're one family. So we had planned our Christmas do and the pet food drive and we will keep doing those things because Kylie would want us to do them.

"We just have to continue on doing the things that she was really passionate about, which was children, dogs, harbour, everything in her name.

"I'll miss her dearly but, as she said to me 'the play must go on'," Baker said.

Tub thumping passion

Newly announced Deputy Mayor Geoff Hayward said he and Wihapi bonded over their concerns about puppy farming and animal welfare in the area about seven years ago.

He said she was adamant that dogs should not be the ones to suffer when their owners were unable to keep up with their responsibilities.

"I remember her just being so proactive, [her] tub-thumping passion in that council chamber," Hayward said.

HUHA founder Carolyn Press-McKenzie (L) says Kylie Wihapi (R) had an infectious and inspiring personality. Supplied

He said Wihapi would lead by example, drawing people into an issue or a cause simply by her desire to "lend a hand' and motivating others to do likewise.

"She reminds me of my mum because she had this real bullshit detector.

"Her eyes would roll whenever she would hear someone going on about something that she didn't agree with.

"She would be very firm in her view [and] never take a step back, but also gave everybody the chance to have their say," Hayward said.

Hayward said he was struck by Wihapi's charm as she chatted to people while the two councillors wrapped Christmas presents for the Rotary Club at Porirua's North City mall.

"She just had a wonderful way of being able to just throw the world's brightest sun bulb on that person and shower them with aroha, just wanting to hear about their lives.

"That's the kind of person you want to hang around with," Hayward said.

Approachable, vibrant and engaging

Founder and CEO of animal welfare group Helping You Help Animals (HUHA) Carolyn Press-McKenzie, described Wihapi as "a whirlwind of passion".

Press-McKenzie said she first met Wihapi when she and Hayward took an interest in her organisation's efforts to build a shelter just beyond the city about five years ago.

"She's somebody you'd want to be friends with. Just incredibly approachable, vibrant, very, very friendly [and] very engaging.

"She just had that infectious personality where she thought we all needed to do better and, with her, you wanted to do better as well," Press-McKenzie said.

Kylie Wihapi (L), Carolyn Press McKenzie (C) and Geoff Hayward. Supplied

She said Wihapi appeared "unstoppable" and it was hard to come to terms with the loss of someone with so much to give.

"We need good people in the world. We need the people who are going to champion whanau and animals and help everyone get things right.

"The community in New Zealand have lost someone who was truly making a tangible difference," Press-McKenzie said.

A 'formidable force' who could move mountains

Speaker for Horouta Marae Raniera Albert said Wihapi was a consistent presence at the marae and regularly attended events, tangi and celebrations.

Albert competed unsuccessfully against Wihapi last year for the role of Māori ward. Wihapi was campaigning for a second term after becoming Porirua's first Māori Ward councillor in 2022.

But Albert said it was the process of campaigning against each other that brought the two more closely together.

"Kylie went out of her way to make contact with me, given that this was my first local elections campaign, to help guide me, provide me sound advice [and] to be a trusted mentor for me," Albert said.

He said he was struck by her steadfast commitment that, regardless of who won the role, the main priority was to "elevate the Māori voice" in the district.

Albert said behind Wihapi's friendly manner and bright smile lay a "formidable force".

"She could move mountains, she could move streams, she could move anything that she put her mind to.

"Regardless of the event, regardless of the kaupapa, anybody was invited to approach Kylie," he said.

"She made herself available no matter the time, no matter the hour, no matter who you were. Whether you're from the richest families or from the poorest."

Speaker for Horouta Marae Raniera Albert. Supplied

Albert said both of the candidates' families grew close and he fondly recalled her sharp sense of humour.

"She was a very good laugh. She had humour ranging from all levels, from the nicest of humours to the darkest of humours, and that's just what made Kylie unique in all ways."

He said her loss would leave "a massive hole" in the lives of those closest to her as well as the community.

"It's a word that is merely slipped off the lips, but Kylie has earned that right to be called a rangatira.

"Kylie has worked so hard for her community, for her constituency, for her whanau," he said.

Wihapi leaves behind her husband Adam, son Cooper, stepchildren Arama and Josh as well as parents Marlene and Rob and siblings Leon, Ariana and Cole.

"She leaves a massive hole in her whanau. The entire family will be feeling the weight and the burden of what the next chapter in this life would entail.

World.title: How exposed is your KiwiSaver to market wobbles?
World.content:
The effects of falling US technology stocks on your KiwiSaver balance will depend largely on the type of fund you are in.

Stocks dropped sharply on Thursday, US time. Media reports blamed the victory of anti-AI candidates in the US midterms, on top of existing fears about how sustainable technology companies' share prices are.

A small number of technology companies' share market returns have risen recently, such as Nvidia, which has increased in price by more than 500 percent over five years, and Apple, which is up 127 percent over five years.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 6.3 percent on Thursday, cutting more than US$2 trillion in market value.

The S&P500 also had its worst day since the introduction of US President Donald Trump's tariffs last year.

In New Zealand, KiwiSaver investors in growth and high-growth funds generally tend to have the most exposure to share markets. How much exposure they have to technology stocks within that depends on the approach of managers.

Audio player for " What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/personal-finance/2388401%2Fhow-exposed-is-your-kiwisaver-to-market-wobbles

What will cost me more, cooling my house down or heating it up? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Passive funds tend to track indices. As technology stocks have become larger parts of those indices, they will have been added to KiwiSaver funds in larger allocations. Active managers decide what they believe is appropriate. Milford, for example, has limited its exposure to technology stocks through its active growth fund because of its concerns about the risk.

An analysis of the top 10 holdings of high growth KiwiSaver funds, as reported by Sorted's Smart Investor tool, shows variation in how much of investors' money was in tech companies.

Milford's aggressive fund had 26 percent in companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom and Micron. Generate's focused growth fund had 22.5 percent. Quay Street's High Growth had 21.6 percent and Kernel's 20.16 percent.

While Milford has been cautious with its active growth fund, its aggressive fund was 5.4 percent invested in Microsoft, 4.56 percent in Nvidia and 4 percent Amazon.

Pathfinder's High Growth had17.5 percent tech exposure and Simplicity's high growth 19.4 percent.

The best performing of those funds over the past year has been Koura' Strategic High Growth fund, which founder Rupert Carlyon credited to being invested offshore.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson said the latest drop was just part of the unpredictability of the market.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson. Supplied / Kernel

"The market is just being volatile at the moment on the back of trying to digest a lot of uncertainty and everyone is ultimately speculating on what moves a democratic House and Senate may make. So we actually have no visibility or clarity.

"These swings in the market are pure speculation as to what may come down the line. It's a great reminder for investors not to be trying to play that game. Overall, I think this is a real positive. I think actually it's kind of healthy to kind of just reset expectations and to dampen some of the euphoric sort of activity that was going on, not only with enlisted markets, but also what we've seen with, you know, some of the smaller AI-related companies in terms of the neocloud data centres."

He said a fall in share prices could help ensure businesses were operating with a focus on sustainability and quality.

"Thinking about our high growth…we've got a reasonable allocation on high growth, about 10 percent, to global infrastructure and global property. Both of those are actually up 7 percent in the past month. So that's actually a great reminder about why being diversified and not just say buying US only and actually having some of these more boring allocations helps in periods like this."

There has been significant dispersion in returns this year as those that have ridden the technology wave have experienced much better results than those who hung back.

While those with more exposure may experience more losses, they would have to drop significantly to undo the returns banked so far.

"If we still keep an eye on what's coming down the line, a lot of these companies are still demonstrating and delivering strong earnings growth," Anderson said.

"And there's still a lot of potential for AI, right? And so I wouldn't be extrapolating the sort of sell-off as interpreting this as that's the end of AI, or that's the end of chemical growth stocks over the next five years."

World.title: Aussie's heroic Paris Masters run ends at the hands of rising French star
World.content:
Rinky Hijikata has finally been awakened from his dream week at the Paris Masters as a new young French tennis hero ended the Australian's bid to reach his first big-time tennis semi-final.

For the third match running, Hijikata, who came from behind to defeat Novak Djokovic in the second round, battled back from a set down with some scintillating tennis as he quieted the home fans cheering for their new hope, Luca Van Assche.

But it was the 22-year-old Paris-based Van Assche, also playing in his first Masters 1000 quarter-final, who rose to new heights as he came from 2-0 down in the final set to prevail 6-4, 6-7 (4-7), 7-5 after a memorable two-and-three-quarter hour duel.

It meant the end of what felt like a major breakthrough week for the 25-year-old Sydneysider Hijikata, who looked early in that final set as if he was going to win his sixth match in seven days and become the first qualifier to reach the last-four at the Paris Masters in nine years.

Ultimately, he was defeated by a young player who said he felt inspired by the crowd as he struggled physically in the deciding set.

"The crowd were so important for me, supporting me so much in the tough moments, and that's why I played my best tennis," said Belgian-born Van Assche, who becomes the 12th Frenchman to make the semi-finals in Paris and will next tackle American Ben Shelton.

Hijikata's consolation will be to start next week as Australia's number two man behind Alex de Minaur as he enters the world's top-60.

Hijikata certainly continued with that fearless, aggressive streak in the second set tiebreak against Van Assche, maintaining his fine form by then earning an immediate break in the third set.

But Van Assche is one of the most highly regarded young talents in the game, and his defensive prowess helped him turn the tide in the final set with some extraordinary wall-like resilience that kept forcing Hijikata to play one shot too many.

Third seed Shelton, bombing down 19 aces, had earlier prevailed in an all-American match-up to reach the Paris semis for the first time, roaring to a 6-4, 4-6, 6-3 win that ended Tommy Paul's quiet late bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin later in November.

The victory sealed qualification for the end-of-season men's championship for another US star, Frances Tiafoe, alongside world number one Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli and Arthur Fils.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Megan Schutt on ADHD, medication and what's changed since her diagnosis
World.content:
The fire in Megan Schutt's belly has driven her to unbelievable heights.

World Cup titles, Commonwealth Games gold, more than 300 wickets across all formats, and 14 years at the top of the game.

Loading Instagram content

An intimidating swing bowler, the 33-year-old has built a successful career on being an aggressive competitor. She is passionate and motivated by an "I'll show you" energy.

That fiery part of her personality comes in handy when on the cricket field, but less so off it.

Since receiving an ADHD diagnosis last year, Schutt has unlocked new insights about herself. The unique ways her brain works and rational explanations for her reactions.

"Cricket has been a great regulator for me," Schutt told ABC Sport.

"I've always been able to control myself on the field and then I'd come off and blow my fuse at spilling a cup of coke or something, so that was a real sign.

"Everything kind of clicked and made sense.

"I was quick to anger as a kid and never understood why that happened when I had a great childhood, happy parents.

"To be able to get my emotions in check has been a big change."

Beyond the rage, Schutt is learning to go easier on herself.

Megan has a daughter Rylee that she shares with ex-wife, Jess. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

"I set really high standards in a lot of areas and am realising they probably aren't achievable," she said.

"I'm getting older and the body wakes up sorer, so I've got to rest more.

"I find that hard, I feel guilty for it, I feel lazy.

"It's made me realise I need to not be so quick to judge myself or feel ashamed."

Seeing real change

Since she started taking ADHD medication, Schutt's Aussie teammates reckon she's more friendly.

"Darcie Brown and Georgia Wareham tell me that I'm a much nicer person when I'm on meds," she said.

Teammates have seen a change in Schutt's mood since she started taking medication. (Getty: Chris Hyde)

"They do make it easier to bat — I no longer have 1,400 shot selections in my head, of which I can only play three anyways — but other than that, I don't think my cricket has changed."

As an elite athlete regularly tested by anti-doping organisations, Schutt requires permission to take her medication with a therapeutic use exemption (TUE) from her doctor and psychologist.

It's a strict process that must be reviewed every 12 months or when her dose changes.

Having that clearance is vital, yet it doesn't bring Schutt complete peace of mind.

Two weeks ago, she was handed a two-match ban for failing to adhere to requirements around the use of prescription medication.

Megan Schutt says ADHD medication helps her with selecting a shot. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

This meant she missed the third T20 International against New Zealand and the opening match of the Women's Big Bash for the Adelaide Strikers.

Schutt returned to play on Thursday at Drummoyne Oval against the Brisbane Heat.

This interview was conducted in September, before the error, and there has been no indication whether the suspension is linked to Schutt's ADHD medication.

In a statement, a Cricket Australia spokesperson said:

"The circumstances of the breach are confidential, but Megan has expressed remorse and is aware of her obligations in this area."

Megan Schutt is back playing after a two-match suspension over prescription medication guidelines. (Getty Images/Cricket Australia: Jason McCawley)

"You do stress," Schutt said.

"I've been drug-tested a few times and I'm like, what if the TUE is inactive or we got our dosing wrong.

"I think you're targeted more being on amphetamines," she said.

Schutt believes the fear of accidentally testing positive for a prohibited substance could put others in her position off medicating.

"Some of the younger players won't take cold and flu," she said.

"You can't even have a protein shake from a cafe in case something is added to the powder.

"If someone cooks you something in their house and it's not approved, you could be done for.

"You've got to think twice, or it could be the end of your career."

As much as Schutt understands the importance of the process, she also gets frustrated about the extra hoops she has to jump through to take essential medicine to function.

Megan Schutt says she does stress about taking medication sometimes. (Getty: Matthew Lewis)

"At the end of the day, you are told a thousand times you are responsible for what you put in your body, but accidents happen," she said.

"What I struggle with is, if you have ADHD, it is obviously no longer a stimulant. I get a little bit angry about needing a TUE in the first place."

Navigating co-parenting and travel

Schutt has a five-year-old daughter, Rylee, with ex-wife Jess.

The pair separated last year and have been adjusting to co-parenting while navigating Rylee's autism and ADHD.

As her daughter started treatment, Schutt recognised her own triggers, which in turn led to her diagnosis.

It's been a tricky balance managing Rylee's appointments while playing professionally.

As a member of the national team, there is a lot of travel involved, and Cricket Australia's parental policies allow children and a carer to come along.

Loading Instagram content

Unfortunately, that hasn't been a viable option for Rylee.

"We had a lot of therapies back in the day — physio, OT, speech, dietitian — and there was no way I was going to pull her out of those routines just to have her on tour," Schutt said.

"It would have been too unsettling.

"It was easier for me to miss them, which was a hard one to wrap my head around because it's not what you picture when you have a child.

"Up until a year ago she preferred being held by myself or Jess anyway, so it really just made it impossible to bring her."

The marriage separation has also presented challenges to travel as Rylee has gotten older and potentially more ready, with it harder to bring along a designated carer.

There are also health and safety regulations that have got in the way.

"The system is not really set up for a single parent to take their kid, so it has been quite frustrating," Schutt said.

"I think the sport could maybe be a little more relaxed and aware of individual situations rather than having blanket rules for everyone."

Going out on a high

This has contributed to Schutt's decision to retire from ICC tournaments, going out on a high at the T20 World Cup as part of the wider squad that won the July final at Lord's.

The Australian team lifts the ICC Women's T20 World Cup trophy at Lord's in July. (Getty: Alex Davidson)

Schutt is still making an impact in the ODI format and was named Player of the Series against Bangladesh last month for taking 10 wickets overall and best figures of 4/16.

However, she's been in and out of the T20I team and hasn't played a Test since 2019.

"I've missed so much of Rylee's life and she's at an age where she can communicate that sadness and it hurts.

"At the back end of the World Cup she said, 'You're never coming back.'

"Every single session of FaceTime would be her asking, 'Are you on the plane yet?'

"It got to a point where me being away was doing more harm than good."

"The guilt is too much and spending more time on the bench makes me question why I'm away.

"Coming home to Adelaide brings a tear to my eye now. It's a realisation of where I want to be."

World.title: Connecting community through sport celebrated at Indigenous Sports Awards
World.content:
When Noongar and Martujarra man Nat Heath was young he was diagnosed with Guillian-Barre Syndrome, an autoimmune disease that attacks the nervous system and causes paralysis.

The diagnosis didn't set him back, but became one of his biggest motivators.

"Getting into triathlon, I just wanted to test my endurance, because the doctor said I would never have the same endurance after having the illness," he said.

After seeing what he achieved from his first triathlon, Heath went on to compete in six ironman events and won a championship in his age division.

"Which was amazing for myself, but there was just no other Black fellas doing the sport," he said.

"So I wanted to create a avenue where more mob could feel like they could participate in the sport of triathlon."

It inspired him to establish TriMob in 2020, an organisation that encourages mob to be physically active, through triathlons or marathons.

TriMob is a First Nations-led organisation encouraging Indigenous people to participate in triathlon. (Supplied: TriMob)

"Connecting community is a big piece of what we do, making sure our programs are culturally safe," Heath said.

"People feel a lot safer to come into our program just try it."

The organisation runs a "Mob the Marathon" program, to train participants from all over Australia to compete in the Sydney Marathon, now a World Major.

Talisha Godwin joined the program at the start of the year as a beginner, having little experience in training for or running a marathon.

"As a woman, as a mum, I just didn't think I couldn't do it," she said.

"I felt supported, I'd pushed so hard for myself to get there. I'd had days where I just couldn't do it, I was too tired, there was too much to do.

"But then one of the things one of the guys said in the group was, 'how can you show up one per cent today?'

"And that's a mantra I just said over and over and over again."

TriMob is a nominee for Team of the Year at the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Sports Awards. (Supplied: TriMob)

Godwin was amazed the community she was able to find in the program

"Showing up at the start line and finding the rest of the mob there in your group and starting together as a group and knowing it doesn't matter where we are on the race, on the track, we're all crossing the line together and supporting each other," she said.

Recognising First Nations excellence

TriMob is one of the nominees for Team of the Year at the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Sports Awards (NATSISAs).

The awards were established by late Aboriginal activist and former international soccer player Charles Perkins in 1986, to use sport as an example of bringing people from all backgrounds together.

It is now organised by former AFL player Nathan Lovett-Murray.

Nathan Lovett-Murray had a long AFL career with Essendon. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

"I recently just found out that my great grandfather, Pastor Sir Doug Nichols, used to host the event," he said.

"Now I'm hosting the event. So it's a bit of family history there and it's something that I'm really proud to be a part of."

As it grew in the 1990s, it showcased the best athletes from a range of sports, and at times became one of the only ways for the sporting contributions of mob to be recognised.

"Played with the Bombers for 10 years in the AFL and I wasn't able to attend the Sports Awards, but I did attend the Deadly Awards that used to be on," Lovett-Murray said.

"I actually won an award for football, so I remember going to those awards and loved seeing all the speeches of all the winners."

The NATSISAs serve as way for First Nations athletes to come together and find community with other mob from different sports.

Nathan Lovett-Murray was instrumental in reviving the NATSISAs after their 20-year hiatus. (ABC News)

This year's event will be held on Gadigal land at the Sydney Cricket Ground tonight, the first time the city has hosted the ceremony since 2001.

Before that it was on 20-year hiatus until 2023 and was brought back to be held in Brisbane and Melbourne.

Lovett-Murray hopes that in future more organisations and sponsors can get on board and support the growth of Indigenous athletes.

"Because when you support the Sports Awards, you're supporting First Nations sports all around the country," he said.

Cathy Freeman will be this year's keynote speaker, and categories include Lifetime Achievement award, Sportsperson of the Year, and National Trailblazer award.

World.title: Fine line between boxing and barbarism breached in 'frightening' KO
World.content:
The reaction from those watching the replays of Nelson Asofa-Solomona's sickening knockout of Paul Gallen speaks volumes.

Former Cronulla Sharks teammate of Gallen, Michael Ennis, looked desperately shaken as he admitted he found it hard to watch.

Tim Tszyu called it "frightening".

In real time, it was even worse.

"Oh jeez, oh no!" cried experienced caller Ben Damon on Main Event's commentary as the footage showed Asofa-Solomona's fist detonating onto Gallen's expressionless features.

"The last one was the worst one boys," Danny Green cried.

"That was the one he didn't need," he added, as Damon said, "that's no good," over the top of him.

"The last one was a bad one," Green reiterated.

"That's hard to watch," a shaken Damon summarised.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona crushed Paul Gallen inside the opening round. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The fight only lasted two minutes and 56 seconds.

In that time, Asofa-Solomona both proved he was capable of taking another step in his quest to climb boxing's Penrose stairs, and similarly unsuitable to do so.

After a steady start, a thunderous right hand from Asofa-Solomona staggered the 45-year-old Gallen back towards the ropes.

Then another left-right combination put him right back against them.

Asofa-Solomona saw Gallen's head roll back, his arms flailing and glimpsed the opening for an upper cut.

He promptly delivered, landing a blow with such hideous force that Gallen was sent to the brink of unconsciousness.

A second upper cut unquestionably delivered him into that foul abyss.

Paul Gallen was left stricken on the canvas. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But Asofa-Solomona wasn't done.

An unnecessary third grazed Gallen's granite chin as he sank to a seated position, his legs folded under him like a grotesquely discarded marionette.

Still, Asofa-Solomona wasn't done.

As referee Chris Condon threw himself between the fighters, a black-shirted angel of deliverance from the punishment Gallen had already endured for too long, Asofa-Solomona aimed another, sickening blow into the head of his stricken rival.

Few will understand this sanctimonious sermonising about such a despicable blow taking place amidst the wanton violence of a boxing bout.

This was boxing, wasn't it?

Hadn't Paulo Aokuso landed such a sweetly-timed left hand onto the head of Mobin Khahrazeh earlier in the night that it had observers positively purring?

Paulo Aokuso delivered a lauded statement KO in his bout. (No Limit)

Isn't it the point to knock your opponent out, to inflict such damage to a fellow human's brain that they lose consciousness in the pursuit of entertainment?

Yes, oddly enough, it is.

But even within the sanctioned barbarism of modern blood sports, there are rules in place to limit the hurt inflicted on a helpless opponent without being accused of hypocrisy.

It's there in almost every rule book you can care to find.

For example, the Australian National Boxing Federation:

55. Some fouls for which a referee may penalise or disqualify a boxer are: (a) Hitting an opponent who is down or is rising from a knockdown.

There can be caveats.

It took eight seconds from the first of those crushing Asofa-Solomona punches to land before referee Condon stopped the fight, but the four punishing upper cuts all came in the space of two-and-a-half horrific seconds.

It's barely enough time for anyone to react, not least a man who is on the charge and fighting for his future as a novice boxer.

But Gallen was clearly down.

Not only that, he was clearly out.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona delivered a devastating quartet of upper cuts. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hundreds of boxers around the world have learned when enough is enough and to stop.

Hitting an unconscious opponent is beyond the pale, an unacceptable sin that breaches the unique brotherhood two fighters join when touching gloves with one another in the squared circle.

But Asofa-Solomona was clearly fired up.

His ill-advised leap into the crowd moments later proved that.

There is a caveat there, too.

Asofa-Solomona added context to his mad dash towards a punter in his post-fight press conference, telling reporters at the TikTok Entertainment Centre that he had been subject to a racist taunt.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona was heckled by someone in the crowd and lowered himself to challenge them directly. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Someone was doing an ape gesture. I stood on the ropes and it looked like someone threw something at me," he was reported as saying.

"If I had my time back, I would, because that's not on. But what that guy did to me, in terms of that gesture, is not on either.

"I'd just seen red."

Nobody should ever be subject to such foul, vindictive and uneducated slop and nobody should ever deign to suggest how someone should react if they are.

But his calamitous dash into the not-so-cheap seats added to the chaotic conclusion of the fight, meaning his indiscretion at its sickening conclusion was largely overlooked.

Asofa-Solomona proved to most onlookers that he has some skill in a ring on Friday night.

But the next time he delivers a knockout blow, he'd do well to stop before he risks inflicting any further damage.

World.title: Khawaja claims Aussies used sandpaper on the ball before notorious Test
World.content:
All players and staff knew about the ball tampering during the infamous 2018 Cape Town Test, Usman Khawaja has told Nine newspapers ahead of the release of his book.

In an explosive claim in his new book Sabr, Khawaja says sandpaper was also used in the previous Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.

"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

"I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."

The claim is at odds with Cricket Australia's assertion that only Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner knew about the tactic. Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon also denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it.

Bancroft was banned for nine months after being caught using sandpaper on the ball during the third Test of the series in South Africa, while captain Smith and vice-captain Warner copped 12-month bans for their parts in the scheme.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith front the media after Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to tamper with the ball. (Gallo Images via Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

In the book, Khawaja claims that lighthearted discussions about the use of sandpaper at St George's Park in Gqeberha during the second Test led to Smith walking out of the rooms and saying that he didn't want to know about it.

He claims Bancroft then volunteered to use sandpaper in the first innings of that Test, where the ball swung significantly. He also said he sat next to Bancroft at Newlands in Cape Town during the third Test and saw who spoke to the young batter during the match that would see the Australian team caught out.

A Cricket Australia spokesperson said they remained comfortable with the initial findings of their investigation.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Khawaja said he was never interviewed by Cricket Australia about the incident. He also said the South Africa team were "far better" at working on the ball and that the Australians were "trying to keep up with them". Then South African captain Faf du Plessis had twice been sanctioned for ball tampering.

Khawaja has been promoting his book across various media outlets over the past weeks. However, the claims made in the ball-tampering chapters had been redacted until today. He said he had dedicated the chapter to Bancroft, Warner and Smith because he had seen how the saga had weighed on all three players.

Khawaja told ABC Radio National's Conversations program that revisiting the 2018 series for the book was particularly difficult.

Loading...

"Everyone in that team, one way or another, was affected and we still are affected by that to this day," he said.

"For me, writing that chapter was more about what I thought was the right thing to do. … I still struggle to talk about it in a lot of respects. There's no easy way to talk about what happened over there. There's no easy way to write about that period of Cricket Australia and that period of my life.

"It's just about telling my story. and what my feelings were particularly at that time and what I saw."

Khawaja said it was a culmination of seven years of playing with a "win at all costs" mentality that made the rest of the cricket world hate them.

He said that started after the 2011 Argus Review, which came in the wake of the team's first home Ashes series loss in 24 years, during which Khawaja made his Test debut as England won by an innings and 83 runs to complete a dominant 3-1 series victory.

"The way we were playing, we were disrespecting other players and I talked to other players in other teams I was friends with and they were just like 'yeah, we hate your boys'," he said.

Usman Khawaja reveals illness he kept secret his entire Test cricket career Cricket great Usman Khawaja could barely walk and thought he had a terminal illness when he was just starting out his Test career. He was soon diagnosed with a crippling disease, which he has kept secret for 17 years.

"This all manifested during that time with sandpaper, and no-one had our backs after that either because why would they? We just acted like idiots for the last seven years."

Khawaja's childhood coach and mentor, Bill Anderson, told Australian Story last month: "Usman actually tried to coerce them all to say 'we all knew what was going on' and some of them wouldn't buy into that. Ussie's view being, 'they're not going to sack us all'."

The 39-year-old told Conversations that if he could have his time over again, he would have stood his ground more resolutely.

The silver lining of the whole affair, Khawaja said, was that it forced the Australian men's team to have a long, hard look at its playing style.

"The best things come out of the worst times. I genuinely believe, for the Australian cricket team, the best thing that came out of Sandpaper is we found humility again," he said.

"JL [Justin Langer] came in as coach and he was honestly probably the best coach we could've had at that time. He put humility back in the Australian cricket team.

"It was just lovely to see. It was beautiful. I really enjoyed it. I really enjoyed seeing where the Australian team went from that point onwards and obviously Pat Cummins, who ended up becoming the captain, was a part of that process and journey."

World.title: Asofa-Solomona leaps into crowd, apologises after 'frightening' Gallen KO
World.content:
A furious Nelson Asofa-Solomona has leaped into the crowd in sensational scenes following his knockout victory over fellow former NRL star Paul Gallen in Sydney.

Gallen, returning to the ring for the final time, was knocked out with 10 seconds remaining in the first round of their five-round heavyweight bout at the TikTok Entertainment Centre.

The 45-year-old was hit with a thunderous right that sent him back against the ropes, before four devastating upper cuts, the last of which was landed despite Gallen already being down.

As Gallen lay stricken on the ropes in considerable distress, Asofa-Solomona leaped onto the corner ropes to celebrate his win.

Then, incredibly, the 200cm, 137.5kg giant leaped over the ropes and ran to someone in the crowd.

Footage appeared to show the former Storm forward swing a wild punch towards a spectator, who was later led out the building by police.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona was heckled by someone in the crowd and lowered himself to challenge them directly. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"I just want to apologise for what I did, I acted like a bloody idiot," Nelson Asofa-Solomona said in the ring.

"I just got in a bit of the heat of the moment.

"I should not behave like that, I'm sorry."

Gallen, meanwhile, who surrendered a 20cm height advantage and more than 33kg in weight, was able to sit up.

He was later shown laughing with his shaken son in the dressing room, seemingly recovered.

Former world champion Tim Tszyu said the knockout was "frightening", while Gallen's former Sharks teammate Michael Ennis was in a state of shock at the sheer violence meted out on his friend.

Paul Gallen was left stricken in terrifying scenes. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"That was really hard," Ennis said.

"It was really hard to watch."

George Rose, promoter of No Limit Boxing, did not criticise Asofa-Solomona, but was adamant that attending his shows was safe.

"One thing that we love with our shows is that we like to make it a safe and enjoyable and entertaining experience for everyone," Rose said on Main Event.

"We want to make sure that it's something that people can be a part of and feel safe to come and enjoy."

Asked later, Asofa-Solomona said: "Someone was doing an ape gesture. I stood on the ropes and it looked like someone threw something at me.

"If I had my time back, I would, because that's not on. But what that guy did to me, in terms of that gesture, is not on either.

"I'd just seen red."

Earlier in the night, Paris Olympian and Commonwealth Games medallist Callum Peters, despite being slightly off colour, maintained his unbeaten record with a unanimous points win against rugged Colombian Juan Diego Ortiz.

Meanwhile Paulo Aokuso delivered a statement knockout to beat Mobin Khahrazeh in the second round of their IBF Inter-Continental light heavyweight title fight.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Ex-CFMEU boss admits to illegal tirade against AFL umpiring boss
World.content:
Former construction union boss John Setka is unapologetic for breaking workplace laws, with his barrister saying he did not "deliberately" wage a public campaign against an ex-building regulator and AFL umpiring chief.

Mr Setka, the former powerful Victorian secretary of the CFMEU, faces a fine of up to $18,730, but could be hit with a much heftier legal bill because the union has refused to indemnify his court costs.

The Federal Court on Friday heard Mr Setka admitted breaching the Fair Work Act by trying to coerce the AFL into sacking its head of umpiring Stephen McBurney in mid-2024.

Mr McBurney was the Australian Building and Construction Commissioner and participated in more than 50 court cases against the union between 2018 and 2023.

Mr Setka's barrister Margo Harris said her client should not receive a severe penalty.

She said he was now retired, in the middle of a divorce, and spent most of his time looking after his elderly mother.

"He doesn't express any remorse but he has made an admission that what he did was wrong," Ms Harris said.

Mr Setka was not in court for Friday's hearing.

Former union boss admits to breaching law

The development comes three days before the start of hearings in Victoria's Royal Commission into the state government's "Big Build" construction projects, which have been dogged by claims of widespread corruption and crime.

Mr Setka, who left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Mr McBurney, is also facing separate criminal charges over alleged harassment of the union's administrators.

In the Fair Work case, Mr Setka was still union boss when he made social media posts and gave media interviews over a two-week period, threatening that the CFMEU would disrupt or delay AFL building projects if it did not get rid of Mr McBurney, the court heard.

"This is going to cost the AFL a lot of f**king money. I hope it's worth it," Mr Setka said.

"Projects without our full co-operation are going to be a f**king misery for them. They will regret the day they ever employed him."

John Setka left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Stephen McBurney. (ABC News)

The Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) prosecuted Mr Setka and the CFMEU, alleging the demands to sack Mr McBurney were made because of his lawful work as ABCC commissioner.

On Friday, barristers for Mr Setka and the CFMEU admitted to the breaches.

Ms Harris said there was no evidence Mr Setka "actively sought" media attention, even though he made statements to newspapers, and appeared in radio and television interviews where he said the AFL should sack Mr McBurney.

Ms Harris also said Mr Setka did not "deliberately" engage in a media campaign against Mr McBurney, prompting Federal Court judge John Snaden to clarify what she meant.

"When I say deliberate, there's a range of deliberateness. It's not a question of being pregnant or not pregnant," she replied.

"It comes in the stream of the interview. There's a question asked of him, he answers it."

However, FWO barrister Marc Felman said Mr Setka was not forced to give interviews.

"There can be no question that this is a media campaign," he said.

During one press conference, Mr Setka said of Mr McBurney: "He's a zealot. He hates unions. He hates workers in general."

He also put up a social media post depicting Mr McBurney in a mock poster containing the words: "(Not) Wanted Dead or Alive".

Penalty to be set for Setka and CFMEU despite claims of new regime

Mr Felman said Mr Setka's breaches of the Fair Work Act were "very, very serious".

He said Mr Setka wasn't the first person to call for the sacking of an AFL umpire, but it became illegal because the demands were connected to Mr McBurney's lawful work in an old job.

Mr McBurney, who has umpired four grand finals, was backed by the AFL at the time and remains the league's head of officiating.

Stephen McBurney adjudicated 401 AFL games and is still employed as the league's head of officiating. (AFLUA Hall of Fame)

The CFMEU, which has since been taken over by administrators, could be fined up to $93,900.

Barrister Andrew White, for the CFMEU, called for the penalty to be moderated because the union's new regime no longer saw breaking the law as "the cost of doing business".

He said the cultural shift had occurred following hundreds of Setka-era officials being removed or leaving their jobs.

"A new culture of lawful but robust unionism is taking hold," he said.

Justice Snaden will set the penalty for Mr Setka and the CFMEU at a later date.

World.title: Baseballer loses sight in one eye in 'horrific freak accident'
World.content:
Adelaide's baseball community is rallying around a "tough cookie" player who lost sight in one eye after a "horrific freak accident" during a weekend game.

Veteran member of the Adelaide Angels Baseball Club, Tyler Forney, was struck in the eye by a foul ball off his own bat, during a double-header against Woodville on Saturday.

Close friend and long-time teammate Chris Congdon said Mr Forney was in the batter's box during the second game when the incident happened.

"His ball ricocheted off his bat and basically collected his right eye," Mr Congdon said.

"[It] resulted in him getting taken off to hospital by ambulance in a bad way and having significant eye surgery that evening.

"However, he's permanently lost vision in his right eye as a result of that.

"Anyone I've spoken to around the club that was there was just really mortified by the accident … it's a really horrific freak accident."

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was an integral member of the club since joining back in 2016, after moving from Arizona in the United States.

He said Mr Forney had a gifted athletic ability which he had honed while playing college baseball.

"He's a really really tough cookie, Ty — I'm sure he played through a broken hand for parts of last season," Mr Congdon said.

"He was a walking highlight reel, he would make plays at shortstop that just no one else could make.

"He just stuck with us and [he's] a massive reason why the last five years we've had huge success."

'So grateful' for support

A GoFundMe page has since raised more than $16,200 by Friday afternoon to cover Mr Forney's medical fees.

"He [Mr Forney] did not realise how much of an impact that he has had on people — not only in our club, but the wider baseball community," Mr Congdon said.

" He's a very humble person, but this has really, really taken him taken by surprise and he's just so grateful. "

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was being supported by his partner, two children and three stepchildren as he recovers.

He said while Mr Forney's playing career may have come to an end, the club is already talking about ways to transition him to a coaching role.

"He's the sort of person that is quite private and reserved, but when he speaks and he does, everybody listens, so I think he wouldn't have thought about coaching," he said.

"He had so much left to do as a player and still so valuable as a player."

Tech.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

Tech.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.

Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.

The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

Tech.title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
Tech.content:
SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.

As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm, which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile, potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network.

SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.

Tech.title: All the latest updates on AI data centers
Tech.content:
Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment.

Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with.
